A R228 million police health contract had gone to the company of businessman Vusimuzi 'Cat' Matlala, who now faces corruption charges, and by July 2026 13 police officers faced criminal charges, among them National Commissioner Fannie Masemola. These are charges, not convictions; Mchunu denies wrongdoing. Before that, national police chief Jackie Selebi, also president of Interpol, was convicted in 2010 over payments from a drug trafficker, and in 2016 police colonel Christiaan Prinsloo was jailed for selling about two thousand police guns to Cape Flats gangs. On building sites, 'business forums', the so-called construction mafia, demand a cut, often 30%, of projects, and try to capture ward councillors by bribery or threats, the Institute for Security Studies reports.

The second strand is 'state capture' under President Jacob Zuma. The Zondo Commission found in 2022 that ministers and heads of state companies acted corruptly for the Gupta family, businessmen close to Zuma. Deputy finance minister Mcebisi Jonas said the Guptas offered him the finance ministry, which decides who gets the state's money, shortly before minister Nhlanhla Nene was sacked in 2015; the Guptas deny it, and the US sanctioned them in 2019. Foreign firms were part of it. Zondo found the US consultancy Bain helped take over the tax service, SARS (Bain denies doing so wilfully). McKinsey, SAP and ABB admitted bribing officials at Eskom, the state power company, and other bodies, and paid US settlements. Thales, the French arms firm, and Zuma still await trial over the 1999 arms deal; both deny the charges.

The older background: from 1948 to 1994 every prime minister and state president belonged to the Afrikaner Broederbond, a secret Afrikaner men's society, and a 1979 report said all but two cabinet ministers were members. Earlier, Alfred Milner's young Oxford staff ran the conquered Boer colonies after 1902; historian Carroll Quigley's claim that they belonged to Cecil Rhodes's secret society is his own. South Africa belongs to the patterns on organised crime inside the state, consultants inside ministries, global firms buying governments and sworn brotherhoods.
South Africa.imp: The offices reached most often are the ones people deal with every day: the police, the tax service, the power company and the rail and port company. Bribes for consulting and engineering contracts end up in electricity prices and in services that fail. Much of this was proven by inquiries and by companies' own admissions, but few people have been convicted in South African courts. Things to watch now: the Madlanga Commission and the charges against senior police, the Thales and Zuma trial, and whether extortion at building sites and in local councils is prosecuted.

South Sudan.d:
In South Sudan the record shows outside forces right around the president. In March 2025, as President Salva Kiir's government detained ministers allied with First Vice President Riek Machar, neighbouring Uganda sent special forces into the capital, Juba. Uganda's army chief, Muhoozi Kainerugaba, said the army 'recognises only Salva Kiir' and that any move against him was 'a declaration of war against Uganda'. Uganda's parliament later endorsed the deployment; South Sudan at first denied Ugandan troops were there.

The second case concerns Benjamin Bol Mel, a businessman close to Kiir. The US sanctioned him in December 2017 under its Global Magnitsky anti-corruption rules. In February 2025 he was made one of the country's vice presidents and deputy head of the ruling party, the SPLM, and in November 2025 a decree removed him from both posts. South Sudan appears under the patterns on governments reaching into other countries and on exposure and reversal. Its conditions score is very high, meaning the state is easy to reach and has few checks, so the two documented cases are likely to be only part of the picture.
South Sudan.imp: For people in South Sudan, the question of who protects the president, and who sits beside him, has been answered partly from outside the country. A foreign army has said openly it stands behind one man, and a businessman under US corruption sanctions reached the vice presidency before being removed. With weak courts and oversight, decisions about security are made by a small circle. Watch who is appointed to senior posts and whether Ugandan troops stay.

Sudan.d:
Sudan is at war, and the outside forces on this map are inside that war now. The Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a paramilitary that grew out of militias of the former ruler Omar al-Bashir, have fought the army since April 2023. A UN Panel of Experts report, leaked in January 2024, found 'credible' evidence that the United Arab Emirates sent weapons to the RSF through Chad; the UAE denies it. The International Court of Justice dismissed Sudan's case against the UAE in May 2025 for lack of jurisdiction, without ruling on the facts. On the army's side, in September 2025 the US sanctioned Finance Minister Gebreil Ibrahim and the al-Baraa bin Malik Brigade, an Islamist militia that has supplied up to 20,000 fighters, saying the brigade got training and weapons from Iran's Revolutionary Guards. Meanwhile Captagon, a drug pill, is reported to be made in Khartoum and Blue Nile; the RSF and Darfur rebels are implicated, though no court has ruled.

The roots go back to 1989, when Bashir seized power in a coup organised with Hassan al-Turabi's National Islamic Front, a movement that came out of the Muslim Brotherhood. Bashir admitted his role at his 2020 trial. After his fall, a committee removed judges and prosecutors placed under his rule; a court overturned some dismissals in 2021. Ali Karti, head of the Islamic Movement, was sanctioned by the US, Canada and the EU in 2023–24 for blocking the move to civilian rule. Russia's Wagner group arrived in 2017, and in 2020 the US sanctioned a Prigozhin-linked gold firm for trying to help crush the 2018–19 protests. In 2017 Sudan handed Gülen-movement schools to Turkey's state Maarif Foundation. Sudan sits in the patterns on movements that sought the state itself, foreign governments, and Russia's networks in Africa.
Sudan.imp: For Sudanese people, outside backers keep the war supplied: weapons reach the RSF from abroad, and an Islamist militia fighting for the army is tied to Iran by US findings. The Islamist network that ran the state for 30 years still has figures in senior posts, including the finance ministry. Gold and drug money give armed groups income no budget controls. Watch for new UN findings on arms routes and for who holds the finance and security posts.

Tanzania.d:
Tanzania hosts one of the more unusual cases on this map, and it is running now. In Kibaha, near Dar es Salaam, the Mwalimu Julius Nyerere Leadership School took its first class in February 2022. It was built with a $40 million grant from the Central Party School of the Chinese Communist Party, and CCP theoreticians teach there. It is run jointly by the CCP and six ruling parties of the region: Tanzania's CCM, South Africa's ANC, Angola's MPLA, Mozambique's FRELIMO, Namibia's SWAPO and Zimbabwe's ZANU-PF. A party school matters because it trains the people who will run government. This is acknowledged openly; it is a training relationship, not a finding of wrongdoing.

The second case is from 2017, when the president read out in public a list of alleged drug traffickers, including a regional commissioner and other public figures, and ordered arrests. Few prosecutions were completed and most people held were released, so the record treats this as a head of state's claim, not as proof. Opus Dei and the Gülen movement are also recorded as present. Tanzania falls under the pattern on organised crime inside the state, as suspected only, and is the home of the Nyerere school.
Tanzania.imp: For Tanzanians, the ruling party's future officials are being trained in a school paid for and partly taught by a foreign ruling party. That shapes how government is run without any vote on it. The 2017 drug list showed that accusations against officials can be made in public and then fade without court findings, which leaves people unable to tell who was guilty. Watch who passes through the Kibaha school into government posts.

Togo.d: Togo's one documented case is unfolding now and concerns Russia. Africa Corps is the force run by Russia's defence ministry that replaced the Wagner group in Africa. In November 2025 President Faure Gnassingbé and Vladimir Putin signed a defence agreement covering intelligence sharing, arms sales, joint exercises and Russian ships docking at Lomé, Togo's port. The Critical Threats project of the American Enterprise Institute reports that Africa Corps officers arrived in January 2026, that about 300–350 soldiers were in Lomé and northern bases by mid-2026, and that on 9 July 2026 the sanctioned ship Mikhail Britnev unloaded vehicles at Lomé for Africa Corps in Mali. These figures are reported by that project, not confirmed by the Togolese government. Three opposition parties have asked for a public debate on foreign troops. The spyware firm NSO Group and the influence firm Archimedes Group are also recorded as present, and French Masonic lodges are likely but undocumented. Togo belongs to the pattern on Russia's networks in Europe and Africa, as a target country.
Togo.imp: For people in Togo, a foreign army is settling into the country's port and bases under an agreement that parliament and the public have not debated. Intelligence sharing means a foreign government may see what Togo's own security services collect. The port also serves as a supply route for Russian forces in Mali, which can draw Togo into conflicts elsewhere. Watch for the opposition's demand for a debate and for the size of the deployment.

Tunisia.d:
In Tunisia today, the leaders of the party that once ran the government are in prison. Ennahda is a party that grew out of the Muslim Brotherhood tradition, though it says it has no organisational link to the Egyptian Brotherhood. Its leader, Rached Ghannouchi, who was speaker of parliament from 2019 to 2021, has been jailed since April 2023. On 5 February 2025 a court gave him a further 22 years for 'plotting against state security' in the so-called Instalingo case; ex-foreign minister Rafik Abdessalem, his son-in-law, got 34 years, and ex-prime minister Hichem Mechichi 35 years in absentia. In July 2025 Ghannouchi received another 14-year sentence. Ennahda calls the case political.

The background is the 2011 revolution. Ennahda won the October 2011 election for the assembly writing a new constitution and led the government: Hamadi Jebali was prime minister from December 2011 to March 2013, and Ali Laarayedh until January 2014. The record lists this as a movement winning power through elections, which is lawful; and the map rates this case only as 'possible'. Tunisia sits in the pattern on movements that sought the state itself. The Trilateral Commission, Hizb ut-Tahrir and the Archimedes Group are also recorded as present.
Tunisia.imp: For Tunisians, the record shows a party that took office by election and whose leaders were later given long sentences by courts under the current government. Readers should keep the two apart: winning an election is not infiltration, and the convictions are disputed by the party as political. What ordinary people cannot easily see is what evidence the Instalingo case rested on. Watch for appeals and for whether other parties' leaders face similar charges.

Uganda.d:
In Uganda, the documented cases are about foreign religious networks inside lawmaking, and a foreign telecoms firm inside the police. The Fellowship, also called The Family, is a US Christian network that runs prayer breakfasts for politicians. David Bahati chairs Uganda's National Prayer Breakfast Fellowship and has been a state minister since 2021, re-appointed in 2026. Journalist Jeff Sharlet reported that Bahati first floated his 2009 Anti-Homosexuality Bill, which proposed the death penalty, at the 2008 prayer breakfast, and a Fellowship member confirmed Bahati's link to NPR.

In 2023 Uganda's parliament passed the Anti-Homosexuality Act, with life imprisonment and in some cases death. A Ugandan activist named Sharon Slater, president of the Arizona-based lobbying group Family Watch International, as having lobbied for it; the group earlier called its position on the 2009 bill 'complicated'. The World Bank halted new lending to Uganda in August 2023 over the law. These links are reported, not found by a court.

In 2019 the Wall Street Journal reported that Huawei technicians working in Uganda's police headquarters helped its cyber unit get into the encrypted messages of opposition MP Bobi Wine. The Journal found no evidence that Huawei in China or the Chinese state directed it, and Huawei denied the report. Uganda belongs to the patterns on churches placing members in the state and China's long arm abroad.
Uganda.imp: For Ugandans, a law that can send people to prison for life was shaped partly in meetings with foreign religious groups that voters never chose. Opposition politicians' private messages may be reachable by police using foreign technical help, which matters to anyone who organises or votes against the government. None of these links has been tested in court. Watch who leads the prayer breakfast and who supplies the police's surveillance tools.

Zambia.d:
Zambia's one documented case is about religion and the state, and it is over but its effects remain. Zambia's 1996 constitution declares the country a Christian nation. In September 2016 President Edgar Lungu turned a religious-affairs desk into a full Ministry of National Guidance and Religious Affairs and gave it to Rev. Godfridah Sumaili, a cleric he appointed to parliament as a nominated MP. She held the post until August 2021. After the 2021 election President Hakainde Hichilema folded the ministry into a department of the Vice-President's office. This was done openly, by the government itself; it is a church network given a seat in cabinet, not a hidden one.

Other groups are recorded as present without a documented case: Huawei, SCL Group / Cambridge Analytica, Pentecostal networks and the Universal Church of the Kingdom of God, a Brazilian church. English Freemasonry, the old bank BCCI and British American Tobacco are likely but undocumented. Zambia belongs to the pattern on churches and movements placing members in the state.
Zambia.imp: For Zambians, the record shows that religious leaders can be brought straight into cabinet by appointment, without election, and that a later government can undo it. The religious-affairs department still sits inside the Vice-President's office. The bigger unknown is what is not documented: foreign tech firms and political consultants are recorded as present, and how they work with government is not on the record. Watch who advises on elections and who supplies state surveillance.

Zimbabwe.d:
In Zimbabwe, a businessman under foreign sanctions now sits in the cabinet. Kudakwashe (Kuda) Tagwirei founded Sakunda Holdings, which grew through fuel trading with the commodity firm Trafigura and a $3 billion state farming contract, 'Command Agriculture', paid in Treasury bills from 2017 to 2019. In August 2020 the US Treasury sanctioned him, accusing him of misappropriating public funds and supporting senior officials; the UK followed in 2021 and the US extended sanctions in 2024. He was co-opted onto the ruling ZANU-PF's Central Committee in October 2025, and in October 2026 President Mnangagwa made him Minister of Economic Development and Investment Promotion. He denies the allegations.

Gold is the other live issue. In 2023 an Al Jazeera undercover investigation, Gold Mafia, recorded intermediaries, one of them an ambassador-at-large, offering to wash cash through the state gold refinery and export it as bullion. The government set up a commission, and the practice continued. This is reported, not proven in court.

Russia's reach is older and smaller: in 2018 a body called AFRIC sent about 40 'election observers' to Zimbabwe's vote, and investigative journalists later found it was organised by people linked to Yevgeny Prigozhin. ZANU-PF is also one of the six parties behind the CCP-funded Nyerere Leadership School in Tanzania. Zimbabwe belongs to the patterns on criminal money in firms, spyware and elections for hire, and Russia's networks in Africa.
Zimbabwe.imp: For Zimbabweans, a man foreign governments accuse of taking public money now helps run economic policy, so the line between state contracts and private fortune is hard to see. If gold can be used to wash cash through the state refinery, the country's main export earns less for the public and more for whoever controls the trade. Watch what contracts Tagwirei's ministry hands out and whether the gold commission's findings lead to charges.

Afghanistan.d:
Afghanistan is ruled by the Taliban, and the map's present-day cases are about who sits inside that government. Since the Taliban took Kabul in 2021, the Haqqani network, a militant group within the Taliban that the US listed as terrorist in 2012, has controlled Kabul's security, and its leader Sirajuddin Haqqani is interior minister. In 2011 the top US military officer told the Senate the network acted as 'a veritable arm' of Pakistan's spy agency, the ISI; Pakistan denies ties. UN sanctions monitors assessed in 2023 that at least three key Taliban government leaders are affiliated with al-Qaeda, and in December 2025 that al-Qaeda keeps close ties with the Taliban while the Pakistani Taliban (TTP), about 6,000 fighters, has strong support from elements within it. The Taliban reject the reports.

Before 2021, under the US-backed republic, the documented cases were about money. Kabul Bank, the largest private bank, paid the salaries of soldiers, police and civil servants. An anti-corruption committee reported in 2012 that it had been run as a fraud: about $935 million taken, most loans going to just 19 people and companies, and money given to a presidential campaign against central bank advice. Shareholders included the brothers of President Hamid Karzai and of the first vice-president; neither was charged. The chairman and chief executive were jailed, and the bailout cost over 5% of the economy. US and UN assessments also described provincial officials and police commanders taxing and protecting opium. US officials named the president's half-brother Ahmed Wali Karzai; he denied it and was never charged. In 2012 the US designated two Kandahar money-exchange houses used by an opium network.

Afghanistan sits in the map's patterns on organised crime inside the state and on banks, and as a country where a foreign spy service is reported inside the government.
Afghanistan.imp: For Afghans, the people who run the police and the interior ministry are, according to US and UN reports, tied to armed groups and a neighbouring spy agency, and there is no independent forum inside the country to test those claims. Before 2021, the bank that paid public salaries was emptied by insiders with family links to the top of government, and the state paid for the rescue. Watch the UN monitors' yearly reports, and money moving through hawala brokers, which leave no bank record.

Armenia.d:
One case is on the map for Armenia, and it is unresolved. Samvel Karapetyan, a Russian-Armenian billionaire, owns the Tashir Group, which ran Electric Networks of Armenia, the country's only power distributor. He was detained on 18 June 2025 over public calls to seize power, made after he backed the Armenian Church in its dispute with Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, and was later charged with money laundering. Parliament then passed amendments allowing the state to take over the grid company. His lawyers call the charges unfounded, and critics see a political case ahead of the 2026 election. No trial result has been reported, and the map rates the alleged plot as only possible.

The case shows the kind of reach that matters in a small country: one private owner holding the company that delivers everyone's electricity. The Russkiy Mir Foundation, a Russian state-backed body, is likely present but undocumented. The conditions scores are moderate. Armenia belongs to no pattern yet.
Armenia.imp: For Armenians, two questions are open: whether the private owner of the national power grid was using that position for political ends, and whether the government is using criminal charges to remove a rival before an election. No court has settled either. Watch the trial, who ends up running the grid company, and whether the takeover law is used again.

Azerbaijan.d:
Azerbaijan's cases show the state and its oil company reaching outward. The economy rests on oil and gas, and the state oil company SOCAR is at its centre. In November 2024 Azerbaijan hosted COP29, the UN climate summit. The summit's president, Mukhtar Babayev, had been SOCAR's vice-president for ecology. Its chief executive, deputy energy minister Elnur Soltanov, was secretly filmed by Global Witness, whose staff posed as investors, discussing possible oil and gas deals in the run-up to the talks. Critics said this broke the code of conduct for summit presidencies. The map rates the case probable and gives it its highest reach score, because it reached into a global body.

Earlier, on 18 June 2014, schools linked to the Gülen movement, a Turkish Islamic movement the Turkish government pursues as a terrorist group, were taken over by a company in which SOCAR holds shares: 11 high schools, 13 university-entrance centres and a private university. The company cited finances; the takeover followed requests from Turkey's Prime Minister Erdoğan for help against the movement.

The map also lists Azerbaijan as the home of the network it calls 'caviar diplomacy', followed in the pattern on foreign money inside Europe's parliaments. Its conditions scores read poorly: a high reading for powerful actors embedded in the state and weak resilience. Azerbaijan also sits in the patterns on industry inside regulators, international bodies, and Turkey's pursuit of the Gülen movement.
Azerbaijan.imp: For people in Azerbaijan, the state, its oil company and its diplomacy are hard to tell apart: the same people move between SOCAR, ministries and the chair of a world summit, and an oil-company affiliate took over a network of schools after another government asked for help. Watch who represents the country abroad and what business they discuss there, and whether SOCAR-linked companies take over institutions that have nothing to do with oil.

Bahrain.d: Nothing is documented on the map yet showing an outside force inside Bahrain's own government, so this is a best guess. The one record runs the other way. In 2018 Bahrain obtained an Interpol Red Notice for Hakeem al-Araibi, a dissident footballer living as a refugee in Australia; Thailand arrested him, Interpol withdrew the notice because its rules bar notices sought by the country a refugee fled, and Thai prosecutors dropped the case in February 2019. The Muslim Brotherhood and the Tony Blair Institute are present. The conditions scores are middling. The most likely route in is Iran's Revolutionary Guards and their allied militia network, listed as likely but undocumented.
Bahrain.imp: For people in Bahrain, the documented risk is the state's own reach: using an international police system to pursue someone who fled. If outside forces are inside the government, the record does not show it yet. Watch for Red Notices against exiles, and for evidence, rather than claims, of Iranian-backed networks.

Bangladesh.d:
Bangladesh's documented cases run through its central bank, its army and the drug route from Myanmar. In February 2016 hackers inside the network of Bangladesh Bank, the central bank, sent fraudulent payment orders for $951 million from its account at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. Most were blocked, but $101 million went out, $81 million of it to the Philippines. US agencies tied the theft to a unit under North Korea's Reconnaissance General Bureau, its military spy agency, and US prosecutors charged a North Korean programmer in 2018. About $66 million was still unrecovered in 2025.

Yaba, a methamphetamine pill, enters almost entirely through Cox's Bazar on the Myanmar border. The district's MP, Abdur Rahman Bodi, appeared on the government's own list of traffickers. He was convicted in 2018 only of concealing wealth; the trafficking allegations never went to trial. The anti-drug campaign there produced hundreds of killings in police custody or 'crossfire', and in 2022 a former Teknaf police station chief and colleagues were sentenced to death for killing a retired army major who had filmed them. The drug trade itself was not disrupted.

In January 2012 the army said it had stopped a coup by serving and retired officers it linked to Hizb ut-Tahrir, a movement that seeks to replace states with a caliphate and has been banned in Bangladesh since 2009. Two retired officers were arrested.

Bangladesh sits in the map's patterns on organised crime inside the state and on movements that tried to take the state itself.
Bangladesh.imp: For people in Bangladesh, the trafficking that runs through Cox's Bazar reached its member of parliament, while the crackdown killed hundreds and ended with police convicted of murder rather than the trade broken. A foreign state's hackers took part of the national reserves, money that belongs to the public. Watch whether trafficking cases against officials reach trial, and how the central bank protects its payment systems.

Bhutan.d: Nothing is documented on the map for Bhutan, and no organisation is recorded as present or even likely, so anything here is a best guess. The conditions scores are moderate: a fairly low reading for powerful actors embedded in the state, and middling resilience, meaning the courts, press and parliament that would catch them. For a small state the likeliest route in would be a larger government's influence, but the record shows nothing of it.
Bhutan.imp: For people in Bhutan, the absence of cases may mean little is happening, or that little has been looked for. If outside forces do reach in, the first signs are usually foreign money in politics and unexplained winners of large public contracts, so those are the things to watch, along with whether the press is free to report them.

Brunei.d: Nothing is documented on the map yet for Brunei, so this is a best guess. One organisation is recorded as present: China's police 'overseas service stations', offices abroad tied to Chinese police. The conditions scores are moderate: a low reading for powerful actors embedded in the state and middling resilience. If anything reaches in, the most likely route is China's reach toward Chinese nationals living there, but no case shows it inside Brunei's government.
Brunei.imp: For people in Brunei, there is nothing on the record yet to point to, which may mean little is happening or that little has been looked for. The one thread worth watching is whether Chinese police offices operate there and what they do, especially toward Chinese nationals, and whether Brunei's own authorities know about them or allow them.

Cambodia.d:
In Cambodia the documented cases are happening now. They centre on scam compounds, premises where trafficked workers are held under debt bondage and made to run online investment fraud, and on people close to the ruling family.

Chen Zhi, born in China and a Cambodian citizen from 2014, built the Prince Group into one of the country's largest conglomerates and was an adviser to Hun Sen, the long-time prime minister, as well as to the interior minister and the National Assembly president. In October 2025 US prosecutors indicted him as head of a cyber-fraud empire run from scam compounds and seized about 127,271 bitcoin, about US$14 billion; the US and UK sanctioned 146 people and firms linked to the group, and more were added in June 2026. In January 2026 Cambodia said it had arrested him, revoked his citizenship and sent him to China. A sitting senator, Kok An, and his network were sanctioned by the US in April 2026. US and UK designations describe political protection as the reason the compounds operate openly; Cambodian courts have prosecuted none of those named.

The money runs through Huione Group, a Phnom Penh financial firm whose payment arm has Hun To, a cousin of Prime Minister Hun Manet, as a major shareholder and director. Cambodia's central bank revoked that arm's licence in March 2025, and in May 2025 the US Treasury found Huione had laundered over US$4 billion, including money from North Korean hackers and scams. Its online marketplace, Huione Guarantee, handled tens of billions of dollars before closing. The UN drugs agency describes the region's 340-plus casinos, online gambling and dollar stablecoin transfers as a parallel banking system for drug, gambling and fraud money.

There is a religious thread too: Hun Sen hosted a 2019 summit of the Unification Church's political arm and accepted two of its awards. The older background includes a 2003 heroin case against a military intelligence general, released within weeks after the seized drugs were publicly burned.

Cambodia is a central case in the map's patterns on scam compounds and criminal money.
Cambodia.imp: For Cambodians, the scam compounds run openly because, according to US and UK findings, people connected to power protect them, and no Cambodian court has tried anyone named. The workers inside are trafficking victims, and the money moves through firms tied to the prime minister's family. Watch whether Cambodian prosecutors act on their own, who takes over Prince and Huione assets, and whether the compounds simply move elsewhere.

China.d:
China's record runs in two directions. Inside the country, the Communist Party sits inside companies by law. Outward, Chinese officials and firms reach into international bodies and into drug supply chains abroad.

Under China's Company Law, any firm with three or more party members must set up a party organisation. In 2020 the party told its United Front departments, the party arm that works with business and overseas Chinese, to 'guide' how private firms are run. ByteDance, owner of TikTok, has had a party committee since 2014, gave a state fund a board seat in 2021, and admitted in 2022 that staff used TikTok data to track journalists. A leaked 2020 list of about 1.95 million party members included staff at foreign banks, drug makers and aircraft firms; it showed membership, not spying.

In international bodies, Meng Hongwei was elected Interpol's president in 2016 while serving as China's vice-minister of public security. He disappeared on a trip home in 2018 and was jailed for 13½ years for bribery; his wife, granted asylum in France, says the case is political.

Chinese chemical companies sit at the source of the fentanyl trade. US indictments since 2018 charge China-based firms and staff with selling fentanyl and its precursor chemicals to Mexican cartels and US buyers, mostly paid in cryptocurrency. These are charges, and the defendants are mostly beyond US reach; China has since controlled some of the chemicals.

In Macau the cases are convictions: in 2023 the heads of Suncity and Tak Chun, junket operators that brought high-stakes gamblers to the casinos, were jailed for 18 and 14 years, though Tak Chun's fraud counts were overturned on appeal. Hong Kong Customs is pursuing about HK$8.9 billion laundered through fake trading.

Foreign firms have reached into Chinese officialdom too. JPMorgan paid $264 million in 2016 after hiring about 100 relatives and friends of officials to win business. ILSI, a group founded by a Coca-Cola executive, had its China office inside the national disease-control agency and steered obesity policy toward exercise rather than diet, a Harvard researcher reported in 2019.

The older background includes a 1993 remark by the police minister that 'patriotic' triads deserve respect, and a 2009–2011 Chongqing campaign in which a former deputy police chief was executed for protecting gangs.

China is a sponsoring state in the map's patterns on governments inside companies and inside international bodies.
China.imp: For people in China, the party is present inside the companies they work for, and inside some of the apps they use, by law rather than in secret, though membership lists are not public. Abroad, the same state placed its own vice-minister at the head of Interpol. Chemical firms selling to cartels are mostly beyond foreign courts. Watch party clauses in company charters, Red Notices against exiles, and whether China prosecutes its own precursor sellers.

Cyprus.d:
Cyprus's cases concern selling access: to passports and to banking. From 2007 to 2020 Cyprus sold citizenship to investors. In October 2020 Al Jazeera aired an undercover film in which House Speaker Demetris Syllouris and MP Christakis Giovanis appeared willing to help a fictional Chinese investor with a money-laundering conviction get a passport. Both resigned and the scheme was closed. A state inquiry led by former judge Myron Nicolatos found that more than half the passports had been granted unlawfully; four men were sent to trial in 2022 and one was cleared in 2023.

Before that, FBME Bank, registered in Tanzania but operating from Cyprus, was named by the US Treasury's FinCEN in 2014 as a primary money-laundering concern over accounts used by organised crime and sanctioned parties. Cyprus wound the bank up; its owners fought the designation in arbitration for years.

Neither case is still running, but both are still felt. The United Grand Lodge of England and Turkey's Grey Wolves are listed as likely present but undocumented. Cyprus sits in the map's patterns on criminal money in banks and on exposure and purge.
Cyprus.imp: For Cypriots, the passport scheme meant the head of parliament was filmed offering to help a convicted launderer become a European citizen, and an official inquiry found most passports were granted unlawfully. The scheme is closed. Watch the remaining trials, whether unlawfully granted passports are withdrawn, and how banks check accounts held by non-residents.

Georgia.d:
Georgia's one documented case concerns the man at the top of its ruling party, and it is rated among the most serious on the map. Bidzina Ivanishvili made his fortune in Russia in the 1990s, founded the ruling Georgian Dream party and, as its honorary chairman, nominates the prime minister. In December 2024 the US Treasury sanctioned him 'for undermining Georgian democracy and advancing the interests of the Russian Federation'. Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia sanctioned him too, and the European Parliament describes him as having 'personal and business links to the Kremlin'. He denies acting for Russia. These are sanctions decisions by foreign governments, not a court ruling, and the map rates the Russian link probable.

The Grand Orient de France and the Gülen movement are recorded as present, and the Atlas Network as likely. Georgia sits in the map's patterns on Russia's networks and on foreign money in European politics, as a target country.
Georgia.imp: For Georgians, the person who chooses the prime minister is under Western sanctions for allegedly advancing another country's interests, and no court has tested that claim. Ordinary voters cannot see what ties, if any, shape his decisions. Watch the government's policy toward Russia and the EU, how protest and dissent are treated, and whether any court examines the allegations.

India.d:
In India, the largest documented presence inside government today is the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), a Hindu nationalist volunteer organisation founded in 1925, from whose political wing the governing BJP grew. Prime Minister Narendra Modi was a full-time RSS organiser before it seconded him to the BJP in 1985. ThePrint counted in 2020 that 38 of the 53 BJP ministers in his second government had RSS roots, as did all eight it listed on the cabinet's economic committee. Vice-President C. P. Radhakrishnan, who chairs the upper house, has been with the RSS since he was 16. The RSS publishes no membership rolls. Membership of a lawful organisation is not wrongdoing; the record shows how many top offices are held by people from one movement.

The second thread is lawmakers facing criminal cases. After the 2024 election, 251 of 543 MPs declared pending criminal cases, 170 of them serious; these are cases, not convictions. Mukhtar Ansari won his Uttar Pradesh seat five times, much of that time from prison, and died in custody in 2024 after eight convictions.

Companies reaching officials: in November 2024 US prosecutors charged Gautam Adani, founder of the ports-and-power conglomerate, with fraud over more than $250 million in alleged bribes to Indian officials for solar contracts; he denies it. A French judge has investigated the Rafale fighter deal since 2021, though India's Supreme Court found no irregularity.

Indian firms also sit in the global drug supply chain. Since 2025 US authorities have charged or sanctioned Indian chemical suppliers for shipping fentanyl precursors toward the Sinaloa Cartel, and investigators traced about $130 million of the opioid tapentadol from more than 60 Indian exporters to West African countries that never approved it.

India's state reaches abroad too. In February 2026 Nikhil Gupta pleaded guilty in New York over a murder-for-hire plot against Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a US citizen and Sikh activist; prosecutors say an officer in India's Cabinet Secretariat, home of the foreign spy agency RAW, directed it. That officer has not been brought to the US.

The older background is the 1919 'dyarchy' reform, which the historian Carroll Quigley traced to a Round Table study group in London.

India sits in the map's patterns on religious nationalism in power and organised crime inside the state.
India.imp: For people in India, many of the top offices are held by people formed in one movement, the RSS, which does not publish who its members are. Nearly half the lower house faces pending criminal cases. The biggest bribery allegations are being pursued by foreign courts, not Indian ones. Watch who is appointed to ministries and regulators, whether Indian investigators act on the Adani charges, and how exporters of opioids and precursor chemicals are policed.

Indonesia.d:
In Indonesia the present-day cases concern religious and paramilitary organisations in politics. The older background is foreign-trained economists, and foreign companies paying officials.

Nahdlatul Ulama, Indonesia's largest Muslim organisation, saw its supreme leader Ma'ruf Amin serve as vice-president from 2019 to 2024 after President Joko Widodo chose him as running mate; he resigned the NU post first. Pemuda Pancasila, a paramilitary group founded in 1959 that took part in the 1965–66 killings, was part of the ruling Golkar party from 1982 to 2001 and is known for extortion and protection work. In the other direction, the government banned Hizb ut-Tahrir Indonesia in 2017 for aiming to replace the state with a caliphate and warned civil servants who were members they would be dismissed; the courts upheld the ban. In 2023 a police inspector general was convicted of ordering seized methamphetamine to be swapped for alum and sold.

Foreign companies have paid their way in. In 2020 the former head of the state airline Garuda was jailed for eight years for bribes that prosecutors traced to Rolls-Royce and Airbus. Monsanto settled US charges in 2005 over a $50,000 bribe to an environment ministry official assessing its genetically modified cotton.

The roots go back to the 1960s. The Ford Foundation paid for University of Indonesia economists to earn doctorates at Berkeley, and after Suharto took power they ran his economy: Widjojo Nitisastro headed the planning agency for 16 years and Ali Wardhana was finance minister for 15. Their programme cut inflation from 650% to 13% by 1969 and opened the country to foreign investors. John Perkins later claimed his engineering firm inflated forecasts so Indonesia would borrow heavily; reporters confirmed his career but not his larger claims.

Indonesia sits in the map's patterns on lenders and trained technocrats, religious movements in the state, and industries inside regulators.
Indonesia.imp: For Indonesians, large mass organisations, religious and paramilitary, are routes into the vice-presidency and the ruling parties. Foreign firms have paid officials at the state airline and at the ministry that assessed GM crops. Watch who mass organisations place on party tickets, how regulators judge foreign companies' products, and whether drug cases against senior police officers keep reaching court.

Iran.d:
In Iran, the state's own armed force sits inside the economy. The Revolutionary Guards (IRGC), Iran's ideological military, control more than 812 registered companies through their engineering arm Khatam al-Anbiya, working in dams, tunnels, oil and gas and defence, with about 1,700 government contracts by 2012; the UN Security Council named it an IRGC entity in 2010. In 2009 a consortium including Guards-linked foundations bought control of the Telecommunication Company of Iran, which runs the network the state uses to watch and filter communications; a Guards unit said in 2018 it had sold its share.

Inside the courts, a defence lawyer has alleged that two Tehran revolutionary court judges who hear drug cases were corrupt. With no independent forum, the claim cannot be tested, and the country hangs hundreds of people a year for drug offences.

The older background is the Shah's era and the early revolution. Nematollah Nassiri, head of the Shah's secret police SAVAK, signed the 1976 Safari Club charter, a pact with the intelligence chiefs of France, Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Morocco. Jafar Sharif-Emami, Grand Master of Iran's Masonic Grand Lodge, was twice the Shah's prime minister, the second time in 1978. After the revolution the Hojjatieh Society, a religious group, suspended itself in 1983 when Ayatollah Khomeini attacked it, and its affiliates were purged; claims that former members later rose high are contested.

Iran's conditions scores are among the worst on the map: the joint highest reading for powerful actors embedded in the state, and weak resilience. It is the sponsoring state in the map's pattern on Iran's armed allies inside other governments.
Iran.imp: For Iranians, the Revolutionary Guards are not only soldiers: they build the dams, run oil and gas projects and for years held the telephone network, so the military shares in the contracts the state awards. Drug courts pass death sentences with little outside scrutiny of the judges. Watch which firms win state contracts, who owns the networks that carry communications, and whether any independent review of drug cases appears.

Iraq.d:
In Iraq, armed groups backed by Iran's Revolutionary Guards are part of the state's own armed forces. The Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) formed in 2014 to fight Islamic State from about 67 mostly Shia factions, almost all backed by the Guards. A 2016 law made them a branch of the armed forces under the prime minister, paid from the state budget. In 2024 the PMF chief of staff said publicly that it took orders from Iran's supreme leader. Kata'ib Hezbollah, which the US lists as a terrorist group, staffs three PMF brigades; the US linked it to a 2024 drone attack that killed three US soldiers. The PMF's chairman, Falih al-Fayyadh, was sanctioned by the US in 2021 over the killing of protesters in 2019 and still holds the post. A 2025 bill to tighten state control was tabled under US pressure.

Money is the second thread. In 2021–22 about $2.5 billion was taken from the tax authority through 247 cheques to five front companies posing as oil firms. In late 2024 a Baghdad court convicted 10 people, including a former head of parliament's finance committee and the former director of Prime Minister Mustafa al-Kadhimi's office. Several former senior tax and bank officials have not been charged.

Drugs are the third. Captagon seizures rose about 3,380% from 2019 to 2023, much of it crossing the 600-kilometre Syrian border, and Iraq has moved from transit route to production site; the state now drug-tests teachers and officials. A former governor's son who worked for the intelligence service got life for drug offences in 2018, then was pardoned.

Iraq is a central case in the map's pattern on Iran's armed allies inside governments.
Iraq.imp: For Iraqis, part of the armed forces paid from the state budget answers, by its own chief of staff's account, to the leader of another country. Public money was taken from inside the tax authority with help from officials close to a prime minister, and only some have been tried. Watch the PMF reform bill, who controls the PMF budget, and whether the remaining tax and bank officials are charged.

Israel.d:
Israel's leading case is in court now. Prosecutors say Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, while also communications minister, gave regulatory decisions worth large sums to Shaul Elovitch, controlling owner of the telecoms company Bezeq, in return for favourable coverage on Elovitch's news site Walla!. Netanyahu is charged with bribery, fraud and breach of trust. His trial began in May 2020; he denies the charges and in November 2025 asked President Herzog for a pardon.

A second investigation concerns a foreign government. In 2025 police arrested two Netanyahu aides, Jonatan Urich and Eli Feldstein, on suspicion of being paid through a US lobbyist's firm to promote Qatar's image in Israel; Qatar mediates in the Gaza war and hosts Hamas's political office. Netanyahu was questioned as a witness, not a suspect, and calls it a political witch hunt. In May 2026 prosecutors announced a separate indictment of Urich over leaking a classified document.

Israeli companies also reach into other governments. NSO Group sells its Pegasus phone-hacking spyware only to governments, under defence ministry export licences; state clients' use of it has been tied to surveillance of journalists and dissidents, and the US blacklisted the firm in 2021. Teva and Allergan settled US opioid claims in 2022 without admitting wrongdoing. Israeli courts have also convicted police officers for passing investigation files to crime organisations.

Israel sits in the map's patterns on industries inside regulators and on spyware for hire, as the spyware firm's home.
Israel.imp: For Israelis, the open questions are whether a prime minister traded regulatory favours for news coverage, and whether his aides took money to promote a foreign state; neither has been decided. Israeli spyware sold to other governments has been used against journalists. Watch the trial's outcome or any pardon, the Qatar investigation, and which governments receive export licences for spyware.

Japan.d:
Japan's prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, elected by the Diet on 21 October 2025, has served in the Diet members' league of Nippon Kaigi, the country's largest nationalist lobby (about 38,000–40,000 members), which campaigns for constitutional revision and patriotic education. Japan Press Weekly, the English service of the Communist Party paper Akahata, reported that 10 of her first 19 ministers belonged to that league and 12 to the league of Shinto Seiji Renmei, the political arm of the Association of Shinto Shrines. These are reported membership lists, not findings that the groups direct policy, and the cabinet reshuffled in September 2026 has not been counted.

The Unification Church, a Korean-founded church, is being dissolved. After Shinzo Abe was shot dead in 2022 by a man who blamed the church for ruining his family, the ruling LDP's own survey found 179 of its 379 Diet members had ties to it, and a minister resigned. In March 2026 the Tokyo High Court upheld the dissolution order, which found 1,559 victims of unlawful donation solicitation and about ¥20.4 billion taken. Church documents seized in South Korea are reported to say it backed 290 LDP candidates in 2021. The roots go back to 1968, when former prime minister Nobusuke Kishi, Abe's grandfather, co-founded the church's anti-communist political arm. Komeito, the party of the Buddhist lay movement Soka Gakkai, governed with the LDP from 1999 until it quit in October 2025; it is now in opposition.

Crime and industry reach in too. Every prefecture now bars business with the yakuza, Japan's crime groups (9,400 members counted in 2025). Regulators found Mizuho Bank let about ¥200 million in loans reach gang members, and police arrested yakuza brokers supplying workers to the state-funded Fukushima clean-up. A Diet commission found in 2012 that the nuclear regulator had been 'captured' by TEPCO, the operator of the plant that melted down. A SoftBank employee was indicted in 2020 for passing network files to a Russian trade official, and a Tokyo 2020 Olympic board member is on trial for bribery, which he denies.

Japan sits in the patterns on churches placing members in the state, religious nationalism in power, organised crime and industries inside their regulators.
Japan.imp: Many of the people running Japan's government belong to lobbies that want to change the constitution and how history is taught, and what the public knows about who belongs comes mostly from press lists, not official disclosure. The church case shows how a religious group's volunteers and votes reached a large part of the ruling party while its followers were pressed for money. Watch the membership counts for the reshuffled cabinet, the church's liquidation, and whether courts and regulators keep acting on gang money and on industries that shape their own safety rules.

Jordan.d:
Jordan is dealing with two separate fights. The first is with the Muslim Brotherhood, a Sunni Islamist movement founded in Egypt in 1928. Its political arm here, the Islamic Action Front, won 31 of 138 seats in the September 2024 election and is the largest party in parliament. On 23 April 2025 the interior minister banned all Brotherhood activities and said its assets would be seized, after the arrest of 16 people, Brotherhood members among them, over an alleged weapons plot the group said it knew nothing about. In January 2026 the US Treasury listed the Jordanian branch as a terrorist group; Jordan's government said the group 'has been dissolved for years'. These are government decisions, not court findings against any official.

The second is with captagon, a pill drug smuggled south from Syria. Jordan's State Security Court has convicted serving and former soldiers of moving captagon and weapons across the border in cases since 2022, which shows the smugglers reached inside the force meant to stop them. Since Assad fell in December 2024, smugglers have switched to GPS-guided helium balloons launched from the empty Hamad desert. Jordan intercepted 128 attempts between July 2025 and April 2026, has struck inside Syria five times, and has seized at least 46 million pills since mid-2025. Whether the balloon trade is tied to firms or money networks inside Jordan is only suspected.

Jordan sits in the patterns on organised crime inside the state, movements that sought the state itself, and governments banning such groups.
Jordan.imp: For people in Jordan, the largest party they voted for in 2024 belongs to a movement their government has banned and the US now lists as terrorist, so what happens to those 31 seats affects who represents them. The captagon convictions show that soldiers guarding the border can be paid to let loads through. Watch the State Security Court cases, how the ban is applied to the Islamic Action Front, and whether balloon seizures lead to anyone on the Jordanian side.

Kazakhstan.d:
Kazakhstan has one case on the map, and it is marked only as possible. The Gülen movement, a Turkish religious network that Turkey's government calls 'FETÖ' and pursues abroad, co-founded 33 Turkish-Kazakh high schools here. After Turkey's July 2016 coup attempt, Ankara asked Central Asian governments to close Gülen-linked schools, and Kazakhstan declined. On 18 October 2016 the sponsoring foundation, KATEV, renamed the schools 'Bilim' Innovative Lyceums; RFE/RL found no Kazakh government order behind the change.

Opus Dei, the Order of Malta, Hizb ut-Tahrir (a movement that seeks a caliphate) and Turkey's nationalist Grey Wolves are recorded as present, and the World Economic Forum, Russia's Russkiy Mir Foundation and Interpol as likely, but none has a documented case. The conditions scores are middling: a fair number of state-embedded actors (6 of 10) and below-average resilience (4.7). Kazakhstan sits in the pattern on Turkey's campaign against the Gülen movement.
Kazakhstan.imp: For families whose children attended those schools, the schools stayed open under a new name, and the government did not hand anyone to Turkey on this record. That sets Kazakhstan apart from neighbours where people were removed. Because Russian and Chinese state bodies are not documented here yet, the map says little about the outside forces most likely to matter. Watch whether the refusal to close schools holds and whether new cases appear involving Russia or China.

Korea, DPR.d:
North Korea is closed to outsiders, so this map records it mainly as a state that reaches into others. Three bodies headquartered here operate abroad: the remote IT-worker programme, the Lazarus Group (state hackers, also called TraderTraitor) and the Reconnaissance General Bureau, its main intelligence agency. It is also one of three countries, with Iran and Myanmar, on the FATF blacklist, the list on which the global anti-money-laundering body calls on others to take action.

The one documented case is disputed. In 2003 the North Korean freighter Pong Su delivered 125 kilograms of heroin to a beach in Victoria, Australia, and was boarded by Australian special forces. In 2006 a jury acquitted the captain and senior crew of importation, not persuaded they knew the cargo, and the ship was later sunk as a bombing target. No court found the state behind it.

The Unification Church, a Korean-founded church, is recorded as present. The conditions scores are near the top of the scale: power held by people embedded in the state (10 of 10) and almost no resilience (1.6). It sits in the organised-crime pattern and in the pattern of courts reversing a finding.
Korea, DPR.imp: People in North Korea have no free press or independent courts that could show who inside the state profits from smuggling, hacking or work abroad, so almost nothing reaches a record like this. What can be seen is the effect outside the country: ships, IT workers and hackers working for the state. Watch foreign court cases and sanctions actions, which are where evidence about North Korea's state businesses usually comes out.

Korea, Rep..d:
South Korea's courts are working through the ties between two churches and its political parties. The Unification Church, a Korean-founded church led by Han Hak-ja, was found to have used its money to expand political influence around the 2022 presidential election. In January 2026 a Seoul court jailed former first lady Kim Keon-hee, wife of ex-president Yoon Suk Yeol, for one year and eight months for taking a Chanel bag worth 12 million won and a diamond necklace worth 62 million won from the church in July 2022. In July 2026 the Supreme Court upheld a two-year term for Kweon Seong-dong, a former floor leader of the then-governing People Power Party, for taking 100 million won from a church official; he lost his seat. In August 2026 Han Hak-ja herself was sentenced to two years, and the church says it will appeal. The money reached the other side too: in December 2025 Chun Jae-soo, oceans minister in the Democratic Party government, resigned after a church official said he had been given cash and two luxury watches. Police booked him as a bribery suspect; he denies it.

The second church, Shincheonji, is accused of signing up at least 56,472 of its members as People Power Party members between 2021 and 2023. Its 94-year-old founder, Lee Man-hee, was indicted in July 2026 under the law that bars forcing anyone to join a party.

Big business reaches into the state as well. Lee Jae-yong, heir to Samsung, the country's largest business group, was convicted in 2017 of bribing entities controlled by a friend of President Park Geun-hye, in the scandal that led to her impeachment; he was pardoned in 2022 and became chairman. Prosecutors also charge that a former Samsung executive copied a Samsung chip plant in China with Chengdu government money, which he denies.

The roots go back to 1978, when a US House inquiry found that a business of Sun Myung Moon's organisation made M-16 rifles for Seoul and that his representatives acted as secret envoys of the government. South Korea sits in the patterns on churches placing members in the state and companies inside other companies.
Korea, Rep..imp: For South Koreans, these cases show that a church's money and members could reach a president's household and party leaders on both sides, and that the courts are now acting on it. Party sign-ups are a quiet route: mass memberships can tilt who gets nominated without voters noticing. Watch the appeals by Han Hak-ja and the church, the Shincheonji trial, the police case against Chun Jae-soo, and whether pardons undo the sentences, as one did for Samsung's heir.

Kuwait.d:
Kuwait has one case on the map, marked only as possible. The Muslim Brotherhood is a Sunni Islamist movement founded in Egypt in 1928 with branches across the region. After Iraq invaded Kuwait in 1990, the Kuwaiti branch broke with the international movement and founded its own party, the Islamic Constitutional Movement, known as Hadas. Hadas regularly won several seats in parliament through the 1990s and 2000s and sometimes had members in the cabinet. A coalition that included it was out of parliament after it boycotted the 2013 elections.

This is an open political party competing in elections, not a hidden network; the case is on the map because of its roots in a movement that crosses borders. The Trilateral Commission, a private forum of business and political leaders, and Gulf-state and private networks that fund Salafi preaching are recorded as present, and the telecoms firm Ericsson as likely, without documented cases. Kuwait sits in the pattern on movements that sought the state itself, where it counts as one that won seats.
Kuwait.imp: For Kuwaitis, the Brotherhood's influence here has come through elections, in the open, which is different from the hidden placement this map records in other countries. Neighbouring Saudi Arabia lists the Brotherhood as terrorist, and the US now designates several of its branches. Watch whether Hadas returns to parliament and the cabinet, and whether outside governments press Kuwait to treat it as other states have.

Kyrgyzstan.d:
Kyrgyzstan's record shows crime networks and a foreign intelligence service getting through the state's customs and border posts. The largest case concerns Raiymbek Matraimov, a former deputy chief of customs. In December 2020 the US Treasury sanctioned him under the Magnitsky Act, a US law used to punish corrupt officials abroad, for a customs scheme that moved hundreds of millions of dollars out of the country. Journalists from OCCRP and Kloop who documented the network were prosecuted or forced out. He settled a domestic corruption case by repaying money and served no prison term at the time.

Kamchybek Kolbayev, a crime boss the US designated as a drug kingpin in 2011, was repeatedly released or lightly sentenced by Kyrgyz courts, a record that points to protection; he was killed in a security operation in 2023.

In mid-2021 Orhan Inandi, a Kyrgyz citizen who headed the Sapat network of Turkish-founded schools, disappeared in Bishkek. On 5 July Turkey's president said on television that Inandi, whom he called a leader of the Gülen movement (a Turkish religious network Ankara calls 'FETÖ'), had been 'captured and taken to Turkey'. Kyrgyz military prosecutors opened proceedings against border officers of the national security committee who let him be taken out.

Conditions are poor: many state-embedded actors (8.5 of 10) and low resilience (3.8). Kyrgyzstan sits in the patterns on organised crime inside the state, Turkey's campaign against the Gülen movement, and outside sanctions.
Kyrgyzstan.imp: For people in Kyrgyzstan, the customs case is about money that should have reached the public purse leaving through the border, with the reporters who exposed it punished rather than the official. The Inandi case shows a foreign government could take a citizen past the state's own border guards. Watch whether the proceedings against those guards reach a result, and whether journalists covering customs and organised crime can keep working.

Laos.d:
In Bokeo province, in the far north-west of Laos, a stretch of the Mekong is run largely by a casino company. In 2007 the Lao government gave Kings Romans Group, headed by the Chinese casino operator Zhao Wei, a 99-year lease to set up and run the Golden Triangle Special Economic Zone. In January 2018 the US Treasury designated Zhao Wei's network as a transnational criminal organisation, saying the Kings Romans casino stored and distributed drugs from Myanmar's United Wa State Army and laundered the proceeds. The owner denied it. The casino kept operating and expanding.

The US State Department reports that the zone is run in part by criminal organisations, that confusion over who is in charge between Lao officials and zone security blocks investigations, and that no complicit official has been investigated, prosecuted or convicted. UNODC has linked the zone to cyber-fraud compounds and flagged a 2020 river port built by a company tied to the organisation. Meanwhile Laos arrested more than 20,000 people for drug offences between 2015 and 2019.

In February 2025 the FATF, the international body that sets anti-money-laundering standards, put Laos on its list of countries under increased monitoring, which brings outside scrutiny to the banks of the state that granted the concession. Hong Kong and Macau triads are likely present but not documented.

Laos sits in the patterns on organised crime inside the state and criminal money inside banks and firms.
Laos.imp: For people in Laos, part of their country is governed under a lease by a group the US calls a criminal organisation, and no official has been prosecuted over it. Tens of thousands of ordinary people have been arrested on drug charges while the zone's owners have not been touched at home. Watch whether Lao authorities ever act inside the zone, what happens to the fraud compounds there, and whether the FATF listing is lifted or tightened.

Lebanon.d:
Lebanon's government includes ministers chosen by Hezbollah, a Shia party with its own armed wing, aligned with Iran and listed as a terrorist group by at least 28 countries including the US and UK. It holds about 14 of 128 seats in parliament, and in Prime Minister Nawaf Salam's government, formed in February 2025, its picks run the health and labour ministries; with its ally Amal it controls six portfolios. In August 2025 the cabinet approved the aim that only the state hold weapons, and Hezbollah- and Amal-aligned ministers walked out. The army presented a disarmament plan in September with no timeline; Hezbollah's leader Naim Qassem rejects disarmament. The US sanctioned two sitting Hezbollah MPs in 2019; one, Muhammad Raad, is now its deputy secretary-general. In January 2026 the US also listed Lebanon's Muslim Brotherhood branch, the party al-Jamaa al-Islamiya, as terrorist.

The banks are the second story. A 2016 study by economist Jad Chaaban found that 18 of the 20 main commercial banks had major shareholders linked to political elites, about 43% of the sector's assets. They lent heavily to the state and to the central bank under Governor Riad Salameh, whose system collapsed in 2019 and froze people's savings. Salameh was detained in September 2024 and charged with embezzling $42 million.

Drug money has moved through the same system. US authorities found the Lebanese Canadian Bank carried cocaine proceeds through used-car sales; its successor forfeited $102 million in 2013 and no banker was prosecuted. The related Joumaa network and the Abou Merhi shipping group were sanctioned; Treasury says the Joumaa ring benefits Hezbollah. In February 2026 a military court gave the captagon trafficker Nouh Zeaiter four months, after twice sentencing him heavily in his absence.

Foreign governments reach in as well: in 2017 Prime Minister Saad Hariri announced his resignation from Saudi Arabia, and Lebanon's president said the Saudis were holding him. Saudi Arabia denied it, and Hariri withdrew the resignation.

Lebanon sits in the patterns on Iran's armed allies inside governments, banks and banking families, criminal money inside banks, and organised crime inside the state.
Lebanon.imp: For people in Lebanon, the banks that held their savings were largely owned by the same political class that borrowed from them, and when the system collapsed in 2019 depositors lost access to their money. An armed party also sits in the cabinet while the state tries to take its weapons away. Watch the Salameh case, whether the army's disarmament plan gets a timeline, and whether any banker or official is ever tried over the drug money that passed through Lebanese banks.

Malaysia.d:
Malaysia's biggest case is the 1MDB affair, and it is still in the courts. 1MDB was a state investment fund. Goldman Sachs bankers Tim Leissner and Roger Ng arranged its bond deals with the financier Jho Low, and US authorities say money was diverted and used to bribe officials in Malaysia and the UAE. Goldman settled with Malaysia in July 2020 for about $3.9 billion; Leissner pleaded guilty and Ng was convicted in New York in 2022. On 26 December 2025 Malaysia's High Court found former prime minister Najib Razak guilty on all 25 counts tied to over $1 billion in his personal accounts and sentenced him to 15 years. He is appealing.

Drug money reaches the police. Malaysia sits on the export route from the Golden Triangle drug-producing region and hosts the busiest transhipment port in the region. Its anti-corruption commission has prosecuted narcotics officers for releasing suspects and reselling seized drugs, mostly in Johor and the Klang valley.

An older case involves Turkey. In May 2017 Malaysian police arrested three Turkish men under a security law allowing 28 days' detention without trial and deported them on 11 May. Turkey accused them of links to the Gülen movement, a religious network Ankara calls 'FETÖ'; Human Rights Watch condemned the deportations.

Opus Dei, Airbus, Russia's GRU military intelligence, and the World Hongmen association of Wan Kuok-koi, a former triad leader, are also recorded as present. Malaysia sits in the patterns on global firms buying governments, organised crime inside the state and Turkey's campaign against the Gülen movement.
Malaysia.imp: For Malaysians, 1MDB is about money from a public fund ending up in a prime minister's accounts, with a global bank arranging the deals. The verdict came years after the US cases. Watch Najib's appeal and what happens to the money recovered from Goldman. The police cases show that drugs seized by officers can be sold again by the same officers, so convictions of officers matter as much as the size of seizures.

Maldives.d: Nothing is documented for the Maldives on this map yet, so what follows is an estimate. No secret society, religious movement, crime group, foreign government or company is recorded here, not even as likely. The conditions scores sit near the middle: a moderate share of power held by people embedded in the state (5.5 of 10) and below-average resilience (4.0), meaning the institutions that could expose capture are not strong. As a best guess, the most likely route in would be money from foreign governments or companies seeking favours from officials over contracts and leases, as the map records in other small states. That is a guess, not a finding.
Maldives.imp: For people in the Maldives, an empty record means no case has yet been documented here, not that none exists. With weak checks on officials, large contracts and leases are the place to look. Watch who wins them, who is behind the companies involved, and whether courts and reporters are able to follow the money.

Mongolia.d:
Mongolia has one documented case, and in it the state stopped a removal rather than helping one. On 27 July 2018 Veysel Akcay, general manager of the Empathy Worldwide Educational Institution, which ran Turkish-Mongolian schools linked to the Gülen movement, was seized in Ulaanbaatar. The Gülen movement is a Turkish religious network that Turkey's government calls 'FETÖ' and pursues abroad. Mongolian authorities temporarily grounded a plane at the airport, and Akcay was released the same day. Turkish Minute and the Stockholm Center for Freedom reported that Turkey's MIT intelligence service carried out the abduction; Mongolian authorities said they had no specific knowledge of one and were investigating. The map marks the case as only possible.

Chinese police 'overseas service stations', offices that Chinese police run abroad, are also recorded as present, and the Unification Church as likely. The conditions scores are middling (state-embedded actors 5.5 of 10, resilience 5.3). Mongolia sits in the pattern on Turkey's campaign against the Gülen movement.
Mongolia.imp: For people in Mongolia, the case shows a foreign intelligence service may have tried to take someone off their streets, and that their own aviation and security officials stopped the flight. Watch whether the investigation the authorities announced ever reports, and whether the Chinese police offices recorded here come under any official review.

Myanmar.d:
Myanmar has been run by a military government since 2021, and much of this record shows that government sharing the state with armed groups and crime networks. Colonel Saw Chit Thu commanded the Karen Border Guard Force, a militia placed under the army. From 2017 he partnered with She Zhijiang's Yatai group to build Shwe Kokko, and dealt with the Dongmei group of Wan Kuok-koi, a former 14K triad leader, over Saixigang. The junta gave him one of its highest honours in 2022; the UK sanctioned him in December 2023 and the US later did the same, over forced labour in scam centres. In Shan State, armed groups made into official border guard forces operate where the largest volumes of methamphetamine are produced; that link is marked only possible.

In the Kokang zone, Bai Suocheng, its first leader and a Shan State MP for the army-backed USDP, ran scam and gambling centres with his family. Myanmar handed him to China in 2024, and a Shenzhen court sentenced him and his son to death in November 2025. He died in custody; four Bai group members were executed in February 2026.

Religion is the second thread. Ma Ba Tha, a Buddhist nationalist monks' group formed in 2014, saw texts proposed by its members become four race and religion laws in 2015, covering religious conversion and marriage between Buddhist women and non-Buddhist men. After the coup the junta dropped sedition charges against the monk Wirathu, a leading Ma Ba Tha figure known for anti-Muslim sermons, and gave him a top honour in 2022. The junta's current spokesman donated to Ma Ba Tha's banned successor in 2019.

Myanmar is one of three countries, with Iran and North Korea, on the FATF blacklist of the global anti-money-laundering body. The older background is the Hong Pang Group, the business arm of the United Wa State Army, sanctioned by the US in 2005 and 2008.

Myanmar sits in the patterns on organised crime inside the state, religious nationalism in power and criminal money inside banks and firms.
Myanmar.imp: For people in Myanmar, armed groups the army has made part of the state run scam compounds and drug production in border areas, and those forced to work there have no court of their own to turn to. Laws drafted from monks' texts govern whom Buddhist women may marry. Action against the bosses has come from China and from foreign sanctions, not from Myanmar's courts. Watch who replaces the Kokang and Karen bosses, and whether the scam compounds simply move.

Nepal.d:
Nepal has one case on the map, marked only as possible, and it concerns China's ruling party. In 2020 the governing Nepal Communist Party was split by a revolt against Prime Minister KP Sharma Oli. In May and July, Chinese ambassador Hou Yanqi met Oli, President Bidya Bhandari and senior leaders Madhav Kumar Nepal and Jhala Nath Khanal, reportedly urging them to stay united. Former ministers and diplomats criticised the meetings as interference. In December 2020 China sent a delegation led by Guo Yezhou of the Chinese Communist Party's International Department, which handles its ties with foreign parties. The embassy said it only wished to see the party united.

The Unification Church and the RSS, an Indian Hindu nationalist volunteer organisation, are recorded as present, and the Atlas Network, which links free-market think tanks, as likely. Conditions are weak: many state-embedded actors (8 of 10) and low resilience (3.9).
Nepal.imp: For Nepalis, the question is whether decisions about who leads their government are shaped by a neighbouring power's diplomats in private meetings. Meetings like these leave little record beyond press reports. Watch for foreign envoys taking sides in party disputes, and for Indian as well as Chinese organisations building ties with Nepal's parties.

Oman.d: Nothing is documented for Oman on this map yet, so what follows is an estimate. Two outside bodies are recorded as likely but unproven: BCCI, the Bank of Credit and Commerce International, which US prosecutors said secretly and illegally took over a Washington bank, and Le Cercle, a private, invitation-only political discussion club. The conditions scores sit near the middle: a moderate share of state-embedded actors (4.5 of 10) and average resilience (5.3). As a best guess, the most likely route in would be private banking ties and personal contacts between ruling circles and foreign figures, the kind of channel those two bodies represent. That is a guess, not a finding.
Oman.imp: For people in Oman, no case means none has been documented, not that none exists. Private banking ties and personal contacts with foreign figures are hard for the public to see in any country. Watch whether information about state finances, foreign advisers and the owners of companies that win state business becomes more open.

Pakistan.d:
Pakistan's record mixes several kinds of outside reach, many of them disputed. The one still in force concerns Turkey: on 28 December 2018 the Supreme Court ordered the government to ban the Gülen movement, a Turkish religious network Ankara calls 'FETÖ', and to hand the Pak-Turk schools it ran to Turkey's state Maarif Foundation, saying Pakistan was bound by an Organisation of Islamic Cooperation declaration.

On money and lending: in May 2019, while Pakistan was negotiating an IMF bailout, Reza Baqir, an IMF staff member, was appointed governor of the State Bank of Pakistan a day after his predecessor was removed; he served until 2022. The map marks any influence through this appointment as only possible. The Karachi-based Khanani group of exchange houses laundered money for drug organisations, designated terrorist groups and Chinese and Colombian networks; its head pleaded guilty in the US in 2016.

In politics: families who hold hereditary custody of Sufi shrines draw income and votes from devotees. One of them, Shah Mahmood Qureshi, custodian of the Bahauddin Zakariya shrine in Multan, was foreign minister twice. Uzair Baloch led the Lyari gang the Peoples' Aman Committee, aligned with the Pakistan Peoples Party that governs Sindh; a military court gave him 12 years for espionage in 2020, and claims that party leaders protected him are disputed. Drug law has also been turned on politicians: Rana Sanaullah, a provincial minister, was charged in 2019 with carrying 15 kilograms of heroin and acquitted in 2022.

The oldest case is from inside the army. In 2012 a military court convicted Brigadier Ali Khan and four majors of links to Hizb ut-Tahrir, a banned group seeking a caliphate, which the army said had tried to recruit officers for a coup.

Pakistan sits in the patterns on organised crime inside the state, Turkey's campaign against the Gülen movement, movements that sought the state itself, and courts reversing a finding.
Pakistan.imp: For Pakistanis, these cases touch the central bank, the army, the courts and the parties, but many are unresolved or disputed. Shrine families turn religious devotion into votes, and a gang's ties to a governing party are claimed but contested. Drug charges have been used against a politician as well as against traffickers. Watch who is appointed to run the State Bank during IMF talks, and whether courts test the claims that gang leaders were protected.

Philippines.d:
Two things lead the Philippine record now: a church that votes as a bloc, and an online gambling industry that reached into town halls before it was banned.

The Iglesia ni Cristo (INC), a Philippine church of about 2.6 million members by the 2015 census, tells its members how to vote and calls it the 'Unity Vote'. It backed Benigno Aquino III in 2010, Rodrigo Duterte in 2016, and in 2022 Ferdinand Marcos Jr., Sara Duterte and 12 Senate candidates. Duterte made its head, Eduardo Manalo, a presidential special envoy in 2018. On 30 June 2026 the church rallied about 12,000 people on EDSA, Manila's main avenue, for Senator Rodante Marcoleta, a member elected with its support who was set to be charged over 75 million pesos in undeclared campaign money. Other preachers reached high office too: Eddie Villanueva of the Jesus Is Lord Church was a deputy speaker, and Apollo Quiboloy, whom Duterte called his spiritual adviser, was arrested in 2024 on child-abuse and trafficking charges and is indicted in the US.

POGOs were Chinese-run online gambling firms licensed from 2016 to serve players in China; Senate hearings in 2024 tied many to fraud, trafficking and torture. Alice Guo, mayor of Bamban, was found to be a Chinese citizen and in November 2025 was sentenced to life for trafficking. A court issued an arrest warrant in 2025 for Harry Roque, Duterte's former spokesman, over another hub; he denies it and has sought asylum in the Netherlands. The industry was banned by executive order in 2024 and by law in October 2025.

The drug war is the third thread. Between 6,000 and more than 30,000 people were killed in anti-drug operations from 2016; the ICC opened an investigation in 2021, and the former president was surrendered to it in 2025. A senator who had investigated the killings was held for almost seven years on drug charges that all failed.

Companies reached in as well. Pharmally, a firm with ₱625,000 in capital, won ₱8.68 billion in pandemic contracts, and graft charges followed against officials. State Grid Corporation of China owns 40% of the national grid operator, which senators questioned in 2019.

The Philippines sits in the patterns on churches in the state, scam compounds and casino money, industries inside their regulators and organised crime.
