Philippines.imp: For Filipinos, a church's bloc vote can help decide Senate seats, and it brings crowds to the streets when one of its members faces charges. The POGO cases show foreign-run businesses got local officials, even a mayor, on their side before the state acted. The drug war killed thousands while the trade went on. Watch the Marcoleta case, the ICC proceedings, the Roque warrant, and whether the banned gambling operations come back under another name.

Qatar.d:
Qatar appears on this map as a target, and both cases point to the United Arab Emirates. In late May 2017 Qatar's state news agency and government social media were hacked and carried false quotes from Emir Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani praising Hamas and calling Iran an 'Islamic power'. On 5 June Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Egypt and Bahrain cut ties with Qatar. In July the Washington Post, citing US intelligence officials, reported that senior UAE officials discussed the hacks the day before they happened; the officials could not say whether the UAE did the hacking or paid for it, and the UAE called the report false.

Separately, Reuters reported in 2019 that Project Raven, a UAE surveillance unit run through the firm DarkMatter and staffed partly by former US intelligence operatives, targeted the emir himself, among others, using an iPhone exploit called Karma. In 2021 three of those former operatives signed deferred-prosecution agreements with the US Justice Department and paid $1.68 million. No court has made a finding against the UAE government.

Gulf-state and private networks funding Salafi preaching, and the group Fight Impunity, are recorded as present; the Muslim Brotherhood and Interpol as likely. Qatar sits in the pattern on governments reaching into other countries.
Qatar.imp: For people in Qatar, these cases show how a neighbouring government's agents could put false words in their ruler's mouth and spy on his phone, and how the hack set off a blockade of the country. Most of what is known comes from journalists and US officials, not courts. Watch for further court cases involving surveillance firms and for new disclosures about who is hacking Gulf governments.

Saudi Arabia.d:
Saudi Arabia appears on this map mostly as a state that reaches into others and into its own companies, rather than one that is reached into. From 4 November 2017 an anti-corruption committee under Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman held princes and business leaders at the Ritz-Carlton hotel in Riyadh, including the chairmen of Saudi Binladin Group and MBC. The government said settlements with 87 people recovered about US$107 billion in property, companies, cash and other assets; 381 people were ordered detained, and some later said they had been beaten and intimidated.

Today the kingdom is the destination market for captagon pills smuggled from Syria and Lebanon. It executed 330 people in 2024, a large share for drug offences and many of them foreign couriers; no Saudi official appears in any adjudicated drug case on the map. Since March 2014 it has listed the Muslim Brotherhood as a terrorist group. It also reaches abroad: in 2017 Lebanon's prime minister announced his resignation from Riyadh, and the map records the kingdom as a state that exports religion.

The roots are older. In 1974, after the Arab oil embargo, the two countries set up a Joint Commission co-chaired by the US Treasury Secretary and the Saudi finance minister. A 1979 report by the US General Accounting Office found it was funded almost entirely from a Saudi account held at the US Treasury and steered US goods and services to the kingdom. Kamal Adham, head of Saudi intelligence until 1979, signed the 1976 charter of the Safari Club, a pact of the intelligence chiefs of France, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Morocco and Iran. He was also a major shareholder in the bank BCCI and, under a US plea agreement, paid a $105 million fine over its secret takeover of a Washington bank.

Saudi Arabia sits in the patterns on governments inside companies, the anticommunist web, banks that carried hidden money, and lenders and trained technocrats.
Saudi Arabia.imp: For people in Saudi Arabia, the 2017 purge showed that the state can take businesses and assets from their owners through a committee rather than a court. The drug cases show the heaviest punishment falls on foreign couriers rather than anyone with power. Watch how the companies and assets taken in 2017 are used, how many people are executed for drug offences, and whether any official is ever charged in the captagon trade.

Singapore.d:
Singapore has strong institutions by this map's measure (resilience 7.8 of 10), and most of its record shows the state catching outside influence rather than being captured by it. Its Foreign Interference (Countermeasures) Act of 2021 lets the Home Affairs Ministry designate people at risk of being used by foreign actors, who must then disclose donations and foreign links. In February 2024 it named the first: Philip Chan Man Ping, a Hong Kong-born businessman, president of the Hong Kong Chamber of Commerce in Singapore and patron of two government-linked grassroots bodies, who had attended China's Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, a united front body, as an overseas delegate. In 2017 the ministry expelled Huang Jing, a US-citizen professor at the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy, calling him an agent of influence of a foreign country it did not name; he denied it.

Money is the second thread. Trident Trust and Asiaciti Trust, two of the largest offshore service providers in the 2021 Pandora Papers, administered structures for sanctioned and criminally implicated clients. Singapore's regulator fined Asiaciti for anti-money-laundering failures; neither firm has been charged over drug money. At street level, 32 men were convicted in 2025 for possessing or moving drug proceeds, facing prison and caning.

The largest case reached the US Navy from here. Leonard Francis ('Fat Leonard'), whose Singapore-based Glenn Defense Marine Asia supplied Navy ships in Asian ports, overbilled the Navy and bribed officers for years; a civilian Navy contracting officer in Singapore quashed an early inquiry. Twenty-two people pleaded guilty, and Francis was sentenced to 15 years in 2024.

Singapore sits in the patterns on China's long arm abroad and criminal money inside banks and firms.
Singapore.imp: For people in Singapore, the government now has a law to name people it believes foreign states are cultivating, and it has used it. That exposes influence, but it rests on ministry judgements rather than court findings. Offshore trust firms are where the ownership of money stops being traceable, and their regulatory fines contrast with prison for small-time launderers. Watch who is designated next and whether trust firms ever face charges.

Sri Lanka.d:
In September 2026 Sri Lanka's Supreme Court ruled that a 2019 presidential pardon of the monk Galagoda Aththe Gnanasara was arbitrary and invalid, and in October the Court of Appeal ordered him to serve the rest of his sentence. Gnanasara leads Bodu Bala Sena (BBS, 'Buddhist Power Force'), a Sinhala Buddhist nationalist monks' group founded in 2012 and accused of stirring anti-Muslim violence; at a 2013 rally he said followers 'must become an unofficial civilian police force against Muslim extremism'. His original six-year sentence was for contempt of court in 2018, during the case over the disappeared journalist Prageeth Eknaligoda. He was also jailed in 2024 and 2025 over statements about Islam. The petitions came from the Centre for Policy Alternatives and Sandhya Eknaligoda.

BBS's ties to power go back to the Rajapaksa family. In 2013 Defence Secretary Gotabaya Rajapaksa, the president's brother, opened the BBS training centre in Galle District as chief guest. After he became president himself, he appointed Gnanasara in October 2021 to chair a task force on 'One Country, One Law' to draft a single legal code. The justice minister said he had not been consulted, and the Bar Association said the task force would take over the work of Parliament and the Justice Ministry.

Two smaller cases. Ranil Wickremesinghe, prime minister several times and president from 2022 to 2024, is listed as a member of the Mont Pelerin Society, an international society of free-market thinkers; no forum has found that it directed his decisions. In 2019 the arrest in Dubai of a trafficking figure, Madush, produced photographs of him with police officers and politicians; he was killed in police custody in 2020 before the inquiry concluded.

Sri Lanka sits in the patterns on religious nationalism in power, private forums where officials meet money, and organised crime inside the state.
Sri Lanka.imp: For Sri Lankans, especially Muslims, the record shows a monk accused of stirring hatred being honoured and protected by those in power, and then the courts reversing that protection. The task force episode shows a movement leader given a role in writing law without Parliament. Watch whether the Supreme Court ruling limits future pardons, whether Gnanasara serves the sentence, and whether the death in custody in the Madush case is ever explained.

Syria.d:
Bashar al-Assad's government fell in December 2024, and Syria's record is now about what it left behind. On 11 August 2026 the Fourth Criminal Court in Damascus sentenced the deposed president and his brother Maher, who commanded the army's Fourth Armoured Division, to death in absentia for murder, torture and crimes against humanity. Both live in Russia, which refuses to extradite them, and Human Rights Watch questioned whether the trial was fair. The convictions are for war crimes, not drugs.

The drug is captagon, a pill trafficked to Jordan and the Gulf. In 2023 the US, UK and EU sanctioned three of Assad's cousins, Maher al-Assad and the manager of the Fourth Division's revenues, and the EU called the trade a regime-led business model. One Latakia factory run by a presidential cousin produced 84 million pills in 2020, according to the US Treasury. A sitting MP, Amer Khiti, was sanctioned over companies that made and moved the pills, and the EU named private security firms as cover for militias in the drug trade. These are government findings; no court has tried the trade. Since the fall, the interior ministry says domestic production has been virtually eradicated, and UNODC counted 15 industrial-scale labs dismantled. But Sweida province has become the main trafficking centre, with labs held by local armed factions, and 177 million pills were intercepted across the Arab region in the year to December 2025.

Foreign forces and companies reached in too. Iran's Revolutionary Guards Quds Force commanded alongside Assad's forces from 2012, with Hezbollah fighters, and was reported to hold 55 bases in 2023, until Iran evacuated its commanders in December 2024. The French cement maker Lafarge paid about $5.92 million to the Islamic State and al-Nusra Front in 2013–14 to keep its Jalabiya plant open; it pleaded guilty in the US in 2022, and a Paris court convicted it and former executives in April 2026.

Syria sits in the patterns on organised crime inside the state, criminal money inside banks and firms, and Iran's armed allies inside governments.
Syria.imp: For Syrians, the old state ran a drug trade through its own army division and members of the ruling family, and those named have fled or face sentences passed in their absence. The trade has not ended; it has broken up among smaller armed groups in places like Sweida that are harder to police. Foreign powers held bases on Syrian soil for more than a decade. Watch whether the new authorities keep production down without new protectors taking over, and whether any trial ever tests the captagon accusations.

Taiwan.d:
Taiwan's courts are now working through a run of cases about the Chinese state reaching into the island's politics. The biggest is still open: on 30 July 2026 the Interior Ministry said it would ask the Constitutional Court to dissolve the Chinese Unification Promotion Party, a registered party founded in 2005 by Chang An-lo, the 'White Wolf', a former leader of the Bamboo Union triad (a criminal gang). The ministry cites work with China on espionage and election interference, attacks on Hong Kong activists, and use of the party as cover for organised crime. Police count 98 crime cases linked to party members since 2010, and 15 temples they say were infiltrated. The court has not ruled.

Some background. China's united front system works to win over or recruit people abroad, including in Taiwan, for the Communist Party, and Taiwan's Anti-Infiltration Act makes taking its money and direction a crime. Several cases have ended in convictions, all open to appeal: Gong He Party chairman Chou Ke-chi got two years in June 2025 for campaigns paid for from Fujian; Lin Hsueh-feng, a former KMT council candidate, got four years for taking village chiefs on trips paid by a Chinese city office; in September 2025 four former DPP aides, including an assistant to the foreign minister and a Presidential Office consultant, were jailed for spying for China's military intelligence; and in September 2026 a retired cabinet official, Hu Peng-nien, got five years. A former lawmaker, Chang Hsien-yao, and two people in a 2022 New Taipei council campaign are charged but not tried, and deny it. The cases touch several parties.

Companies are reached too. In April 2026 a court jailed former TSMC engineers, the main defendant for 10 years, for passing 2-nanometre chip secrets to help Tokyo Electron, and fined its Taiwan unit. The pagers that exploded across Lebanon in 2024, killing 42 people, carried the brand of Taiwan's Gold Apollo, licensed to a Budapest firm the New York Times reported was a Mossad front; Israel's prime minister acknowledged the operation.

Taiwan is a target country in 'China's long arm abroad', and the Cold War-era World Anti-Communist League was based here.
Taiwan.imp: Most of the money and instructions from Beijing found so far land at the local level: small parties, council candidates, village chiefs, and staff working near the president and foreign minister. A voter cannot tell who paid for a trip or a campaign unless prosecutors dig it out. Courts are now testing these cases one by one, and most rulings can still be appealed. Things to watch: the Constitutional Court's decision on the Chinese Unification Promotion Party, and how well the chip secrets much of Taiwan's economy depends on are protected.

Tajikistan.d:
Tajikistan lies on the route that carries Afghan heroin north into Central Asia, and most of what this map records here is that trade reaching into the state. Estimates from 2014 put drug money at up to 30 percent of the country's economy.

The cases reach high. In 2000 Tajikistan's ambassador to Kazakhstan was arrested in Almaty with 86 kilograms of heroin in his car. The next year the deputy interior minister was murdered, and prosecutors argued at trial that he was killed for refusing to pay for a 50-kilogram consignment; this is an allegation made in court, not a proven link. In November 2012 a military court in Khatlon province jailed five Border Guard officers for between three and 21 years, the longest for the former chief of the Vakhsh checkpoint on the Afghan border, where 20 kilograms of hashish were found in his office. A senior Khatlon police official was arrested the same day with 12 kilograms of heroin. Roughly 90 tonnes of heroin cross Central Asia each year, and most arrests are of small dealers, so the record stops at this rank.

The other case is about a religious movement. The Gülen movement, a Turkish Islamic network that ran schools abroad and that Turkey's government now treats as a terrorist group, had seven schools here. In May 2015 President Emomali Rahmon closed them by decree and handed them to the state as schools for gifted children.

Tajikistan belongs to the patterns 'Organised crime inside the state' and 'Turkey's long arm: chasing the Gülen movement'. The conditions scores are poor: very high for state-embedded criminal actors (9 of 10) and low for the ability to resist (2.5).
Tajikistan.imp: For people in Tajikistan, the main finding is that drug money has reached border guards, police and diplomats, and that convictions mostly stop below the top. With a large share of the economy possibly tied to the trade, it is hard to know which officials answer to it. The schools case shows the government closing an outside movement by a single decree. Watch who is prosecuted at border posts and in Khatlon, and whether any case ever reaches above the rank of checkpoint chief.

Thailand.d:
In Thailand the cases still open concern crime money reaching lawmakers and the police. In 2023 a sitting senator, Upakit Pachariyangkun, was indicted on drug trafficking and money-laundering charges tied to a Myanmar businessman arrested in Bangkok in 2022 and sanctioned by the US for supporting Myanmar's military government. His Thai-American son-in-law was among those arrested, and the narcotics board seized property worth over 400 million baht from his homes. The same year the deputy national police chief was removed and investigated over an alleged protection arrangement with an online gambling network; the case split the police leadership in public. Both are charged, not convicted.

The most serious case is older. AlphaBay, a dark-web drug market ten times the size of Silk Road at its peak, was shut down in a joint US and European operation in July 2017. Its administrator was arrested in Bangkok and died in custody a week later, which ended the prosecution before the evidence was tested in court.

One case concerns an elite network rather than crime. The World Economic Forum, the Davos forum, picks people under about 40 for its Young Global Leaders programme. Its class of 2025 included Paetongtarn Shinawatra while she was Thailand's prime minister. Being chosen is not wrongdoing, and the record shows no influence on her decisions. The Constitutional Court removed her from office in August 2025.

Thailand appears in 'Organised crime inside the state', 'Criminal money inside banks and firms' and 'Private forums where officials meet money'. State-embedded criminal actors score 7 of 10.
Thailand.imp: For people in Thailand, the record shows trafficking and gambling money reaching into the upper house and the top of the police, the bodies meant to write the laws and enforce them. Neither case has reached a verdict yet, so the facts are still to be tested in court. Watch the outcome of the senator's trial and the police case, and whether the property seizures hold. The AlphaBay case is a reminder that when a key suspect dies in custody, the public never hears the evidence.

Timor-Leste.d:
Timor-Leste is still living with a deal shaped by spying. In 2004 the Australian Secret Intelligence Service (ASIS), Australia's foreign spy agency, placed listening devices in the government building in Dili, near the cabinet room, to learn Timor-Leste's position in talks over the oil and gas fields of the Timor Sea. For a young and poor country, those fields were its main source of future income. The talks produced the 2006 CMATS treaty, which limited Timor-Leste's claims at sea.

A former ASIS officer, known only as 'Witness K', brought it to light. In 2013 Australia raided him and Timor-Leste's lawyer, Bernard Collaery. Timor-Leste took Australia to the International Court of Justice, which in 2014 ordered Australia not to interfere with Timor-Leste's legal communications, and to the Permanent Court of Arbitration. A new boundary treaty in 2018 replaced CMATS and split revenue 80–20 in Timor-Leste's favour. Australia prosecuted the two men who exposed the operation: Witness K pleaded guilty in 2021 to a secrecy offence, and the case against Collaery was dropped in 2022.

This map has two records of the same events, both rated established. Timor-Leste is the target of a foreign government reaching into its cabinet; its overall score is low because this is the one documented case.
Timor-Leste.imp: For people in Timor-Leste, this case shows how a stronger neighbour used its spy service to gain an edge over the country's main natural wealth. Going to international courts and talks won a fairer deal in 2018. The people punished in Australia were the ones who revealed the bugging, not those who ordered it. When the government negotiates over oil, gas or borders, it is worth asking how its own discussions are protected.

Turkiye.d:
In Türkiye the state itself is the main actor on this map, along with groups tied to people in power. Today a state trustee fund, the TMSF, controls more than a thousand businesses. After a 2013 corruption probe and the July 2016 coup attempt, which the government blames on the Gülen movement (an Islamic network it now calls the terrorist group 'FETÖ'), it seized 784 companies said to be Gülen-linked, worth TL 42.3 billion, including Bank Asya and Koza İpek. More than 600 were later returned. By October 2025 the fund held 1,056 businesses in all.

The purge reached every branch of the state. In 2013 prosecutors opened a corruption case reaching Prime Minister Erdoğan's circle; the government called it a Gülenist plot, sacked the prosecutors and dropped the case. The day after the 2016 coup attempt, 2,745 judges were removed. About 15,000 military personnel and roughly 23,000 police were dismissed, and some 150,000 public employees in all. Courts gave life terms to the coup's air force leaders, who deny the charges. Turkey also reached abroad: the state religious directorate, the Diyanet, had its imams in 38 countries report on Gülen followers, and Interpol refused 773 Turkish arrest requests as political.

Earlier prosecutions have been undone. The 2012 'Sledgehammer' coup-plot convictions of about 300 officers ended in 2015 acquittals after the evidence was found to be forged; the 2013 'Ergenekon' convictions were overturned in 2016 for lack of proof the network existed. The government now blames those prosecutions on Gülen-linked officials.

Organised crime runs underneath. The 1996 Susurluk car crash put a police chief, an MP and a wanted Grey Wolves gunman (the Grey Wolves are the youth wing of the nationalist MHP party) in one car; parliament found state bodies had used the group. Crime boss Alaattin Çakıcı was freed in 2020 under a law passed with the MHP. A rival boss's 2021 accusations against a former interior minister were never tested. Chemicals for heroin are diverted through Türkiye.

The roots go back to the Cold War: a NATO 'Counter-Guerrilla' inside the army, and the MHP leader as deputy prime minister in the 1970s.
Turkiye.imp: For people in Türkiye, the line between catching infiltrators and purging opponents has been hard to see. Courts have both convicted and later cleared the same kinds of people, and huge numbers lost jobs by decree rather than by trial. A state fund now owns over a thousand businesses, which gives the government direct power over jobs and media. Watch what happens to those companies, how trials of alleged Gülenists proceed, and whether ties between nationalist politics and organised crime ever reach a courtroom.

Turkmenistan.d:
Turkmenistan's one documented case is about how the government dealt with the Gülen movement, a Turkish Islamic network that opened schools across Central Asia in the 1990s and that Turkey's government now treats as a terrorist group. The effects are still felt: men convicted in that crackdown were given long sentences.

The schools came first. In 2011 Turkmenistan closed or took over most of the Gülen-linked schools. Then, in late 2016, the year of the failed coup attempt in Turkey, more than 100 people were detained, most with some Gülen link. Eighteen men were convicted in closed trials and given 12 to 25 years for inciting hatred and taking part in a criminal organisation. These facts come from a joint 2017 statement by Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International and the Norwegian Helsinki Committee, and are rated established. Because the trials were closed, the public cannot see what evidence was used.

Turkmenistan belongs to 'Turkey's long arm: chasing the Gülen movement' and 'Churches and movements placing members in the state'. Its conditions scores are among the weakest: state-embedded actors score 9 of 10 and the ability to resist only 2.2.
Turkmenistan.imp: For people in Turkmenistan, the case shows how a movement once allowed to run schools can be turned into a criminal matter almost overnight, with trials held out of public view. People with a past link to a school or group can face decades in prison. Since the courts are closed, outside rights groups are the main source of what is known. Watch for further arrests tied to foreign religious or educational groups, and whether any of the eighteen are released.

United Arab Emirates.d:
The United Arab Emirates appears on this map mostly as a place where money moves and as a government reaching into international bodies. From November 2021 to November 2025 a senior UAE interior ministry officer, Ahmed Naser Al-Raisi, was president of Interpol, the global police cooperation body. Before his election the UAE gave Interpol's foundation donations reported at about $54 million, roughly what the other 194 members pay in their regular dues combined; critics say this helped him win, and Interpol rejects that. Britons Matthew Hedges and Ali Issa Ahmad accuse him of responsibility for their torture in UAE custody, and French anti-terror prosecutors opened a preliminary inquiry in 2022. He and the UAE deny it.

Dubai is where money from several crime networks on this map is settled. US Treasury actions have named exchange houses and trading companies here moving drug money. Free-zone companies can hide who owns them, and that was central to the UAE's place on the FATF 'grey list' of weak anti-laundering countries from 2022 to 2024. A US drug agency case found that a large gold refiner, Kaloti, bought metal from suspected launderers, often for cash; Treasury dropped the case, and the company denies it. In February 2025 North Korean hackers stole about $1.5 billion from Dubai crypto exchange Bybit through a software supplier.

Industry reached a climate summit: in 2023 leaked papers showed that the COP28 president, who also ran the state oil firm ADNOC, had talking points on company deals for meetings with governments. He called the claims false.

The government has also pushed outsiders out. In 2013 a court jailed 56 members of Islah, a group the state ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, for plotting to seize power, and in 2014 the cabinet listed both as terrorist. The background is BCCI, a bank that collapsed in fraud in 1991 when Abu Dhabi's government owned 77% of it; a US Senate report found Abu Dhabi hid what it knew from the auditors.
United Arab Emirates.imp: For people in the UAE, the record shows a state that has bought influence in global bodies and a financial system that criminals elsewhere have used to park money. Ownership of many companies is hidden from the public. The government has meanwhile treated domestic Islamist groups as threats and jailed their members. Watch whether the French torture inquiry goes further, how open company ownership becomes after the grey listing ended, and how the gold and crypto trades are supervised.

Uzbekistan.d:
Uzbekistan's record on this map is about foreign telecom companies buying their way into the country through the president's family. Gulnara Karimova, elder daughter of the late president Islam Karimov, is in prison in Uzbekistan after convictions in 2017 and 2020. Switzerland dropped its own trial of her in 2026.

When mobile phones spread across Uzbekistan, firms needed licences and radio frequencies from the state to operate. Three foreign companies got them by paying firms Karimova controlled. Telia, the Swedish-Finnish telecom group, agreed in September 2017 to pay about $965 million to US, Dutch and Swedish authorities. VimpelCom settled US bribery charges in 2016 for $795 million, and Russia's MTS in 2019 for $850 million. Uzbek prosecutors put her kickbacks at $869.3 million; the reporting group OCCRP said in 2015 she took over $1 billion from Scandinavian and Russian telecom firms. These are settled and convicted cases, rated established.

There are no patterns listed for Uzbekistan on this map. The conditions scores are weak: state-embedded criminal actors score 7 of 10 and the ability to resist only 3.8. Turkey's Gülen movement and its Grey Wolves are likely present, along with Hizb ut-Tahrir, an Islamist group that seeks a single Islamic state, but no case is documented for them.
Uzbekistan.imp: For people in Uzbekistan, this case shows how access to a whole market was sold through one family at the top, and how the money was traced only because foreign prosecutors in the US and Europe acted. Mobile customers ended up paying companies that had paid a bribe to get in. Watch whether licences in other sectors, such as energy or mining, go through the same kind of family-linked firms, and whether the money tied to these cases is returned to the country.

Vietnam.d:
In Vietnam the cases on this map run in two directions: drug networks reaching police, and the state naming an exile party as a threat.

Drug squads have been caught protecting traffickers. Two former officers of a Hanoi district drug team were indicted in 2024 for shielding a Laos–Vietnam network that moved 137 kilograms. In 2025 a court sentenced a senior officer in Viet Tri, Phu Tho province, to life for paying for 12,000 drug tablets that he meant to use in a staged arrest. Vietnam executes traffickers caught with these amounts, which shows how much the officers were covering.

The second case is disputed. Viet Tan is a pro-democracy party founded by Vietnamese exiles in 1982 and based in the United States. On 4 October 2016 Vietnam's Ministry of Public Security labelled it a terrorist organisation, saying it trained people to enter Vietnam and plotted sabotage. Human rights groups and foreign governments reject this, and the US government has said there is no evidence it is a terrorist group. Vietnamese courts have jailed people accused of membership, and the label stays in force.

Vietnam belongs to the patterns 'Organised crime inside the state' and 'Exposure, purge and reversal'. State-embedded criminal actors score 7 of 10.
Vietnam.imp: For people in Vietnam, the drug cases show that the officers meant to stop trafficking can end up protecting it, even under some of the harshest drug laws anywhere. The Viet Tan designation means joining or supporting an exile party can bring a prison term, though outside governments see no evidence it is a terrorist group. Watch whether drug-corruption cases reach above district level, and how the terrorism label is used against people in court.

Yemen.d:
Yemen's government is a coalition at war, and one foreign government built a group inside it. The Southern Transitional Council (STC) was formed in May 2017 with help from the United Arab Emirates to seek a separate state in the south. In April 2022 it joined Yemen's eight-member Presidential Leadership Council, the body that heads the internationally recognised government, and its leader Aidarous al-Zubaidi became a vice-president.

That arrangement has now broken down. After an STC offensive in December 2025 and a Saudi-backed counter-offensive, al-Zubaidi fled to the UAE in January 2026 and was removed from the council. A delegation in Riyadh announced the STC was dissolved; its spokesman, based in the UAE, rejected that. The case is rated probable and still unfolding.

Many other outside forces are present in Yemen, including the Muslim Brotherhood, Hezbollah, and the network of Iran's Revolutionary Guards Quds Force and allied militias, but this map documents only the UAE case so far. Conditions are severe: state-embedded criminal actors score 8 of 10 and the ability to resist only 1.9. Yemen is a target country in 'Governments buying officials in other countries'.
Yemen.imp: For people in Yemen, the top of their own government has included a leader whose movement was created with a foreign power's help, while another foreign power backed the other side. Decisions about the south have been shaped in Abu Dhabi and Riyadh as much as at home. Watch who replaces al-Zubaidi on the leadership council, whether the STC is really dissolved, and which foreign capitals the remaining members answer to.

Australia.d:
Australia's most serious live case is a port. In 2015 the Northern Territory leased the Port of Darwin, near a base used by US Marines, for 99 years to Landbridge, a Shandong company whose owner Ye Cheng has close ties to the Chinese Communist Party. A 2021 review found no security grounds to cancel; in 2025 both main parties pledged to take it back, and in May 2026 Landbridge began arbitration to stop a forced sale. The concern is suspected, not proven.

Crime is inside institutions now. Courts have convicted Border Force and police officers of helping drug imports through Sydney and Melbourne. In 2024 the government put the construction arm of the CFMEU union into administration after reports that bikie gang members held roles on state-funded projects. An alleged administrator of the Ghost encrypted-phone network was arrested in Sydney. Casino group The Star was found unfit for its Sydney licence after extending credit to patrons with reported crime links.

Foreign states have reached into politics. Senator Sam Dastyari resigned in 2017 over links to donor Huang Xiangmo, who chaired a council described as a peak body for United Front groups (the Chinese Communist Party's influence arm). Huang's residency was cancelled on ASIO advice in 2019, and an anti-corruption inquiry found $100,000 in disguised cash from him reached NSW Labor. Di Sanh Duong became the first person convicted under the 2018 foreign interference law. India's spy agency RAW had two officers expelled in 2020 after a 'nest of spies' cultivated politicians and police.

Companies and banks fill out the record: a PwC partner shared confidential Treasury tax plans with 53 colleagues; Commonwealth Bank and Westpac paid record penalties over money-laundering reporting failures; Crown Resorts was found unsuitable over junket links. Philip Morris's challenge to plain cigarette packs was thrown out in 2015. Atlas Network think-tank staff such as Tim Wilson moved into office.

The background includes the Nugan Hand Bank, which collapsed in Sydney in 1980, and a Round Table group from 1910. Australia is a target of China's long arm and a proven case of criminal money in banks.
Australia.imp: For Australians, the main question now is who controls infrastructure, unions and the people at the border. A port lease, a union on public building sites and corrupt border officers each give outside interests a hand in public decisions or public money. Foreign governments have used donors and community leaders to reach ministers. The country has tools that work: ASIO advice, anti-corruption commissions, the 2018 interference law and large penalties for banks. Watch the Darwin arbitration and the CFMEU inquiries.

Fiji.d: Fiji keeps a police cooperation agreement with China, though it has asked China's embedded officers to leave. Under a pact signed in 2011, during military rule, China's Ministry of Public Security, its national police ministry, placed two officers at a time inside the Fiji Police Force from 2013, and posted a police liaison officer to its embassy in 2021. In 2017 Chinese police working with local officials arrested 77 Chinese nationals in Fiji and flew them to China. In March 2024 Home Affairs Minister Pio Tikoduadua said Fiji had asked China to withdraw the embedded officers but would keep the agreement, reviewing it every six months. Fijian officers still train in China. The record is established from the minister's own statement. Fiji also has a documented presence of Shincheonji, a South Korean church. On the map it is a target country in the pattern of China's long arm abroad, with the reach now mostly through training and the standing agreement rather than officers inside the force.
Fiji.imp: The police are who people in Fiji call for help, so it matters who trains them and who works alongside them. For several years, officers of another country's police ministry worked inside the force, and in 2017 dozens of people were taken from Fiji to China. The embedded officers are now gone, but the agreement remains and is reviewed every six months. Watch what those reviews decide and how much training continues in China.

Kiribati.d: Uniformed Chinese police officers work alongside the Kiribati Police Service. Kiribati, a Pacific island nation, switched its diplomatic recognition from Taiwan to China in 2019 and asked China for policing help in 2022. In 2024 the acting police commissioner, Eeri Aritiera, confirmed to Reuters that up to a dozen Chinese officers serve with local police on six-month rotations. They do community policing, teach martial arts and give IT support for a crime database. The arrangement is established: the police service confirmed it. It is not presented as wrongdoing; what it shows is a foreign state's police with a daily role in the national force and access to its records system. The Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic status, also has a documented presence. Kiribati sits in the pattern of China's long arm abroad as a target country, with low scores for criminal actors inside the state.
Kiribati.imp: People in Kiribati now meet foreign officers in ordinary policing, and those officers help run the database where crime records are kept. That gives another government a close view of local policing and possibly of the people in its files. Nothing in the record says this has been misused. Watch whether the arrangement grows, who can see the crime database, and whether its terms are made public.

Marshall Islands.d: The Marshall Islands' documented case ended in convictions, but it still shows how a small parliament can be bought. From about 2016 to 2020, Cary Yan and Gina Zhou, China-born businesspeople who had bought Marshallese passports, paid tens of thousands of dollars to officials, including legislators. They wanted a law creating a semi-autonomous 'Rongelap Atoll Special Administrative Region', a zone with its own rules. Both pleaded guilty in New York; Zhou was sentenced in February 2023 and Yan received 42 months in May 2023. In December 2023 the US State Department barred former president Kessai Note and MP Mike Halferty from entry for taking the bribes; Note denies it. The bribery is established by the guilty pleas; the claims against the two named politicians rest on a US designation, not a local trial. The Sovereign Military Order of Malta also has a documented presence. The case appears in the pattern of industries inside their regulators.
Marshall Islands.imp: A special zone would have taken an atoll partly out of the country's ordinary laws, and lawmakers were paid to push it. The scheme was stopped by US prosecutors, not by a court in the Marshall Islands. For residents, the lesson is that a few votes in a small parliament are cheap to buy. Watch for new proposals for special economic zones and who is behind them.

Micronesia.d: In Micronesia, the documented case is an accusation from the country's own president, and it is unproven. In March 2023 outgoing President David Panuelo of the Federated States of Micronesia sent a 13-page letter accusing China of 'political warfare'. He wrote of bribery and threats meant to keep Micronesia on Beijing's side, or neutral, in any war over Taiwan, and said he had considered switching recognition to Taiwan. China rejected the claims. The record marks this as possible: a head of state made the allegation in writing, but no court or inquiry has tested it, and the map has no named case of a payment. Organisations with documented presence include the Sovereign Military Order of Malta and PRC state proxies, bodies acting for the Chinese state where the United Front is not named. Micronesia is a target country in the pattern of China's long arm abroad.
Micronesia.imp: A sitting president said a foreign power was trying to bribe and pressure his officials. If true, decisions about war and alliances could be shaped by payments residents never see. Nothing has been proven. Watch whether later governments investigate the claims, and how officials explain gifts, trips or funds from foreign governments.

Nauru.d: Nauru's two cases both involve Australian money reaching Nauruan politicians, and both remain open. Australian federal prosecutors have charged Getax Australia, a Gold Coast phosphate trader, with conspiring to bribe Nauruan politicians from 2007 to 2012 to win phosphate deals; phosphate is Nauru's main mineral. The case has been delayed repeatedly. In a related case, Sydney businessman Mozammil Bhojani pleaded guilty to paying over $120,000 to a Nauruan MP and a minister, and was jailed in 2018. Separately, Australia pays contractors to run its offshore asylum centre on Nauru. A 2023 investigation by the Sydney Morning Herald and The Age found subcontracts worth millions went to firms tied to Nauru's leaders, including over $120,000 in suspect payments to justice minister David Adeang and about $2.6 million to a company of Lionel Aingimea, later president. The reporters said they were not claiming the payments were bribes; Adeang denies it. The Getax case is charged, the detention payments only reported.
Nauru.imp: Nauru depends on two outside sources of money: phosphate sales and Australia's asylum centre. Both cases suggest that money from those deals reached the people who decide them. Residents cannot easily see who is paid under these contracts. Watch the Getax trial, if it is ever held, and whether Australia publishes who its contractors pay on Nauru.

New Zealand.d:
New Zealand's current cases are about who sits in government and where crime money surfaces. David Seymour, Minister for Regulation since 2023 and Deputy Prime Minister since 2025, worked in the 2000s for Canadian think tanks including the Frontier Centre for Public Policy, a partner of the Atlas Network, a US-based network of free-market think tanks. Atlas's chair, Debbi Gibbs, is the daughter of a co-founder of his ACT party. These links are reported; no forum has found the network directs his decisions. SkyCity, the casino operator, agreed a NZ$4.16 million penalty in 2024 for failing to monitor high-value play.

On China, National MP Jian Yang, a former Communist Party member who taught at Chinese military institutions training intelligence linguists, left Parliament at the 2020 election. Reports in 2021 said intelligence agencies had raised concerns, and that Labour MP Raymond Huo left for the same reason. This is reported, not proven.

The background includes Ruth Richardson, Finance Minister from 1990, a member of the Mont Pelerin Society, a free-market society of economists; Jacinda Ardern, listed in the World Economic Forum's Young Global Leaders; and a Round Table group from 1910. Membership is documented, influence is not. New Zealand fits the patterns of private forums placing members in office and China's long arm abroad.
New Zealand.imp: For New Zealanders, the record mostly shows ministers who come from or join policy networks with clear views. That is legal and public, but voters may not see how those networks shape rules on regulation or the economy. The case of the two MPs shows that foreign-influence concerns can be settled quietly between party leaders rather than in public. Watch casino money controls and how ministers declare think-tank ties.

Palau.d: Palau's documented case involves a triad boss, a leader of a Chinese organised crime society, who tried to build a foothold in the country. Wan Kuok-koi, known as 'Broken Tooth', once headed Macau's 14K triad; the US sanctioned him in 2020, and the US Treasury says he sits on a body of the Chinese Communist Party's United Front, its influence arm. OCCRP, a journalists' network, reported in 2022 that he visited Palau in 2018 as a 'guest of the government'. A former postmaster general and a former Airai state governor became directors of his Palau Hongmen association, registered in early 2019 to plan a casino zone on Angaur island. President Tommy Remengesau opposed the casino in April 2019, and the association applied to dissolve. OCCRP did not establish that the Chinese state directed the effort. The case is rated probable. Palau sits in the pattern of organised crime inside the state, as a charged or probable case.
Palau.imp: A sanctioned crime boss was welcomed by officials and recruited former office holders to plan a casino zone. Casinos in small states can become channels for laundered money and political favours. In this case the president said no and the plan stopped. Residents should watch for new casino or special-zone proposals and ask who funds them and which former officials are involved.

Papua New Guinea.d:
In Papua New Guinea the police commissioner has said publicly that there are 'criminals in uniform' in the force. That came after a plane carrying 548 kilograms of cocaine crashed on a makeshift runway outside Port Moresby in 2020. The Australian-based organisers were convicted in Victoria and the pilot got 18 years in a PNG jail, but the officers alleged to have enabled the night flights were not charged. The case is probable, not proven.

The biggest finished case is a loan. In 2014 Prime Minister Peter O'Neill's government borrowed about US$1.2 billion through UBS, a Swiss bank, to buy shares in Oil Search, against cabinet advice and before parliament approved it. Treasurer Don Polye, who objected, lost his job. A Commission of Inquiry heard the state lost about $432 million while UBS earned about $83 million; its 2021 report found the loan unlawful and recommended a 10-year ban on UBS. O'Neill was later charged with giving false evidence to the inquiry.

A third claim concerns Paladin, paid A$530 million to run Australia's asylum centre on Manus Island. A former director said in 2023 that more than $3 million went to a businessman close to senior PNG officials; the company's former chief executive denies it. PNG's scores show high levels of criminal actors inside the state and low resilience.
Papua New Guinea.imp: For people in Papua New Guinea, the record shows public money lost on a loan pushed through without parliament, and police who may help traffickers rather than stop them. Both reduce what the state can spend on services and how safe people are. The inquiry worked, but its recommendations depend on follow-through. Watch whether officers tied to the drug flights are charged and whether the UBS ban is applied.

Samoa.d: Nothing is documented on the map for Samoa yet; this write-up is an estimate. The one organisation with recorded presence is Shincheonji, a South Korean church, and no case links it to government. Samoa's conditions scores are low to middling: criminal actors inside the state score low, and its capacity to resist sits around the middle. The best guess for a likely route in comes from its neighbours, where the record shows foreign police cooperation and money paid to members of parliament. That is a guess, not a finding.
Samoa.imp: No case of outside capture is recorded for Samoa. That may mean little is happening, or that little has been looked at. The closest warning signs come from neighbouring islands: foreign police placed in local forces and payments to lawmakers. Residents can watch for new policing agreements and for funds given to MPs from outside the country.

Solomon Islands.d:
The Solomon Islands now has a new prime minister promising to review its security deal with China. Matthew Wale, a critic of the relationship, took office in May 2026. Under a 2022 agreement, Honiara can ask China for police and military personnel. Chinese police advisers arrived in February 2022 after riots in Honiara the previous November, and in 2025 Chinese police began a local trial of the 'Fengqiao' model of community surveillance policing, suspended after local objections.

The roots go back to 2019, when Prime Minister Manasseh Sogavare ended 36 years of ties with Taiwan and recognised China. MPs told reporters that both Beijing and Taipei had offered them money to sway that vote; this is reported only. China then agreed to fund a discretionary fund run by the prime minister's office, as Taiwan had done. At a parliamentary hearing in 2022, the prime minister's secretary said China provided about US$2.49 million spent in 2021, and that 39 of 50 MPs received payments in late 2021, around the time Sogavare survived a no-confidence vote. Wale accused him of using the money to stay in power; Sogavare's office denied it. The payments themselves are acknowledged. The country is a target in the pattern of China's long arm abroad, with high scores for criminal actors inside the state.
Solomon Islands.imp: Most MPs in the Solomon Islands received money from a fund paid for by a foreign government, at a time when the prime minister's job was at stake. Residents cannot easily see what that money bought. Foreign police also have a role in local policing. Watch what the new government's review of the security agreement decides and whether the prime minister's fund is opened to public audit.

Tonga.d: Tonga's documented case is historical, but it cost the country a large share of its money. Before 1997, Tonga sold passports to Hong Kong residents and put the proceeds into the Tonga Trust Fund. Jesse Bogdonoff, an American financial adviser whom King Taufa'ahau Tupou IV named his court jester in 1999, moved the fund into a viatical investment firm, a business that buys people's life-insurance policies. The firm went bankrupt in 2002 and about $33 million was lost, around 40% of a year's state revenue. Tonga sued him, and in 2004 he settled without admitting fraud. The loss is established. The organisation recorded here is the citizenship-by-investment and passport-sale industry, which sells nationality for money. Tonga sits in the banking pattern as a historical case. Its scores show a fairly high level of criminal actors inside the state and middling resilience.
Tonga.imp: A fund built from selling citizenship was handed to one adviser with the king's favour, and most of a year's state revenue disappeared. The people of Tonga paid for that loss through the public budget. The case shows the risk when national funds are run through personal trust rather than public rules. Watch how any future passport or citizenship-sale money is managed and audited.

Tuvalu.d: Nothing is documented on the map for Tuvalu yet; this write-up is an estimate. No organisation has a recorded presence there. Its conditions scores are low: criminal actors inside the state score among the lowest on the map, and its capacity to resist is middling. The most likely route in, judging from neighbouring Pacific states in the record, would be a foreign government offering police cooperation or money to members of parliament, or an outside business seeking a special deal. That is a best guess, not a finding.
Tuvalu.imp: No case of outside capture is recorded for Tuvalu, and no organisations are recorded there. In a very small state a few decisions can be shifted by a few people. If anything changes, it is most likely to come through a foreign aid, police or business deal. Residents can watch who funds such deals and whether their terms are published.

Vanuatu.d: Vanuatu is discussing a wider policing partnership with China. Chinese police advisers have worked in Vanuatu since 2023. On 19 September 2025 the internal affairs minister, Andrew Solomon Napuat, met China's Minister of Public Security, Wang Xiaohong, in Beijing. China donated police equipment worth about NZ$720,000, including motorcycles and drones, and both sides said they were discussing a broader agreement. The case is rated probable and happening now. It is not presented as wrongdoing; it records a foreign state's police ministry gaining a role in local policing, as has happened in Fiji, Kiribati and the Solomon Islands. The organisations present are PRC state proxies, bodies acting for the Chinese state where the United Front, the Communist Party's influence arm, is not named. Vanuatu is a target country in the pattern of China's long arm abroad, with low to middling conditions scores.
Vanuatu.imp: Police equipment and advisers come with ties to the government that supplies them. Drones and training shape how residents are watched and policed. Nothing in the record shows misuse in Vanuatu, but in the Solomon Islands a similar arrangement led to a surveillance-policing trial that was stopped after local objections. Watch whether a new agreement is signed and whether its terms are made public.

Albania.d:
Albania is in the middle of trying to clean out its own state. Since 2017 an EU-monitored vetting has checked every judge and prosecutor in the country, and about half of those assessed have been removed or forced out, mostly because they could not explain their wealth. These are administrative removals, not criminal convictions. A 2015 'decriminalisation' law, agreed across parties, bars people with serious convictions at home or abroad from office; by 2020 seven MPs had resigned or been removed for hiding records, along with three mayors and about 600 state employees.

Drug money is still reaching in. In 2026 Albania's special anti-corruption prosecutor, SPAK, issued 20 arrest warrants and seized over 100 million euros, tracing cocaine money into coastal land and Tirana high-rises. Its file refers to meetings with senior state officials it does not name. These are charges, not verdicts.

The key earlier case reached the interior ministry, which runs the police. Saimir Tahiri was interior minister until 2017. Italian police arrested his cousin in a probe into over 3.5 tonnes of cannabis, and wiretaps mentioned Tahiri. In 2019 he was convicted of abuse of office, but the drug-trafficking counts did not lead to conviction.

A foreign government reached in too. Albania hosts about 3,000 members of an Iranian opposition group, the MEK. In July 2022 a cyberattack shut down many government online services; Albania's government found Iran behind it and cut diplomatic ties. Iran called this baseless.

Albania belongs to 'Organised crime inside the state', where it is proven, and to 'Exposure, purge and reversal'.
Albania.imp: For people in Albania, the vetting and the decriminalisation law are a public admission that courts and parliament had people in them who should not have been there. The new removals are real, but drug money keeps finding new routes, now into land and towers. Watch whether the SPAK case names the officials in its file, whether the vetted courts convict at senior levels, and who ends up owning the coastal land.

Andorra.d:
Andorra is a tiny state in the Pyrenees, and one of its two heads of state is a foreign president. Under its 1993 constitution, the president of France is automatically one of Andorra's two co-princes, together with the Catholic Bishop of Urgell. Emmanuel Macron has held the role since 2017. Acting alone, the French co-prince appoints a member of the Constitutional Tribunal and of the judicial council and must agree to treaties; jointly with Andorra's head of government he appoints the head of government, calls elections and signs laws into force. This is open and written into law.

The other story is its banking. On 10 March 2015 the US Treasury's anti-laundering office, FinCEN, named Banca Privada d'Andorra (BPA) a 'primary money laundering concern', saying senior managers served criminal groups from Russia and China and Venezuelan launderers. Andorra took over the bank the next day and wound it up within a week. The record then splits. FinCEN withdrew its finding in 2016, and Spanish courts dismissed laundering cases against the bank between 2017 and 2019. But in July 2025 an Andorran court sentenced eighteen executives, the former chief executive to seven years and a 30 million euro fine. They are appealing, shareholders argue the bank was closed without tested evidence, and some clients named have never been convicted.

Andorra's conditions scores are strong: few state-embedded criminal actors (1 of 10) and good resilience (8).
Andorra.imp: For people in Andorra, part of their government's top authority sits with whoever France elects, and he takes part in appointing the head of government and signing laws. That is legal and public. The BPA case shows how a single foreign regulator's notice can close a national bank overnight, while courts in different countries reach different answers years later. Watch the appeal of the 2025 sentences and whether the bank's former clients recover their funds.

Austria.d:
Austria's most recent case is a spy story that reached the interior ministry. On 20 May 2026 a Vienna court convicted Egisto Ott, a former officer of Austria's old domestic intelligence agency, of spying for Russia through Jan Marsalek, the fugitive former Wirecard executive. Ott searched police databases for people Moscow wanted to find, passed on journalist Christo Grozev's address, sold a secure laptop for €20,000 and handed over three work phones from the interior minister's office. He got four years and one month and plans to appeal.

Russia's links to politics run deeper. In 2016 the leaders of the Freedom Party (FPÖ) signed a five-year cooperation pact with United Russia, Putin's party; FPÖ ministers then sat in government from 2017 to 2019, and the pact lapsed in 2021. Karin Kneissl, foreign minister for the FPÖ from 2017 to 2019, at whose wedding Putin was a guest, joined the board of Rosneft, Russia's state oil company, in 2021, and moved to Russia in 2023.

Turkey reaches in through religion. In 2018 the government reviewed the permits of about 40 imams of ATIB, the Austrian branch of Turkey's religious directorate, saying it got round a ban on foreign funding. Since 2019 the Grey Wolves salute, used by a Turkish nationalist movement, is banned. 2020 raids against suspected Muslim Brotherhood networks were later ruled unlawful.

Raiffeisen Bank International is under supervisory pressure over its eastern exposure, with no penalty imposed. Former chancellor Sebastian Kurz was a WEF Young Global Leader, which is not a finding of influence.

The background is the Cold War: a secret anti-communist force raised in 1951 by Franz Olah, later interior minister, and more than 80 hidden US weapons caches revealed in 1996.
Austria.imp: For people in Austria, the clearest lesson is that a single insider can open state databases and ministry phones to a foreign power. Russian influence came through open party deals and jobs for ex-ministers, which are legal but shape who politicians listen to. Watch Ott's appeal, any further cases tied to Marsalek, how the Raiffeisen inquiries end, and how the state handles foreign-funded religious bodies without overreaching, as the court found it did in 2020.

Belarus.d:
Belarus's government and army now operate largely inside Russia's plans, and both governments say so openly. After the disputed 2020 election, when Alexander Lukashenko faced mass protests, Vladimir Putin promised him a loan of 1.5 billion dollars. In February 2022 Russian forces launched part of their invasion of Ukraine from Belarusian soil. The same month a referendum changed Belarus's constitution to remove the ban on nuclear weapons and allow permanent Russian bases. In 2023 Russia supplied Iskander-M missiles, which can carry nuclear warheads, and Putin said warheads had been delivered; he has said Russia keeps control of them.

This is the one documented case for Belarus, rated established, severe and happening now. It belongs to 'Russia's networks in Europe and Africa' and 'Governments buying officials in other countries', with Belarus as the target. The Russkiy Mir Foundation, a Russian state body promoting Russian language and culture abroad, and Interpol are likely present but no case is recorded. State-embedded actors score 9 of 10 and the ability to resist only 3.1.
Belarus.imp: For people in Belarus, decisions about war and nuclear weapons on their own soil are now made with Moscow, and Russia says it controls the warheads. The 2022 referendum removed the constitutional limits that once stood in the way. Because both governments state this openly, the question is less what is hidden than what citizens can still decide. Watch for more Russian bases, troop movements and any further changes to the constitution.

Belgium.d:
Belgium hosts the European Union's institutions, so many cases here are about outside forces reaching into them. Qatargate, a Belgian criminal case, is ongoing: in December 2022 police seized about €1.5 million in cash and arrested Eva Kaili, a vice-president of the European Parliament. Prosecutors say Qatar and Morocco paid to influence Parliament, with money passing through Fight Impunity, an NGO run by former MEP Pier Antonio Panzeri, who took a plea deal. Kaili and the others deny the charges; in February 2026 an appeals court let the case go on. A second case concerns Huawei, the Chinese telecoms firm: prosecutors allege people around a former Huawei lobbyist paid MEPs to sign a 2021 letter against curbs on foreign 5G equipment. Eight people have been charged, and in June 2026 Parliament lifted one Italian MEP's immunity. In 2026 the Commission confirmed Hungary's EU mission ran a spy ring against Commission staff from 2012 to 2018. A court ruled in 2025 that Commission President von der Leyen's texts with Pfizer's chief executive over the EU's largest vaccine deal could not simply be withheld. Leaders including NATO's Mark Rutte and five Commissioners attend the private Bilderberg meetings, which is legal.

Inside the Belgian state, cocaine is the main force. Antwerp is Europe's largest cocaine port; workers, police and customs staff have been convicted of extracting containers and passing information, and in 2022 the justice minister was protected after a kidnap plot. Seizures reached 116 tonnes in 2023. Foreign governments reached in too: a former senator took money from China's Ministry of State Security, but a gap in the law blocked prosecution; Belgium ended Saudi control of the Great Mosque of Brussels in 2018, then found Moroccan intelligence officers and a Turkish Diyanet employee in the bodies that followed. Britain's GCHQ hacked the state telecom Belgacom from 2010 to 2013.

The background is Cold War: a 1991 Senate inquiry into the secret NATO stay-behind network, and Westland New Post, a far-right group with links to State Security and gendarmes.
Belgium.imp: For people in Belgium, the country is both a crime-fighting front line and the address of EU decisions that affect 27 countries. Cash from foreign governments and companies has reached lawmakers who vote on rules for everyone, and most of those cases are charges still to be tested. At home, the port's cocaine trade buys staff with access. Watch the Qatargate and Huawei trials, whether Belgium closes the gap that blocked the Chinese spying case, and staff screening at Antwerp.

Bosnia and Herzegovina.d:
In Bosnia and Herzegovina, foreign governments hold real power over the state, some openly and some not. The Office of the High Representative was set up under the 1995 Dayton peace deal and answers to the Peace Implementation Council, a group of foreign governments. Since 1997 its 'Bonn powers' let it impose binding laws and remove officials; by 2004 it had dismissed 139 officials, 58 of them in one day. Germany's Christian Schmidt has held the post since 2021. Russia, China and some Bosnian politicians call his appointment illegitimate and want the office closed.

Russia backs the other side. Milorad Dodik led Republika Srpska, the country's Serb-run entity, and pushed for it to break away. Its police signed a 2016 cooperation deal with Russia's interior ministry, and Dodik met Putin at least five times from 2022. In 2025 a Bosnian court banned him from politics for six years for defying the High Representative. The US had sanctioned him in 2017 for obstructing the peace deal, then lifted the sanctions on 29 October 2025, a day after he met Russia's foreign minister.

Organised crime has reached officials as well. In April 2024, in Operation Black Tie, 23 people were arrested in Sarajevo over trafficking and laundering for the circle of a cocaine boss already sentenced in the Netherlands; Europol said corrupt officials were among them. These are charges, not verdicts.

Bosnia is a target country in 'Russia's networks in Europe and Africa' and appears in 'Organised crime inside the state'.
Bosnia and Herzegovina.imp: For people in Bosnia, laws can still be imposed and officials removed by an envoy who answers to foreign governments, while Russia backs the leaders resisting him. Both shape who governs and how. Ordinary voters have limited say over either. Watch whether the High Representative's office stays open, what Dodik does under his ban, and whether the officials arrested in Operation Black Tie are tried.

Bulgaria.d:
In Bulgaria the open question is who has a hold over the judges. Martin Bozhanov, known as 'the Notary', is alleged to have gathered compromising material on judges and prosecutors and used it to pressure them. Bulgarian National Radio reported he threatened prosecutors as well as judges, and former Prosecutor General Ivan Geshev was questioned. The claims are under investigation and untested in court.

The record on smuggling is clearer. In June 2021 the US used its Magnitsky law, which sanctions corrupt officials abroad, in its largest action ever against a single country. It named Bulgarian officials and business figures, several in customs and border roles, over networks that included protection for smuggling. Bulgarian prosecutions largely did not follow. Customs posts on the Balkan smuggling route sit inside these same institutions.

A Russia case ended in acquittal. Prosecutors charged Nikolay Malinov, a former MP and head of Bulgaria's largest pro-Russia group, in 2019 with collecting state secrets for the Russian Institute for Strategic Studies, a Russian state think tank. While on bail he went to Moscow, where Putin gave him a state award. A Sofia court acquitted him of all charges in May 2026.

Bulgaria belongs to 'Organised crime inside the state', where it is proven, and 'Russia's networks in Europe and Africa'. State-embedded actors score 7.5 of 10.
Bulgaria.imp: For people in Bulgaria, the worry is that the courts and customs, the institutions meant to check crime, may themselves be under pressure or protecting it. Foreign sanctions named officials, but cases at home mostly did not follow. Watch how the 'Notary' investigation develops and whether judges named in it are cleared or charged, and whether any customs or border official named in 2021 is prosecuted.

Croatia.d:
Croatia's documented case is about a foreign oil company buying control of the country's own oil company through the prime minister. INA is Croatia's national oil company. MOL is Hungary's state-influenced oil company. Croatian courts found that Prime Minister Ivo Sanader took a 10 million euro bribe from MOL's chief executive, Zsolt Hernádi, in exchange for giving MOL management control of INA.

The case took years. A first conviction in 2012 was quashed in 2015. Sanader was convicted again in 2020, and Croatia's Supreme Court confirmed it in 2021. It is rated established. The other side has never faced a Croatian court: Hungary has not handed Hernádi over, and MOL denies paying the bribe. The effect is still felt, since MOL's role at INA came out of that deal.

Opus Dei, a Catholic organisation whose lay members are encouraged to excel in public life, and the Order of Malta are present, but no case is recorded for them. Croatia's overall score is low because this is the one documented case; the conditions scores sit near the middle.
Croatia.imp: For people in Croatia, the case shows a prime minister selling control of a national company that belongs to the public, and a foreign government declining to send the other party for trial. Oil and fuel decisions at INA were shaped by that bargain. Watch who controls INA now, whether Hernádi ever faces a court, and how future deals over state companies are made and disclosed.

Czech Republic.d:
The current question in the Czech Republic is the prime minister's company. Agrofert is a large farming, food and chemicals group founded and owned by Andrej Babiš that receives EU farm subsidies. A European Commission audit published in 2021 found that he still controlled it while in government, a conflict of interest. Babiš took back sole ownership in October 2025, became prime minister again in December 2025, and on 20 February 2026 moved the shares into a new trust, saying the conflict was resolved.

Russia's reach is documented too. On 27 March 2024 the government sanctioned Voice of Europe, a website, along with Ukrainian politician Viktor Medvedchuk and an associate. The Czech security service said the network was funded from Russia; a newspaper, citing a foreign ministry source, reported that payments went to politicians in six EU countries.

China appears through Ye Jianming, head of the oil group CEFC and a former deputy secretary-general of a Beijing 'friendship' body, the CAIFC. President Miloš Zeman made him an economic adviser while CEFC bought Czech assets. Ye was detained in China in 2018.

Older cases: Václav Klaus, prime minister and later president, is a member of the Mont Pelerin Society, a free-market thinkers' society; membership is not a finding of influence. In 1939, after Germany occupied Prague, the Bank for International Settlements, the central banks' bank, passed 23 tons of Czechoslovak gold to Germany's central bank.
Czech Republic.imp: For people in the Czech Republic, the main issue is whether the head of government can separate state decisions, including on subsidies, from his own business. That is a question about trust arrangements rather than a crime. Foreign states have tried to buy voices in European politics through Prague. Watch how the new Agrofert trust works in practice, how EU subsidy money flows to it, and whether more politicians are named in the Voice of Europe case.

Denmark.d:
Denmark's newest case involves its closest ally. Greenland is a self-governing part of Denmark that President Trump has said the US should take over. In August 2025 Danish media reported that at least three Americans, said by unnamed sources to have ties to the Trump administration, were stirring anti-Danish feeling there. Denmark's police intelligence service confirmed an influence campaign was under way, and the foreign minister summoned the top US diplomat. Who is behind it is not proven.

The tie runs the other way too. In Operation Dunhammer, an internal review finished in 2015, Danish military intelligence found that it had let the US National Security Agency tap internet cables at Danish stations, and that the NSA used this in 2012–2014 to wiretap German Chancellor Angela Merkel and other German politicians, and reportedly senior figures in Sweden, Norway and France. The defence minister was told in 2020, the intelligence chief was suspended, and the public learned in 2021.

Money is the other thread. Danske Bank pleaded guilty in the US in 2022 to bank fraud conspiracy and forfeited $2 billion over about €200 billion moved through its Estonian branch. Big container shipping lines appear in cocaine seizures as vessel owners; the record does not accuse them.

King Frederik X is a former WEF Young Global Leader, which is not a finding of influence. The background is 'Absalon', a NATO stay-behind network hidden inside military intelligence and disbanded after 1990.
Denmark.imp: For people in Denmark, the record shows the country's own intelligence service helping a foreign power spy on neighbours, and the same ally now suspected of working on Greenland's public. The state's checks found both, but late. Danske Bank shows how a single foreign branch can move enormous sums unseen. Watch what Danish intelligence finds about the Greenland campaign, and how cable-tapping arrangements with allies are overseen.

Estonia.d:
Estonia is pushing a Moscow-run church out of its state affairs right now. The Estonian Orthodox Church of the Moscow Patriarchate has about 150,000 faithful and answers to the Russian church. In January 2024 Estonia refused to renew the residence permit of its head, Metropolitan Eugene (Reshetnikov), calling his support for Russia's war "a security risk", and he left on 6 February 2024. In May 2024 the Riigikogu, Estonia's parliament, declared the Moscow Patriarchate an institution that supports Russian military aggression, and in 2025 it tightened the churches law to cut foreign control.

Private forums reach the top offices. The Bilderberg Meeting is a private yearly conference of about 130 politicians, executives and academics, with no public record of what is said. Its 2024 list named Kaja Kallas, then prime minister; weeks later EU leaders nominated her as the EU's foreign policy chief, a post she has held since December 2024. The World Economic Forum's Young Global Leaders class of 2025, a five-year network for people under about 40, includes Erkki Keldo, the minister of economy and industry. The lists are documented; what was said at the meetings is not.

Banks were the other door. In 2017 the OCCRP and partner newspapers published 16,000 leaked transactions showing about $2.9 billion moved in 2012–2014 through UK shell companies with accounts at Danske Bank's Estonian branch, almost half from an account linked to Azerbaijan's ruling Aliyev family. Recipients included German MP Karin Strenz and Slovenian MP Zmago Jelinčič. In 2018 the European Central Bank, on the Estonian regulator's proposal, withdrew the licence of Versobank, a small bank with mostly foreign clients, for serious anti-money-laundering failures.

Estonia appears in the map's patterns on Russia's networks, foreign money in Europe's parliaments, criminal money in banks and private forums, mostly as a target that has pushed back. The Russkiy Mir Foundation and the Russian Laundromat are likely present but not documented here.
Estonia.imp: The main outside pressure now comes through a church run from Moscow, and Estonia has answered it in the open, with permits and laws anyone can read. The bank cases show how a small country's banks carried billions for a foreign ruling family to politicians abroad without most residents knowing; regulators shut that channel in 2018. Worth watching: which ministers attend private forums like Bilderberg and the Davos network, since those meetings leave no public record.

Finland.d:
Finland's head of state sits in two of the best-known private networks of politicians and business. Alexander Stubb, President since 1 March 2024 and earlier prime minister and finance minister, is listed on his official presidential CV as a member of the World Economic Forum's Young Global Leader network (2009) and of its Global Future Council on Europe (2018). The Forum, best known for its Davos meeting, picks people under about 40 each year for this network. Stubb also appears on the official Bilderberg lists for 2024 and 2025, each time as sitting President. Bilderberg is a private yearly conference of about 130 European and North American politicians, executives and academics, with no public record of what is said.

Former prime minister Sanna Marin (2019–23) was on the 2025 Bilderberg list, and a 2021 paper by the German Bundestag's research service lists her among Young Global Leaders participants. Being picked is a Forum decision; no forum has found that either network directed Finnish government decisions.

The older story is a hidden army. After the September 1944 armistice with Moscow, Colonel Valo Nihtilä and Lieutenant Colonel Usko Haahti of Military Headquarters began hiding weapons across the country, planned for 8,000 men but estimated to equip about 35,000. Between 5,000 and 10,000 people took part. Exposed in spring 1945, it led the security police to question more than 5,000 people, and under a retroactive law of January 1947, 1,488 were convicted, most receiving one to four months in prison.

Finland belongs to the map's patterns on private forums and on the anticommunist networks of 1945–1990. The Club of Rome is likely present but not documented.
Finland.imp: For people in Finland, nothing on the record shows an outside group steering the state today. What is documented is that the President and a former prime minister move in private forums where officials meet business leaders behind closed doors, with no minutes. That is legal and openly listed, but what is discussed there stays out of view. Watch whether positions taken at home match what leaders say they heard in those rooms.

France.d:
In France the outside forces reaching into the state today are mostly companies, consultants and foreign governments, with an older layer of lodges and Cold War networks underneath.

Start with the consultants. A Senate inquiry reported in 2022 that the state's use of private consultants since 2017 was "sprawling and opaque" and shaped policy, including during Covid. It referred McKinsey, the US consulting firm, to prosecutors over its French taxes; on 4 September 2026 French and Brussels prosecutors announced a €65 million seizure, and the investigation continues. The Uber Files, 124,000 leaked company documents, suggest that Emmanuel Macron as economy minister (2014–16) brokered a secret deal for Uber inside the cabinet; Macron said he was proud of supporting the company. Macron had been a partner at Rothschild & Cie before joining the Élysée in 2012; no court or inquiry has found that the bank directs his policies, and the claim that he is "the Rothschilds' president" is a form of an antisemitic conspiracy theory.

Big firms have been caught paying abroad and at home. Airbus agreed in 2020 to pay about €3.6 billion to French, British and US prosecutors over bribes to win contracts in many countries. Servier was convicted in 2021 over its drug Mediator, and the medicines regulator was fined €303,000 for failing to act.

Foreign governments and crime reach in too. Marine Le Pen's party took a €9 million loan from a Moscow bank in 2014. The interior minister accused Azerbaijan of stirring New Caledonia's 2024 riots, which Baku denies. France dissolved Turkey's Grey Wolves movement in 2020; the ban stays in force. Officers of Marseille's anti-crime brigade were convicted of stealing seized cannabis and money, and a former head of the national anti-drug office is under formal investigation, which he denies. A 2025 state report warned of Muslim Brotherhood "entryism" in town halls, while finding no sign that Muslims in France seek an Islamic state.

The roots run deep. In 1901–1904 the War Ministry sorted officers for promotion using files gathered through Grand Orient lodges, and the government fell. The CIA ran the Congress for Cultural Freedom from Paris, an operation its own historians now praise. The Gaullist militia SAC was dissolved in 1982, and French lodges chartered lodges in former African colonies.
