France is a central case on the map: banks, consultants, regulators, organised crime and the anticommunist web all run through it.
France.imp: For people in France, the strongest documented pull on the state today comes from companies and consultants who write advice ministries follow, and from former bankers moving into top office; those moves are lawful and on the record. Courts have acted on bribery, a deadly drug and police theft, and a large consultancy probe is still open. Watch the McKinsey case, who the state hires for advice, and how foreign governments try to work through parties and overseas territories.

Germany.d:
Germany is where foreign spy services are most often caught inside the political system right now, and where the line between business and government runs straight to the top.

Start with who is inside today. China: on 30 September 2025 a Dresden court sentenced Jian Guo, aide to AfD MEP Maximilian Krah, to 4 years and 9 months for working for China's Ministry of State Security, including passing on European Parliament business; three Germans are on trial in Düsseldorf, charged with passing naval technology to the same service. Russia: Jan Marsalek, chief operating officer of the payments firm Wirecard until its 2020 collapse over €1.9 billion that did not exist, is wanted and, German investigators say, worked with Russian intelligence since at least 2010. Munich prosecutors are investigating AfD politician Petr Bystroň over cash from the Russian-funded Voice of Europe network; he denies it and no charge had been reported. Former chancellor Gerhard Schröder chaired Rosneft's board until 2022. In 2024 the state banned the Islamic Centre Hamburg as an outpost of Iran's government.

Inside its own forces, prosecutors charge that a Berlin judge and former MP was to be justice minister in the Reichsbürger group of Heinrich XIII Prinz Reuss, which planned to storm the Reichstag; the trials are running. Customs officers at Hamburg and Bremerhaven have been convicted of clearing cocaine containers.

Business reaches the top. Chancellor Friedrich Merz chaired BlackRock's German arm from 2016 to 2020; Jörg Kukies went from Goldman Sachs to finance minister. Diaries of banker Christian Olearius record meetings with Olaf Scholz as Hamburg mayor before a €47 million tax claim on Warburg bank was dropped; Scholz denies any influence. The financial regulator BaFin turned on Wirecard's critics, and a study found the risk agency copied industry text into its glyphosate review, which it rejects. Ministers and the Bundestag president appear on Bilderberg lists.

The background: the US spy agency NSA monitored Chancellor Merkel's phone; the CIA funded Radio Free Europe from Munich until 1971; the BND's NATO stay-behind network was dissolved in 1991; the 1924 Dawes Plan put the Reichsbank under a creditor board.

Germany sits in almost every pattern on the map, as both target and base.
Germany.imp: For people in Germany, the clearest documented risk today is foreign intelligence working through staff, companies and politicians, and courts are convicting people for it. At the same time, top offices pass between finance houses and government, which is legal but means the same people sit on both sides. Watch the spy trials, the Reichsbürger verdicts, and who Germany's leaders worked for before office.

Greece.d:
Greece's present is shaped by debt deals and by a party a court has called a criminal organisation. Kyriakos Mitsotakis, prime minister since 2019, appears on the official list for the private Bilderberg conference of June 2025, held with no public record of what is said.

Golden Dawn, a far-right party, won 21 seats in May 2012 and was the third-largest party in parliament by 2015. On 7 October 2020 an Athens appeal court found its leader Nikolaos Michaloliakos and six others guilty of running a criminal organisation "dressed in the mantle of a political party", in a trial that included the 2013 murder of rapper Pavlos Fyssas; on 4 March 2026 a court upheld 42 convictions. Ties to the police are suspected: in 2012 police polling stations in Attica gave the party just over 20%, against about 6% nearby, and the Council of Europe's rights commissioner said in 2013 he had strong evidence of links.

Then the debt. In 2001, as Greece entered the euro, Goldman Sachs arranged swaps that worked as a hidden loan of about €2.8 billion; Bloomberg reported that Greece paid about €600 million in fees and that the obligation grew to €5.1 billion. Goldman said the deals met EU rules. Lucas Papademos, central bank governor at the time, became unelected prime minister in 2011–12 to secure the second bailout; he never worked for Goldman. Lazard advised the government on the 2012 bond swap. Bribery cases against ex-ministers over Novartis were dropped, though Novartis paid about $347 million in the US partly over bribing Greek hospital staff.

The roots are military. IDEA, a secret officers' society, prepared the 1967 coup, and the colonels ruled until 1974; their leaders were convicted of high treason in 1975. A NATO stay-behind branch operated until 1988.
Greece.imp: For people in Greece, the debt the country carried into its crisis was partly hidden through a bank deal that cost far more than shown, and those decisions were made by a small circle of officials and advisers. A party that sat in parliament has been convicted as a criminal gang, with suspected support inside the police. Watch the remaining appeals, who advises the finance ministry on debt, and how police handle far-right violence.

Hungary.d:
Hungary has invited China's police onto its streets. In February 2024 Interior Minister Sándor Pintér and China's Minister of Public Security agreed that Chinese officers may patrol alongside Hungarian police in tourist areas and at large events. The ministry denied that Chinese police stations exist in Hungary, though the rights group Safeguard Defenders had listed two in Budapest, in the Józsefváros and Kőbánya districts. Elsewhere such stations have been used to pressure people China wants back.

The second case runs through the European Parliament. Béla Kovács sat there for Jobbik, a Hungarian nationalist party. Prosecutors accused him of spying on EU institutions for Russia, and in September 2022 Hungary's top court, the Curia, sentenced him in absentia to five years in prison; he lives in Russia.

Only two cases are documented, so the overall score is low, but Hungary's conditions score is high: state-embedded actors are strong and resilience is weak, which makes outside reach easier. Scientology, the Ordo Iuris institute and the Viktor Medvedchuk network are likely present but undocumented. Hungary belongs to the patterns on China's long arm and on Russia's networks in Europe, as a target country.
Hungary.imp: For people in Hungary, the patrol deal means foreign police can work beside your own, under an agreement made by ministers and with stations the government says do not exist. The Kovács case shows a Russian spy can reach a seat in the European Parliament. With weak checks on power, watch how far the Chinese policing deal extends and who it is used against.

Iceland.d: Nothing is documented on this map for Iceland yet; what follows is an estimate. The Mont Pelerin Society, a network of free-market economists and politicians, has documented presence, and the fishing company Samherji is based here. A NATO stay-behind network is likely but not documented. Conditions are strong: state-embedded actors score very low and resilience very high, so outside groups have few easy openings. The most likely route in, as a best guess, is through large home companies and their dealings abroad, or through policy networks that shape economic ideas, rather than through hidden placement in the state.
Iceland.imp: For people in Iceland, there is no documented case of an outside group steering the state. The strong conditions scores mean it would be hard to do quietly. If anything appears, it is most likely to come through big companies based here and their dealings abroad, so that is where to keep an eye.

Ireland.d:
Ireland's current leaders appear in the World Economic Forum's network for rising politicians. The Forum, best known for its Davos meeting, picks people under about 40 each year for its Young Global Leaders programme. Its 2025 class includes Simon Harris, the former Taoiseach (prime minister) who is now Tánaiste (deputy prime minister). In 2018 the Forum named Leo Varadkar while he was sitting Taoiseach, and he was on the official list of the private Bilderberg conference in 2024, weeks after stepping down. These are documented selections, not findings of influence.

China's police reached into Dublin. In 2022 the rights group Safeguard Defenders reported that Chinese city police ran unofficial "overseas service stations" abroad to pressure people China wanted back; one, run for Fuzhou police, was on Capel Street. In late October 2022 Ireland's foreign ministry ordered it to close.

The older story is a Catholic brotherhood. The Knights of Saint Columbanus, a lay Catholic order based in Ireland, had members at the top of the first Inter-Party government of 1948: Taoiseach John A. Costello and Justice Minister Seán MacEoin, who reportedly assured the Order that conflict between Church and State would be avoided. The government gave Maynooth seminary a special grant, and a Knight in the Labour party is reported to have worked against the Mother and Child health scheme that Archbishop McQuaid opposed. These accounts rest mainly on two biographies.

Ireland sits in the map's patterns on private forums, on China's long arm and on sworn brotherhoods.
Ireland.imp: For people in Ireland, the documented ties of today's leaders are to open, listed networks where politicians meet business leaders, not to hidden groups; what is said there is not public. The Dublin station showed that a foreign police force can try to reach people living here, and the state shut it. The older Knights story is a reminder to ask whose voice shapes health and social policy.

Italy.d:
Italy has the most crowded record on this map, and much of it is still moving. Organised crime is the largest part. The Sicilian Mafia (Cosa Nostra), the Calabrian 'Ndrangheta, the Neapolitan Camorra and the Puglia clans reach into town halls, ports and building firms. Since a 1991 law, the national government can dissolve a town council when an inquiry finds a mafia group steering it; by September 2025 there had been 402 such decrees, covering 288 towns and 6 health authorities, and courts had annulled 24. In 2012 Reggio Calabria became the first provincial capital dissolved this way. The 'Ndrangheta reaches furthest: the Rinascita-Scott trial convicted 207 people in November 2023, including former senator Giancarlo Pittelli, and appeals are running. The Aemilia trial showed its firms running construction in Emilia-Romagna, and in 2024 Reggio Emilia's prefect barred 80 firms from public contracts as EU recovery money flowed in. Investigators document its control over hiring at Gioia Tauro, Italy's largest transhipment port. Higher up the state, Sicily's former president Salvatore Cuffaro was jailed for aiding Cosa Nostra (final in 2011), Berlusconi's aide Marcello Dell'Utri was convicted as his go-between with the Mafia (2014), and economy undersecretary Nicola Cosentino's 10 years for helping the Casalesi clan became final in 2023. Seven-time prime minister Giulio Andreotti was acquitted; appeal judges found ties to mobsters before 1980 but too old to prosecute.

Foreign governments are present now too. The Lega, whose leader Matteo Salvini is deputy prime minister, signed a cooperation pact with Putin's United Russia party in 2017, reported renewed to 2027; a Milan judge closed the inquiry into 2018 talks on Russian oil money for the party, finding them aimed at illegal funding but never completed. China's former vice-minister Qu Dongyu heads the Rome-based UN food agency (FAO), and in 2023 Italy limited Chinese state firm Sinochem's control of tyre maker Pirelli.

The older background is the lodge P2. A list seized in 1981 held 962 names: ministers, 44 MPs, 195 officers and the heads of all three intelligence services. It led to the 1982 ban on secret societies, still used today. Italy is the proven centre of the patterns on organised crime inside the state and criminal money in firms, and the coordinating centre of the Cold War anticommunist web.
Italy.imp: For people in Italy the clearest sign is local. When a town council is dissolved, appointed commissioners run the town for 18 to 24 months, and contracts for building, waste, ports and transport are where clans look for money. Much of the anti-mafia system works in the open: prefects' bans, dissolution decrees and maxi-trials are public records worth following. Nationally, watch agreements between Italian parties and foreign ruling parties, foreign state ownership of strategic companies, and lodge membership among judges and police, which the Anti-Mafia Commission recommended banning in 2017.

Latvia.d:
Latvia's documented record is about Russia and about money passing through its banks. In 2022 Latvia's parliament, on a bill from President Egils Levits, made the Latvian Orthodox Church fully independent of any church authority abroad. Until then it was a self-governing part of the Russian Orthodox Church under the Moscow Patriarchate. As of mid-2026 no Orthodox church had recognised the new status. In January 2024 leaked emails showed Tatjana Ždanoka, a Latvian member of the European Parliament from 2004 to 2024, reporting to officers of Russia's security service, the FSB, from at least 2004. Latvia's State Security Service opened a criminal case, which is still an investigation, and the European Parliament penalised her for breaking its code of conduct.

The banks are the second part. In 2018 the US Treasury named ABLV Bank, which served shell-company clients, a primary money-laundering concern; depositors ran and the bank wound itself up within weeks, with no trial. In 2021 the US designated Chatex, a crypto exchange with support companies in Latvia and Estonia, as a successor to an already-sanctioned operation. Latvian banks were also a channel for the Global Laundromat, money moved out of Russia through Moldovan courts. Latvia appears in the patterns on Russia's networks in Europe and on criminal money in banks, mostly as a target that has pushed back.
Latvia.imp: For people in Latvia, the documented risk is a neighbouring government using familiar institutions as channels: a church, an elected representative, a bank. The state has acted each time, with a law on the church, a criminal case against a former MEP, and a bank closed after outside pressure. What to watch is whether those steps hold: the outcome of the Ždanoka case, and whether banks and crypto firms check where their clients' money comes from.

Liechtenstein.d: Nothing is documented on the map for Liechtenstein yet. The only organisation recorded as present is the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order, and its presence is not a case. The conditions scores are very low: almost no sign of outside actors embedded in the state, and strong resilience (8.4 out of 10). As a best guess, if an outside force did reach in, the most likely route would be finance, through banks, trusts and company registration, which is how other small financial centres such as Malta and Monaco appear elsewhere on this map, rather than through lodges or churches. This is an estimate, not a finding.
Liechtenstein.imp: For people in Liechtenstein there is no recorded case to point to today. If anything is worth watching, the best guess is the financial sector: who owns the trusts and companies registered there, and whether checks on foreign clients' money keep pace with what neighbouring financial centres have been caught missing.

Lithuania.d:
Lithuania's current cases are about criminal money passing through. Matrix, an invitation-only encrypted phone network that appears in Lithuania's record, was taken down in December 2024 after French and Dutch investigators read 2.3 million of its messages over three months; it ran on more than 40 servers and had been found on the phone of a man convicted of murdering a Dutch crime journalist. In February 2026 a group selling cocaine, MDMA, ketamine and methamphetamine in Iceland was charged with laundering the money through property in Lithuania, with 24 arrests in five countries. Both are at the charge stage.

The best-known case is older. Yuri Borisov, a Russian businessman who ran the helicopter firm Avia Baltika, reportedly gave about $400,000 to Rolandas Paksas's 2002 presidential campaign and then received Lithuanian citizenship by Paksas's decree. On 31 March 2004 the Constitutional Court found Paksas had broken the constitution and his oath, and on 6 April parliament removed him, the first European head of state impeached. The European Court of Human Rights later found his lifetime ban from parliament disproportionate. Lithuania appears in the pattern on criminal money in banks and firms, and as a country where parliament exposed a foreign donor's hold on a president.
Lithuania.imp: For people in Lithuania, the record is less about secret groups in government and more about money: a foreign donor reaching a president, and drug profits from abroad turning into property at home. The 2004 impeachment shows the courts and parliament can act against the highest office. What to watch: who funds election campaigns, who receives citizenship or favours afterwards, and who buys property with money that has no clear source.

Luxembourg.d:
Luxembourg has one documented case, and it is old and unresolved. Between May 1984 and April 1986, 18 bombs went off in Luxembourg, hitting targets such as electricity pylons. In 2013 two former officers of the Gendarmerie's mobile brigade, Jos Wilmes and Marc Scheer, went on trial for them. Their defence argued the bombings were the work of NATO's stay-behind network, the secret Cold War units meant to resist a Soviet invasion, known in Italy as Gladio. A 2006 recording of Prime Minister Jean-Claude Juncker, Justice Minister Luc Frieden and intelligence chief Marco Mille speculating about stay-behind involvement was played in court, and the prosecutor said 88 of 125 pieces of evidence had disappeared. The trial was suspended in 2014. Eight former officers were later sent to trial for false testimony, not for the bombings. The stay-behind link remains only a suspicion.

Luxembourg also appears as the place where BCCI Holdings was registered; the bank's operating centre was in London, and regulators in several countries closed it on 5 July 1991. Luxembourg sits in the Cold War anticommunist web and in the pattern on banks that carried hidden money.
Luxembourg.imp: For people in Luxembourg, the record shows a two-year bombing campaign that was never settled in court, and evidence that went missing from the state's own files. There is no documented case of outside capture today. What to watch is the financial sector, where the country's other appearance on this map comes from: which companies and banks register here, and what supervisors know about who stands behind them.

Malta.d:
Malta's main case is in court now. Electrogas built Malta's gas power station under a state contract. One of its directors, businessman Yorgen Fenech, was identified as the owner of 17 Black, a company registered in the UAE. Leaked papers showed that Panama companies belonging to Keith Schembri, the prime minister's chief of staff, and Konrad Mizzi, the energy minister, expected payments from 17 Black. Journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia was investigating these companies when a car bomb killed her in 2017. Fenech is charged with complicity in her murder, and that trial began in mid-2026. Schembri and Mizzi resigned in November 2019, and in February 2025 the three men were charged with corruption over the power station. A 2021 public inquiry found the state had created an 'atmosphere of impunity'. None of these charges has reached a verdict.

The second part is Malta as a licensing centre. Italian investigations found Calabrian and Sicilian mafia groups using online betting firms licensed in Malta to collect bets and launder money, though some executives were later acquitted. Pilatus Bank lost its licence in 2018 after its owner's arrest in the US; his conviction there was later vacated over the prosecution's conduct. Crypto exchanges Binance and OKX, which appear in Malta's record, pleaded guilty in the US to money-transfer and sanctions failures. The EU's top court ruled against Malta's sale of citizenship for investment, and in 2018 the US designated Maltese brokers for smuggling Libyan oil. Malta is a proven case in the pattern on criminal money in banks and firms.
Malta.imp: For people in Malta, the record shows how a state energy contract, offshore companies and senior officials can sit in one chain, and that a journalist was killed while tracing it. The trials now running will decide what is proven. What to watch: the verdicts in the Fenech, Schembri and Mizzi cases, how licences are granted to betting, banking and crypto firms, and who is buying Maltese citizenship or residence.

Moldova.d:
Moldova's biggest case reached a verdict this year. In 2014 about $1 billion, equal to 12% of the country's GDP, was drained from three banks through loans repaid with new loans and moved through UK and Hong Kong shell companies. Vlad Plahotniuc, who led the Democratic Party and was widely described as controlling the government and the parliamentary majority, fled in 2019. He was arrested in Greece in July 2025, extradited, and on 22 April 2026 sentenced to 19 years. At parliamentary hearings the deputy head of the security service said President Nicolae Timofti had known of the theft since 2013.

Russia is the other present force. In 2023 the Constitutional Court declared the Șor Party of businessman Ilan Shor unconstitutional for serving a foreign state's interests. Its candidate, Evghenia Guțul, won the governorship of Gagauzia, an autonomous region, and met Vladimir Putin in 2024. In August 2025 a court sentenced her to seven years for financing the party with undeclared Russian money.

The older background: between 2010 and 2014 Moldovan judges approved fake debts that let an estimated $20–80 billion leave Russia, the scheme known as the Global Laundromat, and prosecutors later charged judges. In 2018 Moldova's intelligence service sent seven Turkish teachers from schools linked to the Gülen movement, which Turkey's government pursues abroad, to Turkey; the European Court of Human Rights ruled it an illegal transfer. Moldova is a proven case of organised crime inside the state and a target of Russia's networks.
Moldova.imp: For people in Moldova, the bank theft cost about 12% of a year's national output, and the record shows judges, banks and party leaders serving as routes for it and for Russian money. Courts have now convicted at the top. What to watch: where party money comes from, especially from abroad; whether the judges who approved fake debts are held to account; and whether the security services act within the law, which the European Court found they did not in 2018.

Monaco.d:
Monaco's present situation is unusual: France holds key posts inside its state, openly and by treaty. The head of government, the Minister of State, is appointed after the prince consults the French government; until a 2002 constitutional change the post had to go to a French citizen chosen from names Paris put forward. Since July 2025 it has been held by Christophe Mirmand, a French senior civil servant. Key judicial posts are held by French magistrates proposed by the French government, a French officer commands the police, and France is responsible for Monaco's defence. This is an agreed arrangement, not a hidden one.

The other cases involve people and bodies based in Monaco. Lamine Diack led world athletics' governing body (the IAAF, now World Athletics, based in Monaco) from 1999 to 2015. In 2020 a Paris court convicted him of corruption for helping hide Russian athletes' doping in return for money; he died in 2021 with appeals pending. Russian billionaire Dmitry Rybolovlev, owner of AS Monaco football club, was made a suspect in 2018 in a probe into whether he courted Monaco officials, including a former public prosecutor. The courts closed the case in 2025 after ruling the phone evidence unlawfully obtained, so nothing was proven. Monaco sits in the patterns on foreign governments placing officials and on international bodies.
Monaco.imp: For people in Monaco, the main fact is that France fills the top government, police and judicial posts under treaty. It is public, but it means key decisions rest with officials proposed by another country. The record also shows that a sports body headquartered here was bought from outside. What to watch: who is appointed to those posts, and how complaints involving wealthy residents and officials are investigated and decided.

Montenegro.d:
In Montenegro the top of the justice system is in court. On 28 January 2026 the High Court in Podgorica sentenced Vesna Medenica, who led the Supreme Court until 2020, to 10 years for using her position to protect a cigarette and drug smuggling network run by her son Miloš. He received 10 years and 2 months and fled while under house arrest. She was acquitted of creating a criminal organisation, and prosecutors are appealing for longer sentences. Much of the evidence came from Sky ECC, an encrypted phone service whose messages Europol passed to Podgorica. The same transcripts led to charges against a former chief special prosecutor, a former assistant police director and his son, a state security officer, for protecting the cocaine trade of the Kavac clan, a criminal group. Other indictments name two former police directors and the mayor of Budva. These are charges, not yet verdicts.

Separately, the World Economic Forum, the Davos forum, named Prime Minister Milojko Spajić to its 2025 class of Young Global Leaders, a five-year network of meetings and courses. The record shows the membership only, not any influence on his decisions. Montenegro is a proven case in the pattern on organised crime inside the state.
Montenegro.imp: For people in Montenegro, the record shows smuggling and cocaine networks reaching the people whose job is to stop them: the highest judge, the special prosecutor and police chiefs. When those posts are compromised, cases that should reach court may never get there. The appeals and trials now running will show whether the courts can hold their own former leaders to account. Watch those verdicts, and who is named to lead prosecutors and police next.

Netherlands.d:
The Netherlands' record is large because two things meet here: Europe's busiest port, and the international courts in The Hague. Most current cases are about cocaine. Crews take drugs out of containers at Rotterdam, sometimes with PIN codes supplied by terminal staff or with IT contractors moving a box's position in the system; several have been convicted. In July 2023 customs found 8,064 kg of cocaine in a banana shipment from Ecuador, the largest seizure in Dutch history. The network of Ridouan Taghi, sentenced to life in 2024, reached into the legal system: in the Marengo trial a lawyer and a police employee were prosecuted for leaking information, a witness's brother, his lawyer and a journalist were murdered, and in May 2026 Taghi's own lawyer, Inez Weski, was convicted of relaying messages for his organisation. Banks ING and ABN AMRO paid €775 million and €480 million to settle laundering failures.

Foreign governments reach in through companies and the international bodies. In October 2025 the state took control of chipmaker Nexperia, owned by Wingtech, a Chinese firm almost 30% traceable to the Chinese state; China answered with an export ban and the order was suspended in November. A former ASML and NXP engineer was jailed in 2025 for sending chip files to a contact in Russia. In 2018 four officers of GRU, Russian military intelligence, were caught trying to hack the chemical weapons watchdog (OPCW). In 2024 journalists reported that Israel's Mossad spied on International Criminal Court staff for years and pressed its prosecutor; Israel denies it. A 2020 parliamentary inquiry found Gulf donors and Turkey's religious authority influencing Dutch mosques.

Companies reach government too: memos showed Shell and Unilever lobbied for the 2017 plan to scrap the dividend tax, later dropped. King Willem-Alexander attends Bilderberg, a private yearly forum his grandfather founded. The Netherlands is a proven case of criminal money in firms and industries inside their regulators.
Netherlands.imp: For people in the Netherlands, much of the documented risk sits in ordinary jobs: a port worker's access code, a contractor's login, a lawyer's prison visit. Drug networks pay for these because they open doors without force. At national level, foreign states reach for chip companies and for the international courts in The Hague. What to watch: insider cases at the ports, how the Nexperia dispute ends, and whether banks that settle laundering cases ever see individuals charged.

Norway.d:
Norway has two documented cases, and neither is active now. The more recent concerns Eirik Jensen, who ran the Oslo police narcotics section for years. He was convicted of aggravated corruption and of helping import around 14 tonnes of hashish with an informant he handled, and sentenced to 21 years; the Supreme Court refused his appeal in 2021. It is the most senior police conviction of its kind in Scandinavia.

The older case comes from the Cold War. In 1978 police found weapons and radio equipment at a mountain cabin and arrested businessman Hans Otto Meyer, who said Norwegian intelligence had supplied them. The find exposed Norway's stay-behind network, secret units meant to resist an occupation. Defence Minister Rolf Hansen then said the network 'was not in any way answerable to NATO and had no CIA connection'.

The conditions scores are low: few signs of outside actors embedded in the state, and strong resilience. Norway sits in the patterns on organised crime inside the state and the Cold War anticommunist web.
Norway.imp: For people in Norway, the record shows that even with strong institutions, the officer in charge of fighting drugs ended up helping to import them. The courts caught it, and that case is closed. What to watch now: how police manage their informants, and whether Swedish criminal networks, which the map lists as likely present but not yet documented in Norway, begin reaching into Norwegian institutions.

Poland.d:
Poland's current cases centre on a legal campaign group and on China. Ordo Iuris, the Institute for Legal Culture, is a Polish legal think-tank; in 2016 it drafted a near-total abortion ban that parliament rejected after nationwide protests. Its co-founder Aleksander Stępkowski became deputy foreign minister in November 2015 under the new Law and Justice government. In 2019 he was appointed to the Supreme Court with no prior judicial experience, nominated by the reconstituted National Council of the Judiciary, and in May 2020 President Andrzej Duda made him the court's acting First President. Przemysław Wipler, reported by Gazeta Wyborcza to be an Opus Dei supernumerary (Opus Dei is a Catholic organisation whose lay members are encouraged to excel in public life), sits in the Sejm and since 2024 has been vice-chair of its inquiry into the Pegasus spyware. These are reports of membership and appointment, not findings of wrongdoing.

On China: in January 2019 Poland arrested Wang Weijing, a senior Huawei employee, and Piotr Durbajło, a cybersecurity expert who had worked for the Internal Security Agency, and charged both with working for Chinese intelligence. Both pleaded not guilty; the trial opened in 2021, closed to the public. Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski is on the official Bilderberg lists for 2024 and 2025. A 2026 case describes Rzeszów as a hub on a methamphetamine route running out of Western Europe into Ukraine. Poland appears in the patterns on churches and movements placing members in the state and on China's long arm.
Poland.imp: For people in Poland, the record shows a campaign group's co-founder moving into the foreign ministry and then to the head of the Supreme Court, the court whose rulings shape the law everyone lives under. The record reports appointments, not wrongdoing, but how judges are chosen affects whether courts are trusted as independent. What to watch: who is named to the courts and by which council, the outcome of the Huawei spying trial, and which ministers attend closed forums.

Portugal.d:
Portugal's main current case is a trial. Banco Espírito Santo was run by one of the banking families that had been close to power since the Salazar dictatorship; its chief, Ricardo Salgado, was nicknamed 'owner of all this', and the bank collapsed in 2014. In Operation Marquês prosecutors charge that former Prime Minister José Sócrates (2005–11) received undue payments, including money they link to the Espírito Santo group, and charge Salgado with three counts of corruption and eight of money laundering. A judge threw out most charges in 2021, the Lisbon Court of Appeal reinstated them in 2024, and the trial began on 3 July 2025; all defendants are presumed innocent. In a separate case from the same investigation, Salgado's sentence for breach of trust was raised to eight years on appeal in 2023.

Portugal's coast also sits on a cocaine route. An April 2026 operation between the Canaries and the Azores seized 11 tonnes from mother ships that pass loads at sea to small boats landing on remote Portuguese and Spanish coastline.

The older background is Aginter Press, set up in Lisbon in 1966 under Salazar and run by former French officer Yves Guérin-Sérac. It called itself a news agency but trained members in bombing and sabotage; an Italian magistrate told parliament in 1997 that its instructors taught Italian neo-fascists to use explosives. José Manuel Durão Barroso, later prime minister and European Commission president, was on a 1993 World Economic Forum young leaders list, a selection rather than a finding of influence. Portugal sits in the patterns on banks and banking families and the Cold War anticommunist web.
Portugal.imp: For people in Portugal, the record shows a bank tied to a powerful family reaching, by the prosecution's account, as far as a prime minister. Whether that is proven is now up to the court. What to watch: the Operation Marquês verdict, how the ownership and lending of large banks is supervised, and the remote stretches of coastline where cocaine is being landed from boats at sea.

Romania.d:
Romania has two documented cases, and both are still open questions. In September 2019 the magazine Newsweek România, citing anonymous Masonic sources, reported that Mihai Fifor, then interim interior minister and deputy prime minister, had joined Freemasonry in 2008, and that General Constantin Florea, head of the Gendarmerie, a national police force, belonged to the same lodge, Loja Basarab. Neither had declared membership in their interest declarations, which the magazine said the law required. Fifor neither confirmed nor denied it. The claim rests on that one outlet, and being a Mason is lawful; the question it raises is the undeclared interest. In the same report Costin Mihalache, head of the Government Chancellery and a former foreign-intelligence officer, said he had been a Mason but no longer was.

The second case is about money. In February 2026 French and Romanian authorities broke up a network laundering €306 million of drug and tax-evasion proceeds through front companies and property, using invoices for services never performed; 13 people were arrested and the case is at the charge stage. Romania sits in the patterns on lodges inside police forces and courts and on criminal money in banks and firms.
Romania.imp: For people in Romania, the record raises two questions rather than answering them: whether officials who run the police declare the private networks they belong to, as the law requires, and how easily front companies can move criminal money with fake invoices. What to watch: whether interest declarations are checked and enforced, and the outcome of the 2026 laundering case.

Russia.d:
Today the Russian state reaches into companies more directly than almost any country here. In April 2023 President Putin signed Decree 302, which lets the state take "temporary management" of businesses owned by companies from "unfriendly" countries. On 16 July 2023 the federal property agency, Rosimushchestvo, took control of Danone's Russian business and Carlsberg's Baltika Breweries. Yakub Zakriev, Chechnya's agriculture minister and a nephew of Ramzan Kadyrov, was made head of Danone Russia, and Taimuraz Bolloyev, a former Putin campaign representative, head of Baltika. Carlsberg said it was not told. The utilities of Fortum and Uniper had been taken the same way that April.

Money is the second thread. Bank Rossiya was refounded in 1991 by businessmen who later shared the Ozero dacha cooperative with Vladimir Putin. In 2014 the US Treasury called it "the personal bank for senior officials", and it remains under US and EU sanctions. Exchanges and mixers run from Russia, among them BTC-e, Suex, Garantex and Cryptex, have been sanctioned or prosecuted abroad for moving darknet and ransomware money. Garantex lost its Estonian licence and kept operating from Moscow.

Russia also reaches into international bodies. Richard McLaren's 2016 reports for the World Anti-Doping Agency found that the sports ministry and the FSB, Russia's main security service, ran a cover-up that hid at least 643 positive samples. Interpol, which lets police forces share wanted-person alerts, refused Russian requests against critics as political, and since March 2022 checks every Russian alert before it goes out. The US says the antivirus maker Kaspersky has ties to the FSB; Kaspersky denies it, and the US banned its sales in 2024.

At home, courts convicted a Krasnodar gang that operated under police protection until it murdered 12 people in Kushchyovskaya in 2010, and Moscow drug officers who planted narcotics on a journalist. Other cases failed: Spain acquitted Duma deputy Vladislav Reznik of mafia laundering in 2018, and investor Michael Calvey's conviction was vacated in 2024. Russia itself banned the US-funded National Endowment for Democracy in 2015 and the Moscow Church of Scientology; no independent body has found NED working inside Russian institutions.

The oldest background is Alexander Kerensky, head of a Masonic lodge, who became prime minister in 1917, and a claim that banker Jacob Schiff funded the Bolsheviks, an antisemitic myth that his firm's records contradict. Russia is the sponsoring state behind the map's networks in Europe and Africa.
Russia.imp: For people in Russia, the state and its security services can take over a business, choose who runs it, and protect a bank tied to the president's circle, and few courts will undo it. Russian services that move criminal money keep working at home after being sanctioned abroad. How far Kaspersky shares data with the FSB is a US claim the company denies, not a proven fact. Watch which foreign-owned firms are put under "temporary management" next, and who is appointed to run them.

San Marino.d:
San Marino's entry is one bribery case, and its final ruling came in March 2022, when an appeal court upheld most of the convictions with lower sentences. The case is known as "Conto Mazzini", after a bank account at Banca Commerciale Sammarinese held in the name of "Giuseppe Mazzini". Prosecutors said construction and banking entrepreneurs drew cash from it to pay politicians for building permits and banking licences, the permissions that decide who may build and who may run a bank in the country.

Twenty-one former political figures, including former state secretaries Fiorenzo Stolfi and Claudio Podeschi, went on trial in 2015 for criminal association to launder bribes, and about 200 million euros were seized. Several were convicted in 2017. The network was based in San Marino, and the map scores its reach outside the country as low.
San Marino.imp: For people in San Marino, the case showed that building permits and banking licences could be bought, and that courts did convict former state secretaries for it. In a state this small, a few officials decide who can build or open a bank, so a handful of payments can shape the whole economy. Watch how licences are granted now and what becomes of the money that was seized.

Serbia.d:
A court case now running in Belgrade asks how far Serbia's state security service was tied to a violent criminal group. Prosecutors charging the Belivuk-Miljkovic group from 2021 produced evidence that its members held state security identification and could enter protected facilities, and a former head of the security service was later charged in connection with them. The case is not concluded, and who is to blame remains contested in Serbian politics.

It has a precedent. In 2003 Prime Minister Zoran Djindjic was shot by a serving commander of the interior ministry's special operations unit, the JSO, which had merged with the Zemun criminal clan, a group with a share of the Balkan heroin trade. Twelve people were convicted in 2007 and the unit was disbanded.

The older background is the army's secret brotherhoods. In 1903 officers led by Dragutin Dimitrijević "Apis" killed King Alexander Obrenović and Queen Draga. In 1911 Apis and others founded Unification or Death, the Black Hand, which dominated the army, and in 1913 he became chief of military intelligence. Many scholars hold he sanctioned the 1914 Sarajevo assassination. He was court-martialled and shot in 1917; in 1953 Serbia's Supreme Court acquitted him for lack of proof. A rival group, the White Hand, put General Petar Živković in office as prime minister in 1929.
Serbia.imp: For people in Serbia, the question is whether parts of the police and security service still work with criminal groups, as the special operations unit did when it killed a prime minister in 2003. The Belivuk case may answer that, but it is still in court and the charges are not proven. Watch how the trial of the former security chief ends and whether the evidence about state identification cards is tested in open court.

Slovakia.d:
No case on Slovakia's record is listed as happening now, but the two that matter most still shape its politics. In February 2018 journalist Ján Kuciak and his fiancée Martina Kušnírová were shot dead. His unfinished article, published by OCCRP partners on 28 February 2018, described Antonino Vadalà, an Italian businessman running farm companies in eastern Slovakia who had been named in investigations into the 'Ndrangheta, the Calabrian mafia. It showed that Mária Trošková, who had co-founded a company with Vadalà in 2011, had become chief state adviser to Prime Minister Robert Fico. Trošková and Security Council secretary Viliam Jasaň stepped aside, saying their names were being misused, and Fico resigned in March 2018 after mass protests. No court has found that the prime minister's office acted for the 'Ndrangheta.

The second case involves a foreign government. In July 2017 Trinh Xuan Thanh, a former Vietnamese state-company executive seeking asylum, was seized in Berlin; Germany blamed Vietnamese intelligence. In 2019 a Slovak journalist found a €17,000 interior ministry invoice to Vietnam for a flight to Moscow on 26 July 2017, and former president Andrej Kiska wrote that then interior minister Robert Kaliňák was behind lending the plane. Thanh was later given life in Hanoi. Slovakia sits in the map's patterns on organised crime inside the state (suspected) and governments buying officials abroad (target country).
Slovakia.imp: For people in Slovakia, these cases show two routes in: a businessman named in mafia inquiries getting close to the prime minister's office, and a foreign spy service apparently using a Slovak government plane. Neither has been proven in a Slovak court. Kuciak's reporting brought down a government, which shows public pressure can work. Watch who sits close to the prime minister, and how ministries account for the use of state aircraft.

Slovenia.d:
Slovenia has one documented case, and it ended without a valid conviction. Patria is a Finnish state-owned arms maker. In 2006 Slovenia signed a 278 million euro deal with it for 135 armoured vehicles. In 2008 the Finnish broadcaster YLE alleged that Patria paid bribes to win the contract, partly aimed at Prime Minister Janez Janša.

A Ljubljana court sentenced Janša to two years in prison on 5 June 2013. The Constitutional Court annulled the verdict, and in 2016 the case lapsed. In Finland the defendants were acquitted on appeal, and in Austria one middleman was convicted. The map places Slovenia under "exposure, purge and reversal" because a court overturned the finding. Other bodies listed as present, such as Azerbaijan's "caviar diplomacy" network and the Trilateral Commission, have no documented case here, and Slovenia's overall score is minimal.
Slovenia.imp: For people in Slovenia, the Patria case shows how arms contracts, worth hundreds of millions of euros, invite bribes, and how hard they are to prove: the only conviction of the prime minister was annulled. One middleman was convicted in Austria, so money did move, but no court has said who in Slovenia received it. Watch how future defence purchases are tendered and who acts as go-between.

Spain.d:
Today Spain's most active cases are about cocaine and the people paid to let it through. Algeciras, the country's largest container port, sits eight miles from Morocco, and the smuggling networks around it recruit from the municipal police, customs and the port workforce. In April 2024 a municipal officer and two national police officers were each sentenced to more than seven years for guarding a 367-kilogram cocaine load; a 2022 operation arrested five municipal officers, a customs official and others over 6.2 tonnes. Prosecutors have also charged airport ground staff with moving drugs past security, charged crime figures with using football clubs and transfer fees to clean money, and in January 2025 arrested 23 people running a laundering service for other criminals that handled around 100 million euros.

At the top of government, Pegasus spyware, which its maker NSO sells only to governments, was found on Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's phone in 2021. The High Court reopened the case in April 2024; no state has been named. Two ministers attended the private Bilderberg conference in Madrid in 2024, and King Felipe VI was reported present.

The older story is Opus Dei, a Catholic organisation whose lay members follow its spiritual programme in ordinary jobs. From 1957 Franco appointed its members to run finance, trade, development planning and foreign affairs; historians count eight among his 116 ministers. After the 1969 MATESA export-credit scandal, Franco pardoned the charged ex-ministers before any verdict, and the new cabinet had eleven members tied to Opus Dei. Jorge Fernández Díaz, interior minister from 2011 to 2016, is reported to be a member. A 2024 book claims the failed Banco Popular channelled money to Opus Dei causes; Opus Dei calls this false.

Further back sit Operation Necora (1990), which exposed Galicia's cocaine clans, and a 1990 inquiry into a stay-behind network. Spain belongs to the map's patterns on organised crime, criminal money and religious movements in government.
Spain.imp: For people in Spain, the clearest danger today is police, customs and port staff being paid to let cocaine through, which courts have proven in Algeciras. Spyware on the prime minister's phone shows a foreign government may have reached the top, though no state is named. Opus Dei's hold on Franco's ministries is history; its influence now is reported, not proven. Watch the port and airport prosecutions and the reopened Pegasus case.

Sweden.d:
Sweden is a country with strong institutions, but its main problem today is criminal networks getting inside them. A November 2023 research review by Carina Gunnarson for the SNS think tank found that criminal networks have infiltrated government agencies, run companies in the welfare sector and exploit social insurance, with incorrect welfare payments estimated at SEK 13–16.3 billion a year. Municipalities, which spend much public money locally with weaker oversight, are the most exposed. Swedish courts have convicted police employees of passing register data to the networks, and a Security Service officer of unauthorised disclosure.

Banks are the second thread. In 2020 the Swedish regulator fined Swedbank 4 billion kronor over high-risk flows through its Baltic branches, and Nordea and SEB were censured over similar flows; how much was drug money has never been separated out.

The Wallenberg family is the third. Its foundations own about 23% of Investor AB but hold just over 50% of the votes, and through it the family has major stakes in Ericsson, ABB, Saab, SEB and others; one 2025 estimate puts its share of the Stockholm market at about 35%. This control is legal and disclosed. In the Second World War the government used the family's bankers for trade talks, and the US seized American Bosch in 1943, treating the bank's purchase as cloaking enemy property.

In June 2025 the private Bilderberg conference met in Stockholm, and Reuters reported Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson attended though he was not on the published list. The older background includes the 1973 IB affair, when journalists revealed a secret military intelligence bureau spying on the left.
Sweden.imp: For people in Sweden, the risk is less about the top of government and more about everyday services: welfare companies, municipal contracts and police registers that criminal networks have reached, as courts and researchers have shown. A single family's voting control over much of the stock market is legal and public, but it concentrates economic power. Watch how municipalities check welfare contractors, and whether the Prime Minister's private meetings appear on published lists.

Switzerland.d:
Switzerland is home to many of the bodies other countries' stories run through, and much of its record is about what happens in them now. Swiss courts have convicted the commodity traders Glencore and Trafigura of bribery failures, and in 2022 Credit Suisse became the first major Swiss bank convicted of a crime, for failing to stop laundering by a Bulgarian cocaine group. In 2024 a Zug software firm running encrypted messaging apps was sanctioned by the US under its drug order, and in 2026 investigators followed a laundering service used by both the Camorra and the 'Ndrangheta through Swiss shell companies.

Foreign governments hire Swiss firms too. From 2017 the United Arab Emirates paid the Geneva firm Alp Services at least €5.7m to build files on about 1,000 people and feed names into bank-compliance databases; criminal cases were reported open in 2025, and Alp says some files were falsified.

Geneva and Basel host international bodies that outsiders try to sway. Leaked documents reported in 2017 showed Philip Morris campaigning to weaken the WHO tobacco treaty. The Gates Foundation was the WHO's second-largest funder in 2020, mostly for its own chosen programmes. In Basel the Bank for International Settlements, owned by central banks, hosts governors' closed meetings and writes the bank-capital rules parliaments adopt; its outlines are public.

The biggest past case is Crypto AG, a Swiss firm that sold encryption machines to over 120 governments. The CIA and West Germany's BND secretly owned it from 1970 and read customers' messages; a 2020 Swiss inquiry found Swiss intelligence knew and benefited. FIFA's base in Zurich brought US bribery charges over the 2018 and 2022 World Cup votes and the exit of attorney general Michael Lauber over unrecorded meetings with FIFA's president. Older still are P-26, a secret army dissolved in 1990, and the Rockefeller Foundation's funding of the League of Nations.
Switzerland.imp: For people in Switzerland, the country's banks, traders and lawyers are where much of the world's dirty money and influence is handled, and courts have now convicted several big names. Decisions made in Geneva and Basel, on health, tobacco and bank rules, affect people far beyond Swiss borders. The Crypto AG case shows that Swiss authorities knew of foreign spying and benefited. Watch the commodity traders, the UAE-Alp cases, and who funds the WHO.

Ukraine.d:
Ukraine's record is mostly current and mostly about money and the war with Russia. In November 2025 the National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) said a group led by Timur Mindich, a friend of President Zelensky, ran a $100 million kickback scheme on contractors of Energoatom, the state nuclear power company. Mindich left Ukraine hours before his home was searched. A former deputy prime minister was charged, Zelensky asked the justice and energy ministers to resign, and chief of staff Andriy Yermak later became a suspect.

Russia reaches in through companies and the church. In October 2022 the security service detained Viacheslav Bohuslaiev, former president of the engine maker Motor Sich, who is on trial for treason over hidden supply channels to Russia arranged with the Russian state corporation Rostec. In August 2024 parliament banned the Russian Orthodox Church, whose patriarch backs the war, and gave linked Ukrainian bodies nine months to cut ties.

Banks are the older thread. Ihor Kolomoisky co-founded PrivatBank, the largest bank, and was a regional governor in 2014–15. The state nationalised the bank in 2016 with a $5.6 billion bailout; he was arrested in 2023 and charged with embezzling about $250 million. Customs and border officers at the Zakarpattia crossings have been charged with running smuggling channels into the EU. In 2022 BlackRock agreed with Zelensky to help design a framework for rebuilding the country.
Ukraine.imp: For people in Ukraine, the money most at risk is the money that keeps the country running: the nuclear power company, the largest bank, and the funds for rebuilding. Anti-corruption bodies are charging people close to the president, which shows they can act, but most cases are charges, not verdicts yet. Russia's reach through companies and the church is being cut by law. Watch how the Midas and Motor Sich trials end and who controls reconstruction money.

United Kingdom.d:
Britain's record is one of the longest on the map, and much of it is still moving. Since December 2025 the Metropolitan Police, London's force, makes officers and staff declare membership of the Freemasons, a fraternal society whose members meet privately in lodges. By February 2026, 397 had declared, and the High Court refused the United Grand Lodge of England's challenge. Foreign states are reaching in too. In 2022 MI5, the domestic security service, warned MPs that solicitor Christine Lee had worked covertly with the Chinese Communist Party's United Front Work Department, its influence arm; a tribunal upheld the warning in 2024. Businessman Yang Tengbo, a guest of Prince Andrew, was excluded in 2023. The China spying charges against parliamentary researcher Christopher Cash were dropped in 2025. On Russia's side, former MEP Nathan Gill was jailed in November 2025 for taking bribes to make pro-Russian statements for a network linked to Viktor Medvedchuk, and six Bulgarians run from Moscow by ex-Wirecard executive Jan Marsalek were jailed for spying. Google reports North Korean IT workers taking jobs in British firms. Hizb ut-Tahrir, a party calling for a caliphate, has been banned as terrorist since January 2024.

Companies and money form the second strand. The Grenfell inquiry (2024) found cladding makers Arconic, Celotex and Kingspan deceived the fire-safety testing system before a fire that killed 72. PPE Medpro must repay about £122 million from pandemic 'VIP lane' contracts. Big Four accountants were seconded to the Treasury to help write tax law (2013). The Serious Fraud Office dropped its BAE Systems inquiry in 2006 under Saudi and British pressure. HSBC, Standard Chartered and Entain settled over money laundering and bribery, and Scottish Limited Partnerships let anonymous companies be formed for a few pounds. Shipping lobbies sit inside the London-based UN maritime body's climate talks.

The older background: a 1997 Commons committee examined Freemasonry in police and courts, after cases such as Operation Countryman. Rothschild banks moved Britain's war money in 1814 and lent for the Suez shares in 1875; the claim that the family profited from early Waterloo news is an antisemitic myth historians reject. Carroll Quigley described a Milner–Round Table network placing men near power; that account is his.

Britain is a target of China's and Russia's networks, a home for lodges, banks and private forums, and a proven case of industries inside regulators.
United Kingdom.imp: For people in Britain, the main risks today are less about secret oaths than about who writes the rules and who checks them. Firms that seconded staff to the Treasury, cladding makers that gamed safety tests and contractors given fast-track deals all reached decisions that affect homes, taxes and health. Foreign governments have tried to buy or cultivate MPs and researchers. Some protections now exist: Freemason declarations in the Met, a foreign-interference alert system, court cases that end in prison terms. Watch whether the Grenfell contract bans happen and whether MPs' outside roles are declared.

Vatican City.d:
The Holy See, the government of the Catholic Church, runs from Vatican City, and its main live case is a trial that has not finished. Cardinal Angelo Becciu, the Secretariat of State's number two from 2011 to 2018, was convicted of embezzlement in December 2023 over a €350 million London property deal. In March 2026 the Vatican appeals court nullified the indictment, citing unpublished papal decrees and undisclosed evidence, and ordered a retrial from 22 June 2026. The conviction is not standing.

The Vatican also reaches outward. The Sovereign Military Order of Malta is a Catholic order recognised as a sovereign body, with diplomatic ties to 115 states and UN observer status. In 2017 Pope Francis forced out its Grand Master; in September 2022 he rewrote its constitution and named its governing council himself, and the Order re-elected his appointees in 2023.

The background is the Vatican Bank, the Institute for the Works of Religion (IOR). It was the main shareholder of Banco Ambrosiano, an Italian bank that collapsed in 1982, and its letters of comfort stood behind loans to Panama shell companies. In 1984 it paid creditors $224 million, citing 'moral involvement'. Milan magistrates issued a warrant for its president, Archbishop Paul Marcinkus, in 1987, but Italy's top court ruled the 1929 Lateran Treaty shielded him and he was never tried. In 2021 the Vatican court convicted former IOR president Angelo Caloia of embezzlement. In 2016 a finance official was jailed for leaking documents.

It belongs to the banking and hidden-money patterns as a bank headquarters, and to the exposure pattern as a place where a court reversed a finding. Its conditions scores borrow Italy's figures.
Vatican City.imp: Few people live in Vatican City, but the Holy See handles money given by Catholics worldwide. The cases show that its own bank and offices have lost or misused large sums, and that a treaty once kept its bank chief out of an Italian court. Its own court now tries cardinals, but the Becciu retrial shows how papal decrees made outside public view can undo a verdict. Watch the retrial and whether the rules it turns on are published.

North Macedonia.d: North Macedonia's foreign minister is part of a World Economic Forum programme. The Forum, the organiser of the yearly Davos meeting, picks people under about 40 each year for its Young Global Leaders programme, a five-year network of meetings and courses. Its class of 2025 included Timčo Mucunski, North Macedonia's Minister of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade, the office that handles relations and trade deals with other countries. The record rates this probable and current. Membership is documented; no forum has found that the programme directs his decisions, and joining it is not wrongdoing. Also present are the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic status, and the Gülen movement is thought likely to be present though undocumented. North Macedonia sits in the pattern of private forums where officials meet money, as a country with a member placed in office. Its scores show a fairly high level of criminal actors inside the state and middling resilience.
North Macedonia.imp: A minister in charge of foreign trade is meeting regularly with a network of business and political figures chosen by a private forum. That is legal and public, but residents do not see what is discussed or whether it shapes trade positions. Watch how the minister declares outside programmes and whether trade decisions favour firms linked to the forum.

Antigua and Barbuda.d:
Antigua and Barbuda's documented case is finished, but its effects are still felt. R. Allen Stanford, a Texan financier, ran Stanford International Bank from Antigua and was convicted in the US of a $7 billion fraud. A bank of that size in a small country depends on its regulator, the body meant to check the bank's books. A June 2009 US indictment charges Leroy King, then head of Antigua's Financial Services Regulatory Commission, with taking more than $100,000 in bribes from Stanford to ignore the bank's real assets and to help obstruct an investigation by the US Securities and Exchange Commission. Antigua extradited King to Houston in November 2019. The charge against King is an indictment, not a conviction.

The Order of Malta and the Sun Kian Ip Group of Ng Lap Seng are also recorded as present. Antigua belongs to the pattern on banks and banking families, as a case that is over but still felt, and is the home of the Stanford group.
Antigua and Barbuda.imp: For people in Antigua and Barbuda, the case shows how one bank can grow larger than the office meant to supervise it. If the head regulator was paid, as charged, the checks that protect depositors and the country's name in banking did not work. Small offshore centres depend on trust from foreign banks, and a scandal like this raises costs for everyone. Watch how the regulator is staffed and who oversees it.

Barbados.d: Nothing is documented for Barbados on this map yet. English Freemasonry, the United Grand Lodge of England, is likely to be present but has no recorded case. The conditions score is low: the state has few signs of outside actors embedded in it and fairly strong checks and balances. As a best guess, the most likely route in would be through the island's banking and offshore business, as in other small Caribbean financial centres on this map, rather than through the cabinet or police. This is an estimate, not a finding.
Barbados.imp: For people in Barbados, the map has no case to report, and the conditions are better than in most countries. A blank record means nothing has been documented, not that nothing could happen. The area to watch is offshore finance: who sets up companies there, and how foreign banks and regulators treat the island.

Belize.d:
Belize's one documented case is historical and contested. In September 2013 Prime Minister Dean Barrow removed Elvin Penner, minister of state for immigration, after Penner was accused of selling and issuing a Belizean passport to a South Korean man, Kim Won Hong, who was then jailed in Taiwan. An immigration minister matters because he controls who can become a citizen and travel on the country's passport. Penner was charged in March 2014, but the charges were dropped in July 2014 for lack of evidence, so nothing was proven.

The Order of Malta and the citizenship-by-investment industry, which sells passports to foreign buyers in several countries, are recorded as present. Belize falls under the patterns on organised crime inside the state and on exposure and reversal, both as a disputed case. The conditions score is moderate.
Belize.imp: For Belizeans, a passport is worth something only if other countries trust how it is issued. The Penner case was dropped, but it shows that a single official with power over passports can be a target for buyers abroad. Watch how passports and citizenship are granted and who checks the immigration department.

Colombia.d:
Colombia's sitting president, Gustavo Petro, was designated by the United States under its illicit-drug sanctions order in October 2025, citing rising coca cultivation and the handling of intelligence channels. This is a US executive designation, not a criminal charge; Colombia rejects it. Below the presidency, the drug trade is still reaching into the state: in 2023 a serving prosecutor was charged with holding property in her name for a front man of the Gulf Clan, the country's largest cocaine organisation. In February 2026 the last of the 'Cartel de la Toga' sentences came down: two former Supreme Court presidents, a magistrate and the national anti-corruption prosecutor were convicted of taking bribes to shelve cases against members of Congress.

Those Congress cases are the 'parapolítica' files. From 2006 roughly 30% of Congress was investigated over collusion with the AUC, right-wing paramilitaries who were also major cocaine traffickers; by 2012 five governors and 32 legislators had been convicted. Earlier, the Proceso 8000 case found the Cali cartel funded the 1994 presidential campaign. President Uribe's police security chief admitted aiding the AUC in a US court.

Companies are the second route. Chiquita pleaded guilty in 2007 to paying the AUC. The Brazilian builder Odebrecht put illegal money into President Santos's 2010 campaign, which he acknowledged. US Treasury lists show a stream of front companies, farms, emerald mines, a football club, property firms, run for La Oficina de Envigado and other groups, replaced about as fast as they are named. One Clan del Golfo trafficker used his laundered money to fund mayoral candidates.

Religion appears too: the MIRA party, tied to the Church of God Ministry of Jesus Christ, holds three Senate seats. Colombia is a proven case of organised crime inside the state and of criminal money inside firms.
Colombia.imp: For more than 30 years cocaine money has reached elections, Congress, the police and the top courts, and convictions have followed. Ordinary Colombians cannot easily see which local businesses are fronts or which candidates were funded by armed groups. The US designation of the president is disputed and untested in court. Watch prosecutions of officials who hold assets for traffickers, the Gulf Clan's reach into local politics, and whether further judges are investigated.

Costa Rica.d:
Costa Rica's documented cases are recent and come from drug trafficking through the country. In June 2025 police arrested Gamboa Sánchez, a former vice-minister of public security who later sat as a judge, on a US extradition request. The US Treasury designated him in August 2025, saying he helped move tens of millions of dollars' worth of Colombian cocaine through Costa Rica and used his government contacts to learn about counter-narcotics investigations. His removal became possible weeks after a constitutional change, signed in May 2025, allowed Costa Rican nationals to be extradited for drug trafficking. In the 2026 'Caso Colorado', five police officers stationed at Guápiles and Cariari de Pococí were charged with tipping off a trafficking group about raids and checkpoints on the Caribbean corridor. Neither case has reached a verdict.

The other entry is religious politics. Fabricio Alvarado, an evangelical Christian singer, reached the 2018 presidential runoff on opposition to a regional human-rights court ruling on same-sex marriage, and sat in the Legislative Assembly again from 2022 to 2026. That is an open political campaign, not a hidden network.

Costa Rica's overall score is low. It belongs to the patterns of organised crime inside the state and of churches placing members in government.
Costa Rica.imp: Trafficking groups are trying to buy information from inside the security ministry and local police, so raids can be warned of in advance. Both cases are charges, not convictions. The new extradition rule means officials accused of helping traffickers can now be sent for trial in the United States. Watch the Caso Colorado court case and whether more officials are named.

Cuba.d:
In Cuba the documented reach-in runs the other way: the state reaching into a private body. Since 2024 the Ministry of Justice, which registers all associations, has refused to recognise the newly elected leadership of the Grand Lodge of Cuba, the country's main Freemasons' organisation, after about $19,000 meant for a Masonic retirement home went missing and the Grand Master was expelled. This was reported by the independent outlet 14ymedio. A former senior lodge official who left in 2023 said a state-security officer had told him agents had watched Cuban lodges for over 40 years.

There is an earlier, admitted case. José Manuel Collera Vento became Grand Master in 2000 after government pressure. In 2011, after WikiLeaks cables exposed him, he said on state television that he had worked for state security as 'Agente Gerardo' and had been placed at the top of the lodge so the government could monitor Freemasons.

The older background is crime inside the state. In 1989 General Arnaldo Ochoa and an Interior Ministry colonel who ran the state's hard-currency operations were court-martialled for moving cocaine through Cuban waters and airspace, and executed in July 1989; the interior minister was jailed in the same purge.

Cuba scores minimal overall. It appears in the patterns of lodges watched by police and of organised crime inside the state.
Cuba.imp: For Cuban Freemasons, the record shows the government has placed its own agent at the head of their lodge and now decides whose election counts. Members cannot know who among them reports to state security. Watch whether the Justice Ministry recognises a lodge leadership, and whether other associations face the same treatment.

Dominica.d:
Dominica sells citizenship to foreign buyers, and that trade is the route into its government on this map. A 2023 investigation by the reporting network OCCRP found about 7,700 people had bought Dominican passports, among them Afghanistan's former spy chief and sanctioned Russians. The one documented case is an allegation, not a finding. Al Jazeera's investigative unit reported in November 2019 that Iranian businessman Alireza Monfared gave hundreds of thousands of dollars to Prime Minister Roosevelt Skerrit's 2014 election campaign in return for an ambassadorship and a diplomatic passport, which a witness said Skerrit handed over in Kuala Lumpur. Monfared was later jailed in Iran for stealing oil revenue. Skerrit denies any trade, and no court or inquiry has ruled on the claim.

Dominica's overall score is minimal, and the case is marked as only possible. It belongs with the citizenship-sale industry.
Dominica.imp: When a country sells passports and diplomatic titles, people with money from abroad can gain the protection of a government post. Dominicans cannot see who has bought citizenship or a diplomatic role. The Monfared claim is unproven and denied. Watch who is given diplomatic passports and whether the buyer lists are ever published.

Dominican Republic.d:
The Dominican Republic's two documented cases are both about money from outside reaching officials, and both still shape the country. The larger one involves Odebrecht, the Brazilian construction group. In 2016 it admitted to the United States that it had paid 92 million dollars in bribes in the Dominican Republic to win public works. In October 2021 a Dominican court convicted businessman Ángel Rondón, named as the channel for the bribes, and former public works minister Víctor Díaz Rúa; four other defendants were acquitted. An appeal court upheld both convictions on 19 May 2023.

The other case is drug trafficking inside the security forces. Three senior officials of the National Drug Control Agency (DNCD) were arrested while guarding traffickers waiting for a shipment to Puerto Rico; a navy port-security officer was accused of moving 800 kilograms to Spain; and in 2008 nearly twenty officials, mostly navy, were accused of killing seven Colombian traffickers to take 1.3 tonnes. Since 2009 more than 700 DNCD staff have been removed, about 200 suspected of trafficking, and police expelled about 1,400 officers from 2010.

The country belongs to the patterns of global firms buying governments and organised crime inside the state.
Dominican Republic.imp: A foreign builder paid ministers to win public works, and Dominicans paid for those contracts. Drug groups have recruited the very agencies meant to stop them, and the large number of dismissals shows how widespread it was. Watch how public contracts are awarded and whether the anti-drug agency's purges continue.

Ecuador.d:
Ecuador is living through the fastest rise of cocaine gangs on this map, and the gangs have reached its courts. The 'Metastasis' case began when prosecutors decrypted a trafficker's phone. In November 2024 the National Court sentenced 20 of 21 defendants, judges, prosecutors, police commanders and prison officials, for fixing cases and protecting traffickers; the former head of the Judiciary Council got more than nine years. A second file, 'Caso Purga', charges judges and a former legislator in Guayas province over paid releases. In 2026 the US listed the Chone Killers gang as a terrorist organisation, after Los Choneros and Los Lobos in 2025, and sanctioned a Manta fishing fleet that refuels cocaine boats at sea using state-subsidised fuel. Cocaine also leaves inside banana shipments through Guayaquil, with exporters, port staff and customs officials prosecuted.

President Daniel Noboa announced a deal in March 2025 with Erik Prince, founder of the US security firm Blackwater, to support Ecuador's forces against the gangs.

Foreign companies have bought officials before. Vice-President Jorge Glas was sentenced in 2017 for taking about $13.5 million from Odebrecht, the Brazilian builder; police seized him inside Mexico's embassy in 2024. In 2024 the Geneva oil trader Gunvor paid about $661 million in US and Swiss penalties and was convicted in Switzerland of corruption in Ecuador.

Guillermo Lasso, president from 2021 to 2023, has been reported as an Opus Dei supernumerary, a married lay member of the Catholic organisation; that is membership, not a finding of wrongdoing.

Ecuador is a proven case of organised crime inside the state and of criminal money inside firms, and a country where global firms paid officials.
Ecuador.imp: Gangs that move cocaine have paid judges, prosecutors and police, so a court ruling or a release order may have been bought. The Metastasis verdicts show some of it can be proven, and the court asked prosecutors to look at others named but not charged. Ordinary exporters, fishermen and port workers are recruited into the routes. Watch the Caso Purga trial, the role of Prince's contractors, and who is investigated next.

El Salvador.d:
El Salvador's government is accused by the United States of making a secret deal with its biggest street gangs. MS-13 is a gang that spans Central America and the US. In December 2021 the US Treasury sanctioned prisons director Osiris Luna and Carlos Marroquín, head of the government's Social Fabric Reconstruction Unit, for negotiating with MS-13 and Barrio 18 leaders: privileges and money inside the prisons in exchange for fewer killings and electoral support. A US indictment of 13 MS-13 leaders, unsealed on 23 February 2023, says the meetings 'were organized by the government of El Salvador and prison officials', that leaders got benefits and one wanted by the US was released, and that the gang backed President Bukele's Nuevas Ideas party in the 2021 election. Much of this was first reported by the newspaper El Faro from 2020.

President Bukele's government denies any pact, and no court has tried the claims against the officials. The indictment is against the gang leaders, not the officials.

El Salvador belongs to the pattern of organised crime inside the state.
El Salvador.imp: If the US findings are right, the fall in murders was partly bought from the gangs, and elections were touched by gang support. Salvadorans have no domestic court ruling on this, only US sanctions and an indictment, and the government denies it. Watch how the US case against the MS-13 leaders proceeds and what evidence it puts on the record.

Grenada.d:
Grenada sells citizenship to foreign investors and has given ambassador titles to foreign businessmen; that trade is the route in on this map. The one documented case is an allegation. Al Jazeera's investigative unit reported in November 2019 that investor Eric Resteiner claimed he paid about half a million dollars to Prime Minister Keith Mitchell. Mitchell said he received only 15,000 dollars, for travel costs. In the same report, US businessman Leo Ford said a partner was offered a diplomatic post in return for kickbacks on state projects, which the government denies. No court or inquiry has ruled on any of it.

Grenada scores minimal overall, and the case is marked as only possible. It sits with the citizenship-sale industry.
Grenada.imp: Where passports and diplomatic titles are for sale, foreign investors can buy closeness to the head of government. Grenadians cannot see who has paid for these posts or what was promised in return. The claims are disputed and unproven. Watch who receives ambassador titles and whether the government publishes who has bought citizenship.

Guyana.d:
Guyana is now treated by the United States as a route for cocaine heading north and across the Atlantic. On 5 June 2025 the US Treasury published a chart of how traffickers use the country, and designated six people: two men it says run Guyana's largest trafficking organisations, two Colombians managing hidden airstrips, a serving police officer accused of arranging safe passage for Mexican and Venezuelan traffickers, and a former officer wanted over the 2024 abduction of a policeman. None has been tried. Semi-submersible boats leave from Guyanese and Surinamese ports, and cocaine has been found buried in bunkers on jungle airstrips. Treasury called Guyana a close partner but named corruption as an obstacle.

Gold is the other route. In June 2024 the US sanctioned gold trader Nazar Mohamed, his son Azruddin and Mohamed's Enterprise for keeping over 10,000 kilograms of gold off customs declarations and evading more than 50 million dollars in duty. It said the firm bribed customs officials and paid for favours in court matters and state contracts. It also sanctioned Mae Thomas, a permanent secretary in the home affairs ministry, for taking cash for contract, gun-permit and passport favours. The Mohameds deny wrongdoing.
