The background is the Phantom Squad. In the mid-2000s trafficker Roger Khan ran an armed group that worked alongside the state during a wave of killings; he was convicted in New York. Its tie to the government was never settled in a Guyanese court.

Guyana is a proven case of organised crime inside the state and criminal money in firms.
Guyana.imp: Drug routes and gold smuggling both depend on police, customs and ministry officials who look away for money, according to US findings. Guyanese courts have not ruled on most of these cases. Watch whether the designated officers are charged at home, how gold exports are checked, and what happens to the airstrips in Barima-Waini.

Haiti.d:
Armed gangs, joined since 2023 in the Viv Ansanm alliance, control much of Haiti's capital, and the record shows politicians paying them. A UN panel of experts' report released in October 2026 accuses former legislator Alfredo Junior Antoine of arming groups and sponsoring a 2025 attack that killed more than 100 people, and former senator Nenel Cassy of controlling a gang in Miragoâne. It says former senator Youri Latortue's long use of gangs fuels violence ahead of elections, that a member of the new Cité Soleil municipal commission is an active gang member, and that some police officers supply gangs with guns and information. Antoine and Cassy deny it; these are allegations. Canada had already sanctioned Latortue and Senator Joseph Lambert in 2022 for financing gangs, and the US designated former president Michel Martelly in 2024 for sponsoring gangs and trafficking. Martelly denies it, and no court has heard it.

Jimmy Chérizier was a serving police officer until 2018 and then led the largest gang federation in Port-au-Prince; he was the first person on the UN's Haiti sanctions list.

A private company is now inside the security effort. Vectus Global, run by Blackwater founder Erik Prince, took part in anti-gang raids, as Haitian authorities confirmed in January 2026; Reuters reported Prince planned to stay ten years and help collect taxes.

The background includes Guy Philippe, a former police commander seized in 2017 days after winning a Senate seat and jailed in the US for laundering drug money; he returned to Haitian politics in 2023.

Haiti is a proven case of organised crime inside the state.
Haiti.imp: In Haiti the line between politicians and gangs is thin: officials and former lawmakers are accused of arming and paying groups that terrorise neighbourhoods. Most of this rests on sanctions and UN reports, not court verdicts. A foreign private company now takes part in policing. Watch who runs in the coming elections, what powers Vectus Global is given, and whether any accused politician is tried.

St. Kitts and Nevis.d:
St Kitts and Nevis has sold citizenship to foreign investors since 1984, and the industry that sells passports this way is based here. That programme is the country's one documented case. On 20 May 2014 the US Treasury's financial crimes unit, FinCEN, warned banks that several Iranians under US sanctions had obtained Kittitian passports through the programme, which it said 'maintains lax controls', and that Iranians kept getting them even after a 2013 suspension. A passport from a small country lets its holder travel and open accounts under a new nationality, which is why a sanctions agency cared.

The situation has since changed. FinCEN withdrew the warning on 24 February 2026, after the passports had expired and the programme had been reformed. The case is over but still affects how banks treat Kittitian citizenship. The country's overall score is minimal. It sits in the map's pattern on exposure, purge and reversal, where a government acts after a scheme is exposed.
St. Kitts and Nevis.imp: For people in St Kitts and Nevis, the record is about what the state sells rather than who sits inside it: citizenship bought by outsiders, including people under sanctions. The warning hurt the country's standing with banks until the programme was reformed. Watch who buys passports now, how buyers are checked, and whether outside agencies raise new concerns.

St. Lucia.d: Nothing is documented on this map for St Lucia yet; this write-up is an estimate. The only organisation recorded as present is the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order that holds diplomatic relations with many states; no case ties it to any wrongdoing here. The conditions scores are low: state-embedded actors at 3.0 out of 10 and resilience at 5.5, meaning there are few signs of outside groups embedded in the state and moderate ability to resist them. As a best guess, the likeliest route in would be money rather than membership, the kind seen in nearby small island states on this map, such as the passport sales recorded for St Kitts and Nevis.
St. Lucia.imp: For people in St Lucia, there is no recorded case of an outside group capturing part of the government. That is not proof that none exists, only that nothing has been documented. If a problem appears, the record of neighbouring islands suggests it would most likely come through financial services or schemes that sell something the state controls, so those are the places to watch.

St. Vincent and the Grenadines.d: Nothing is documented on this map for St Vincent and the Grenadines yet; this write-up is an estimate. The only organisation recorded as present is the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order that holds diplomatic relations with many states; no case ties it to any wrongdoing here. The conditions scores are among the lowest in the region: state-embedded actors at 2.0 out of 10 and resilience at 5.4, meaning few signs of outside groups inside the state and a moderate ability to resist them. As a best guess, the likeliest route in would be money, as on nearby islands on this map such as St Kitts and Nevis, where passport sales drew a US warning.
St. Vincent and the Grenadines.imp: For people in St Vincent and the Grenadines, no outside group has been recorded capturing part of the government. That means nothing has been documented, not that nothing could happen. Neighbouring islands suggest the risk lies in money: financial services, or anything the state can sell to outsiders. Those are the places to watch.

Suriname.d:
Suriname's record centres on one family at the top of the state, and its main cases are now closed, though their effects remain. Dési Bouterse was head of state and was later elected president twice. In 1999 a Dutch court convicted him in absentia of trafficking almost 500 kilograms of cocaine and sentenced him to eleven years, but with no extradition treaty the sentence was never carried out. A separate Surinamese case over the 1982 killing of fifteen political opponents, the 'December murders', took 16 years and ended in a 20-year sentence upheld in December 2023. He did not surrender, disappeared in January 2024 and died in hiding in December 2024, having served no time for either conviction.

His son Dino Bouterse ran Suriname's Counter-Terrorism Unit while his father was president. The DEA lured him to Panama and arrested him in August 2013. He pleaded guilty in New York to cocaine trafficking, weapons offences and offering a base in Suriname to people he believed were from Hezbollah, the Lebanese armed movement; they were in fact DEA informants. He was sentenced in March 2015 to about 16 years.

The US-funded National Endowment for Democracy is also recorded as present. Suriname's conditions score is high at 7.67, with signs of outside actors embedded in the state and weak resistance to them. It belongs to the pattern on organised crime inside the state, as a case where a head of state and the head of a security unit were both proven traffickers.
Suriname.imp: For people in Suriname, the record shows a president convicted of cocaine trafficking who still won two elections, and his son using a counter-terrorism unit while dealing drugs. Neither conviction was enforced at home in the father's lifetime. The conditions score suggests the weaknesses that allowed this remain. Watch who controls the security services, and whether courts can enforce their rulings against powerful people.

Argentina.d:
Argentina's record runs from the 1970s to now, and the cases that matter most today are in the courts and the economy ministry. Former President Cristina Fernández de Kirchner faces two trials. In the 'Notebooks' case, which opened in November 2025 with 87 defendants, prosecutors allege construction and energy contractors paid officials cash for public-works contracts from 2003 to 2015; she denies it. Separately, the Supreme Court ruled in December 2024 that she must stand trial for covering up for Iran over the 1994 bombing of the AMIA Jewish centre, through a 2013 pact with Iran. These are charges, not verdicts.

Drug money has reached the police and the courts. Hugo Tognoli, head of Santa Fe province's police, was convicted in 2016 of protecting a trafficking network around Rosario, and a federal judge in Orán was sentenced in 2019 to 13 years for selling rulings to traffickers.

Today's government draws on two networks. Luis Caputo, a former JPMorgan and Deutsche Bank executive, has been economy minister since December 2023, and the central bank president, Santiago Bausili, also worked at JPMorgan. President Javier Milei won a prize from Fundación Atlas in 2018, and the Atlas Network, a US-based network of free-market think tanks, says its partners helped push his reforms; that is the network's own claim. Holding office after working at a bank or think tank is not wrongdoing; the record shows where the people come from.

The older background is the P2 lodge, a secret Italian Masonic lodge led by Licio Gelli. Lists seized in 1981 named Argentine ministers and commanders as members, including interim president Raúl Lastiri, welfare minister José López Rega, whose ministry funded the Triple A death squad, and junta member Admiral Emilio Massera. In 1974 Perón's government gave Gelli a state honour and a diplomatic post. In 2016 an Argentine court convicted 15 officers, including ex-dictator Reynaldo Bignone, for Operation Condor, the coordinated repression of regional dictatorships. Argentina sits in the patterns on organised crime in the state, banks and banking families, private forums, and the anticommunist web.
Argentina.imp: For Argentines, the record shows that public-works money, the courts and provincial police have been reached by contractors and traffickers, and several of those cases ended in convictions. The economy and central bank are run by people from the big foreign banks Argentina owes money to, which shapes how debt is handled. Watch the Notebooks and Iran-pact trials, how Atlas-linked groups shape new laws, and whether trafficking cases in Rosario and Salta reach officials.

Bahamas.d:
The Bahamas has two cases, both about banking. The one happening now is quieter: global banks have been withdrawing 'correspondent' relationships, the links that let local banks move money abroad, from small Caribbean countries faster than anywhere else, on grounds of compliance cost. International bodies such as the IMF and World Bank report that legitimate remittances and trade then move to less transparent channels, while trafficking money never depended on those links. This is marked as possible, not proven.

The older case is Banco Ambrosiano Overseas in Nassau, a subsidiary of Banco Ambrosiano, the bank run by Calvi. Archbishop Paul Marcinkus, president of the Vatican Bank, had been a director. After Ambrosiano collapsed in 1982, Bahamian authorities suspended the Nassau unit's operations. The Nassau and Luxembourg units owed about half of the $1.2–1.4 billion lent to shell companies in Panama. The Bahamas sits in the patterns on banks and banking families and banks that carried hidden money, as a booking centre. English Freemasonry and BCCI are likely but undocumented.
Bahamas.imp: For people in the Bahamas, the banking rules made abroad decide whether ordinary families can send and receive money cheaply. When foreign banks pull out, legitimate users are pushed to costlier or less visible channels, while criminal money finds other routes. The Ambrosiano case shows how an offshore unit can hold a large share of hidden debt. Watch for further bank withdrawals and for how the regulator responds.

Bolivia.d:
In Bolivia, the people meant to fight the drug trade have been the ones reached by it. In October 2025 a US jury in Manhattan convicted Maximiliano Dávila, head of the national anti-narcotics force (FELCN) until 2019; he was sentenced in March 2026 to 25 years. Prosecutors showed he steered investigations away from allied traffickers and assigned armed officers to guard cocaine loads. An earlier FELCN commander, René Sanabria, pleaded guilty in Miami in 2011 after a sting and got 14 years. In June 2025 the Financial Action Task Force, the global anti-money-laundering body, added Bolivia to its list of countries under increased monitoring.

The background is the 1980 'cocaine coup', in which General Luis García Meza seized power. His interior minister, Luis Arce Gómez, was given a life sentence by a Rome appeals court in 2019 in the Operation Condor case. Journalist Robert Parry reported that the Unification Church of Sun Myung Moon backed the coup, that Moon's aide Bo Hi Pak met García Meza, and that Bolivian investigations found Moon's group invested about $4 million; this rests on one author's account. Bolivia sits in the patterns on organised crime inside the state and the anticommunist web.
Bolivia.imp: For Bolivians, the anti-drug police, the body meant to protect them from traffickers, was twice led by men later convicted of working for them. Both cases were proven in US courts, not Bolivian ones. Being on the international watch list makes banking with the outside world harder and costlier. Watch who is appointed to lead the anti-narcotics force and whether cases are brought at home.

Brazil.d:
Brazil has the fullest record in this group, and the largest current case is organised crime inside companies and the money system. The PCC (Primeiro Comando da Capital) is Brazil's largest criminal organisation. In 2024 São Paulo prosecutors charged that two city bus companies, Transwolff and UpBus, laundered PCC money through public transport contracts, and the city took both over. From August 2025 Operation Carbono Oculto traced about 26 billion reais of PCC money through investment funds and fintechs in São Paulo's financial district, and a fuel chain with more than a thousand petrol stations selling adulterated petrol. Firms named deny wrongdoing; most of this is still under investigation. Officials are reached too: São Paulo police are charged with shielding PCC members, and in February 2026 the Supreme Court convicted the Brazão brothers, a federal deputy and an audit-court counsellor, of ordering the 2018 murder of councillor Marielle Franco, linked to land in militia-held west Rio.

Companies have bought officials. The trader Trafigura pleaded guilty in the US in 2024 to bribing officials at the state oil company Petrobras. Operation Car Wash charged 429 people, but former President Lula's convictions were annulled in 2021 because the court lacked jurisdiction. JBS owner Joesley Batista's recording led to bribery charges against President Temer in 2017, which Congress did not let proceed.

Churches are organised inside Congress, openly. The Evangelical Parliamentary Front registers 213 of 513 deputies; the Republicanos party was founded by Universal Church pastors, and its leader is a bishop. André Mendonça, a Presbyterian pastor, sits on the Supreme Court. The farm caucus's agenda is drafted by a think tank funded by groups including Bayer, Cargill and JBS.

The older background includes a CIA-linked institute funding 1962 candidates, the 1964 coup, US NSA spying on President Rousseff in 2013, and the 2005 'mensalão' vote-buying scheme run through Banco Rural. Brazil sits in nearly every pattern, from organised crime in banks and firms to churches in the state.
Brazil.imp: For Brazilians, criminal money now runs through things they use daily: city buses, petrol stations and investment funds. Adulterated fuel harms drivers directly. Large firms have paid officials at Petrobras, and some politicians accused have had cases dropped or annulled. Churches and agribusiness are organised in Congress openly, so their influence is legal but large. Watch the Carbono Oculto prosecutions, the São Paulo police case and how fintechs are now regulated.

Canada.d:
Canada's most serious open file today is about other governments. A federal public inquiry led by Justice Marie-Josée Hogue reported on 28 January 2025 that China is the 'most active' state interfering in Canada, working through diplomats, proxies and the United Front Work Department, the Chinese Communist Party body that builds influence over overseas Chinese communities and foreign elites. It named India second and cited intelligence that India's proxy agents may have given, and may still give, illicit money to Canadian politicians. A parliamentary security committee had reported in June 2024 that some unnamed MPs and senators were 'witting' participants; Hogue found no 'traitors' in Parliament but some 'concerning conduct'. China and India reject the findings.

The Indian case turns on the 18 June 2023 killing of Sikh activist Hardeep Singh Nijjar in Surrey. In October 2024 Canada expelled six Indian diplomats, and the RCMP said agents of India's government had used the Lawrence Bishnoi gang to target Sikhs in Canada. Canada listed the gang as a terrorist entity in September 2025; a US indictment of July 2026 charges Bishnoi with directing the killing but does not allege an Indian government role. On China, a consular officer was expelled in 2023 over a plan to target MP Michael Chong's relatives, while the RCMP closed its probe of alleged Chinese 'police stations' without charges, and ex-officer William Majcher was acquitted in May 2026 (prosecutors are appealing).

Organised crime reaches inside too. Cameron Ortis, a senior RCMP intelligence director, was convicted of offering police material to targets including the head of the encrypted-phone firm Phantom Secure, and was jailed for 14 years. Border officers have been convicted of waving drug loads through. Inquiries found Mafia cuts on Montreal public works and bags of cash accepted at BC casinos.

Among companies, the ethics commissioner found in 2019 that Prime Minister Trudeau broke conflict law by pressing his attorney general to help SNC-Lavalin, the Montreal engineering firm. Prime Minister Mark Carney spent 13 years at Goldman Sachs; that is a career fact, not a finding.

The older background is lodges: four prime ministers were Orangemen, Toronto's mayors were for a century, and Scientology was convicted in 1992 of planting members in Ontario police and justice offices. Canada is a target country in the foreign-interference patterns and a proven case of organised crime inside the state.
Canada.imp: Foreign governments compete for influence in Canadian elections and diaspora communities, and the inquiries say some politicians took part knowingly, though no names have been published. Voters cannot see who funded a nomination race or who is passing information to a foreign mission. Criminal groups have bought a top police intelligence officer and border staff. Watch whether the Hogue inquiry's 51 recommendations are carried out, how the Majcher appeal ends, and how the Bishnoi case is tried in the United States.

Chile.d:
Chile's president today is José Antonio Kast, who took office on 11 March 2026. Two press reports, from BBC Mundo and El Mercurio, say he was raised in and belongs to the Schoenstatt Movement, a Catholic lay movement founded in Germany in 1914. His under-secretary of justice, Luis Silva, is reported to be an Opus Dei numerary, a celibate member of the Catholic organisation that encourages lay members to excel in public life. Membership of a lawful movement is not wrongdoing, and nothing on the map shows either group directing policy. Meanwhile prosecutors are charging Carabineros police officers with reselling seized drugs and protecting dealers, as Chile shifts from drug market to transit route.

Companies reach in as well. From 2015 prosecutors traced fake invoices that SQM, the lithium and fertiliser miner whose main shareholder is Pinochet's former son-in-law, paid to politicians across the spectrum. SQM settled US bribery charges in 2017 and in 2024 agreed a lithium partnership with the state copper company. Cristián Larroulet moved from Libertad y Desarrollo, an Atlas Network think tank, into President Piñera's cabinet in 2010.

The roots are in the dictatorship. Chile's intelligence service DINA called the founding meeting of Operation Condor, the joint campaign of South American military regimes against opponents, in Santiago in 1975. Its chief Manuel Contreras was convicted over the 1976 Washington killing of Orlando Letelier; Pinochet was indicted in 2004 but died unconvicted. The Rettig commission found DINA held prisoners at Colonia Dignidad, a German sect compound. Economists trained under a US-funded Chicago-Catholic University programme ran the finance, economy and planning ministries and the central bank, among them Miguel Kast, the president's brother.

Chile is the coordinating centre of the anticommunist web, a case of trained technocrats running an economy, and a country where religious movements hold top office now.
Chile.imp: The people at the top of the government today come partly from Catholic lay movements whose internal guidance the public does not see; the record shows membership, not direction. The bigger proven problems are money and police: a mining company paid politicians through fake invoices, and some Carabineros are charged with protecting drug sales. Watch the Carabineros cases, the SQM-Codelco lithium deal, and whether appointments under Kast draw from the same networks.

Guatemala.d:
Guatemala lost its main tool against criminal networks inside the state in 2019, and the trafficking cases since then are mostly brought in US courts. CICIG was an international commission set up with the UN in 2006 to help Guatemalan prosecutors take apart those networks. In 2015 it exposed 'La Línea', a customs-bribery ring reaching President Otto Pérez Molina and Vice-President Roxana Baldetti; he resigned and both were sentenced to 16 years in 2022. When CICIG began looking at President Jimmy Morales's campaign money, he ended the agreement; its mandate ran out in September 2019. By 2023 more than thirty judges and prosecutors who had worked such cases had left the country under threat of arrest.

The drug cases continue. In July 2026 the mayor of Santa Lucía, Escuintla, pleaded guilty in Washington to using his office to help a cocaine shipment pass as cement. A former congressman pleaded guilty in 2024. A sitting Central American Parliament deputy faces a US cocaine indictment, untried. The mayor of a border town was designated with his 'Los Pochos' organisation, which supplies the Sinaloa Cartel, and its companies were relisted in 2024. In April 2026 two Guatemala City import firms were sanctioned for moving fentanyl chemicals from India. Baldetti also faces a US cocaine charge that has never been tried.

International bodies were reached too: a Guatemalan judge pleaded guilty in the US FIFA bribery case.

The older background is the Cold War. Mario Sandoval Alarcón, a leader of the World Anti-Communist League, was vice-president from 1974 to 1978; historians link his party to the Mano Blanca death squad.

Guatemala is a proven case of organised crime inside the state.
Guatemala.imp: Mayors, legislators and police chiefs have worked for traffickers, and with the anti-corruption commission gone, many of these cases are now heard only abroad. Guatemalans lose the chance to see them tried at home, and prosecutors who pursued them have fled. Watch the Freddy Salazar Flores case, whether Los Pochos keeps a hold on local politics, and the precursor route through Guatemala City firms.

Honduras.d:
Honduras is the clearest case on this map of a head of state convicted of drug trafficking. Juan Orlando Hernández, president from 2014 to 2022, was convicted in New York and sentenced to 45 years in June 2024. On 1 December 2025 he received a full US presidential pardon and was released; Honduras then asked Interpol to act on a 2023 arrest order written for exactly that event. The conviction stands, but the sentence is not being served. His brother Tony Hernández, a congressman, is serving life after a 2019 conviction, with testimony that drug money funded the National Party. Former police chief Juan Carlos 'El Tigre' Bonilla pleaded guilty in 2024 to protecting cocaine loads.

The trafficking reached the family of an earlier president too. Fabio Lobo, son of President Porfirio Lobo, was sentenced to 24 years for arranging police escorts for shipments. Porfirio Lobo himself was named by witnesses in others' trials and put on a US list of corrupt actors, but has never been charged.

Banks were used. In 2015 the US designated the Rosenthal family, including a former vice-president and a congressman, as launderers for the Cachiros trafficking group, and their Banco Continental was liquidated within days; Yani Rosenthal pleaded guilty in 2017. Former president Rafael Callejas pleaded guilty in the US FIFA bribery case in 2016.

In the background, in 1984 a group headed by the armed forces commander took $50,000 from a front for the Unification Church, the Korean-founded religious movement, before officers ousted him.

Honduras is a proven case of organised crime inside the state and criminal money in banks.
Honduras.imp: Traffickers reached the presidency, Congress, the police command and a bank, and US courts proved much of it. The pardon of Hernández means the top convicted figure is free, which Hondurans are trying to answer with their own arrest order. Watch whether he is arrested, whether Honduran courts try any of these cases, and how campaign money is checked.

Jamaica.d:
Jamaica's documented cases are both from the past but still shape how people see the state. The most recent concerns Christopher 'Dudus' Coke, leader of the Shower Posse gang based in Tivoli Gardens, West Kingston. When the United States asked for his extradition, the government resisted for nine months and hired a Washington law firm to lobby against the request. The security operation that followed killed at least 69 people. Coke pleaded guilty in New York in 2011. The prime minister had already resigned over the affair, and a 2016 commission of enquiry found the operation unjustified in how it was carried out.

The older case is about a bank. BCCI, the Bank of Credit and Commerce International, collapsed in 1991 amid fraud and laundering. A 1992 US Senate report found that under Prime Minister Edward Seaga, BCCI handled most of the government's foreign-currency accounts, with loans of $33.9 million to the central bank and $45.4 million to the state oil company Petrojam. A BCCI officer said the bank 'handled every penny' of Jamaica's foreign currency.

Jamaica belongs to the patterns of organised crime inside the state and banks that carried hidden money.
Jamaica.imp: A gang leader was protected by his government until the cost became a deadly security operation, and a corrupt bank once held the state's foreign money. Both show how close outside interests have come to the centre of power. Watch how extradition requests are handled and who holds the government's banking business.

Mexico.d:
The largest case on Mexico's record is still open. In April 2026 US prosecutors in Manhattan charged the sitting governor of Sinaloa, Rubén Rocha Moya, and nine other current and former officials, among them the mayor of Culiacán and a senator, with protecting the Chapitos faction of the Sinaloa Cartel. They allege cartel members stole ballot boxes to help him win in 2021 and that he then let them take over the state's police. He resigned on 1 May 2026, calling the case a political attack. Mexico says the extradition request lacks evidence and has opened its own inquiry; none of the ten is in custody. Tabasco's former security chief, Hernán Bermúdez Requena, is in prison accused of running a CJNG-linked gang from his office.

The cartels also reach into ordinary businesses. In 2026 the US Treasury listed tequila distilleries and gas stations as CJNG fronts, a Puerto Vallarta resort whose customer lists fed timeshare scams costing about 6,000 Americans roughly $300 million, and a Guadalajara pharmacy pressing fentanyl pills. In 2025 naval officers and customs officials were arrested over fuel imported as 'lubricant additive'. Avocado and lime growers in Michoacán pay criminal groups a fee per hectare and per shipment.

Behind this sits a long run of proven cases. Genaro García Luna, who ran the federal police from 2006 to 2012, was convicted in New York of taking Sinaloa Cartel payments. Two former governors and Nayarit's chief prosecutor admitted guilt in US courts. In Iguala in 2014, town police acting for Guerreros Unidos took 43 students, who disappeared. Other cases collapsed: US charges against defence minister Salvador Cienfuegos were dropped in 2020. Witnesses in US trials testified that a serving president took bribes; no document backs this and no one was charged.

Companies and churches appear too. Ex-Pemex chief Emilio Lozoya is accused of taking about $10 million from Odebrecht, a Brazilian builder, and denies it; a Vitol oil trader was convicted in 2024 of bribing Pemex officials. A 2003 book claimed El Yunque, a secret Catholic group, had members in Vicente Fox's cabinet; the party called this fiction. Older roots: a J.P. Morgan partner advised President Calles as US ambassador from 1927, and a 1943 Rockefeller Foundation farm programme began the Green Revolution. Mexico is the map's central case of organised crime inside a state, and home to El Yunque, the Legion of Christ and La Luz del Mundo.
Mexico.imp: The officials meant to protect people in Mexico, from town police to a federal security minister, have in proven cases been paid by the groups they were supposed to stop. Most of what is known comes from US courts and US Treasury lists rather than Mexican verdicts, and the people who authorised these arrangements are tried less often than junior staff. Cartel money also runs through everyday businesses: petrol stations, resorts, distilleries, pharmacies and farm supply chains. Watch whether the Sinaloa indictment reaches a courtroom and whether Mexico's own inquiry produces charges.

Nicaragua.d:
Today the one active case on Nicaragua's record is a Russian one. In October 2017 Russia's Interior Ministry, which runs Russia's police, opened a training centre in the Las Colinas district of Managua as an affiliate of the ministry. Russia's ambassador and Laureano Ortega Murillo, the president's son, attended the opening. It trains Nicaraguan police and later officers from Central America and the Caribbean. On 15 May 2024 the US Treasury sanctioned the centre, saying it trains officials of the Ortega-Murillo government in the Russian government's 'playbook of oppression' and is a key actor in repressing civil society.

The older background involves foreign money in both directions. Roberto Calvi's Banco Ambrosiano opened a Nicaraguan unit in 1977–78 and funded both the Somoza dictatorship and the Sandinista opposition. In 1985 President Daniel Ortega cancelled its licence by decree. Later in the decade the US-funded National Endowment for Democracy (NED) spent about $2 million in Nicaragua between 1984 and 1988, half of it on La Prensa, the newspaper run by Violeta Chamorro, according to historian William LeoGrande. In 1989 the US Congress approved a further $9 million to boost the opposition, and Chamorro won the February 1990 election. Critics compared this to CIA operations in Chile; NED says its grants are public and nonpartisan.

Nicaragua's overall score is low because few cases are documented, but its conditions score is high: power is concentrated and checks on it are weak. It belongs to the map's patterns on Russia's networks abroad, governments buying officials in other countries, the anticommunist web and the money behind international NGOs.
Nicaragua.imp: For people in Nicaragua, the documented case is about their own police: a foreign government trains the force that the US says represses civil society, with the president's family present from the start. Earlier, both a foreign bank and a US-funded foundation put money into Nicaraguan politics, on different sides. Because few checks on the government remain, other arrangements may exist that no court or inquiry has recorded. Watch who trains and equips the police, and where political funding comes from.

Panama.d:
Panama's biggest trial is under way now. Odebrecht, a Brazilian construction group, admitted in 2016 paying $788 million in bribes across Latin America and Africa, and says $59 million went to Panamanian officials during Ricardo Martinelli's 2009–2014 presidency. The main money-laundering trial opened on 12 January 2026 with more than 20 defendants. Martinelli, who received asylum in Colombia in 2025, takes part by video and pleads innocent. Two of his sons and former president Juan Carlos Varela are to be tried separately by the Supreme Court.

Panama's role on the map is as a place where money is moved and hidden. The Colón Free Zone, the largest in the Americas, lets goods pass without entering Panamanian customs; laundering studies and several US sanctions run through it, and Panama has tightened ownership rules without the volume falling. In 2016 the US named a free-zone trading group and its bank, Balboa Bank & Trust, as a laundering network; Panama's regulator seized and closed the bank. Two law firms that create offshore companies are on the record: Mossack Fonseca, at the centre of the Panama Papers, whose founders and 26 others were acquitted of laundering in 2024 for lack of proper evidence, and Alcogal, which appeared throughout the Pandora Papers, says it followed the law and has not been charged.

The background is General Manuel Noriega. In 1982 he opened an account at the bank BCCI in the name of Panama's Defense Forces, holding about $25 million at its height, and had BCCI pay off the mortgage of Nicolás Ardito Barletta, his chosen candidate, who became president in 1984. After the US invasion, a Miami court convicted Noriega in 1992 of drug trafficking for the Medellín Cartel. Panama belongs to the patterns on global firms buying governments, criminal money in banks and firms, and banks that carried hidden money.
Panama.imp: For people in Panama, the country's banks, law firms and free zone are tools that others use to move and hide money, and the record shows cases ending in acquittals or no charges as often as convictions. A former head of state was a trafficker, and a former president now faces trial from abroad. Watch the Odebrecht verdicts, the separate Supreme Court cases, and whether ownership rules ever reduce what passes through the Colón Free Zone.

Paraguay.d:
In Paraguay a drug case reaching into the courts is still running. In February 2022 prosecutors opened A Ultranza Py, an investigation into a cocaine network moving drugs along the Hidrovía river route. It produced charges against police officers, a serving prosecutor, court officials and a sitting member of the Chamber of Deputies, and the seizure of hundreds of properties. Several principals fled before arrest, and one of the case's own prosecutors was later removed.

The second present-day thread involves Hezbollah, a Lebanese armed movement and party that the US lists as a terrorist group, with money networks in the Tri-Border Area where Paraguay meets Argentina and Brazil. On 26 January 2023 the US Treasury sanctioned former president Horacio Cartes and the sitting vice-president, Hugo Velázquez, for corruption, saying both had ties to Hezbollah members and that their representatives collected bribes at Hezbollah events in Paraguay. The US lifted the sanctions on Cartes and several of his companies in 2025. Nearby, in Ciudad del Este, a trading network whose principals the US designated had its assets frozen by Argentina in 2018.

The roots go back to the dictatorship of Alfredo Stroessner. In December 1992 a lawyer and a judge found his secret police's files, the 'Archives of Terror', in a police station outside Asunción. They proved Operation Condor, the joint work of South American military regimes against opponents, existed, and later helped a truth commission document 9,923 victims. A US Senate report records a $5 million central bank deposit at BCCI in 1989, with ties built through a Saudi businessman's friendship with Stroessner. In 2005 the Senate voted to expropriate land around Puerto Casado from the Unification Church. Paraguay belongs to the patterns on organised crime inside the state and Iran's armed allies.
Paraguay.imp: For people in Paraguay, the current cases show traffickers reaching police, prosecutors, judges and a lawmaker, and US claims of armed-group links reaching the presidency, with those sanctions later lifted for Cartes. Many principals escape before arrest. The dictatorship's files show how long such arrangements can stay hidden until someone finds the paperwork. Watch how A Ultranza Py ends, whether prosecutors who pursue it keep their jobs, and what the Tri-Border trade is used for.

Peru.d:
Peru's record is mostly about money from a foreign company, and the courts are still working through it. Odebrecht, a Brazilian construction group, admitted in 2016 paying $788 million in bribes in a dozen countries. In October 2024 a Lima court sentenced former president Alejandro Toledo to 20 years for taking about $35 million in return for the Interoceanic Highway contract. In April 2025 former president Ollanta Humala and his wife Nadine Heredia were each sentenced to 15 years for laundering Odebrecht money; Heredia left for Brazil under diplomatic asylum, and both deny the charges.

Other cases are open now. Prosecutors in Junín say a network in the regional transport office has sold driving licences since 2012, and argued in 2021 that the money funded Perú Libre, the party that won that year's presidential election; party leader Vladimir Cerrón has been a fugitive since 2023 in a separate case. In 2025 a TV programme reported that Prime Minister Eduardo Arana is a senior Freemason and that a lodge member was hired while he was justice minister; he said membership is no grounds to assume favours, and this remains a report. Rafael López Aliaga, a self-described member of Opus Dei, a Catholic organisation whose lay members are encouraged to excel in public life, was mayor of Lima and has sat in the Senate since July 2026. ENACO, the state coca buyer, pays less than traffickers, so most legal coca leaves its channel.

The background includes Vladimiro Montesinos, Fujimori's intelligence chief, who ran much of the military, courts and press and was convicted of drug trafficking and more, partly from his own bribe videos. In 2018 wiretaps exposed judges trading sentences in Callao; the first trial conviction came in November 2025. Earlier threads run through BCCI, which held Peru's central bank reserves, and Banco Ambrosiano. Peru belongs to the patterns on global firms buying governments and organised crime inside the state.
Peru.imp: For people in Peru, three recent presidents have been convicted or sentenced over money from one foreign company, and earlier cases show an intelligence chief and judges selling the state's power. Cases take years: the Callao judges waited seven years for a first verdict. Some of today's questions are only reported or alleged, including the Junín licence money and lodge ties at the top of government. Watch whether those reports lead to inquiries, and whether people convicted abroad or in absentia ever serve their sentences.

Trinidad and Tobago.d: No case of capture of Trinidad and Tobago's own government is documented on this map yet, so this write-up is an estimate. One related case is filed under FIFA, world football's governing body, because the money ran through it. Jack Warner, FIFA vice-president until 2011, sat in the cabinet from 2010 to 2013, latterly as national security minister. US prosecutors indicted him in 2015 for fraud, racketeering and laundering, including a $10 million payment tied to South Africa's World Cup bid; FIFA banned him for life. In September 2025 Trinidad's High Court blocked his extradition. Opus Dei is present; English Freemasonry is likely. Conditions scores are moderate. As a best guess, sport and international bodies are the likeliest route in.
Trinidad and Tobago.imp: For people in Trinidad and Tobago, a man US prosecutors charged with taking bribes as a football official sat in the cabinet, including in charge of national security. The charges have not been tested in court, and he will not be sent to the US. Watch how officials who also hold posts in international bodies are vetted.

United States.d:
Right now the United States is being reached into from many directions at once. Start with foreign governments. A hacking group called Salt Typhoon, widely attributed to China's Ministry of State Security (its spy service), sat inside at least nine US phone companies from about 2023, with access to call records and the systems used for court-ordered wiretaps. North Korea gets its programmers hired by US firms under stolen identities; one Arizona "laptop farm" placed them in more than 300 companies,. Huawei, China's largest telecom-equipment maker, is on trial in Brooklyn for racketeering and stealing trade secrets. In Arcadia, California, the mayor pleaded guilty in 2026 to acting as a Chinese agent. Senator Bob Menendez is in prison for acting for Egypt, and a Republican National Committee fundraiser, Elliott Broidy, pleaded guilty as an unregistered foreign agent and was pardoned.

Inside the government, private networks supply both people and drafts. People who wrote or advised on Project 2025, a governing plan organised by the conservative Heritage Foundation, now run the budget office, the FCC and the CIA. Under President Biden nearly 70 staff of the Center for American Progress, founded as its Democratic counterpart, took administration posts. Goldman Sachs leaders ran economic policy under Clinton (Robert Rubin) and Trump (Gary Cohn). In statehouses, the corporate-funded American Legislative Exchange Council writes model bills with legislators; a 2019 study found 10,000 near-copies introduced and more than 2,100 passed. Belonging to these groups is lawful.

Boeing staff still do much of the FAA's safety certification, and the criminal case for deceiving the FAA was dropped in 2025. FirstEnergy paid about $60 million to Ohio's House Speaker, now serving 20 years. Drug cartels reach in through border officers (over 200 corruption convictions in a decade) and banks: TD Bank became the first US bank to plead guilty to money-laundering conspiracy in 2024, yet in 2025 no US bank faced a major penalty. A televangelist named among New Apostolic Reformation figures, Paula White, heads the new White House Faith Office.

The roots go deep: a secret order took the whole Massachusetts legislature in 1854, the Ku Klux Klan elected governors in the 1920s, and the CIA hid money in foundation grants. Two famous claims are not supported: that the Rothschilds own the Federal Reserve, an antisemitic myth, and that the Rockefellers run a secret world government.

On this map the US is a proven case of police captured by drug gangs, industries inside regulators and criminal money in banks; a target of China's long arm and of governments buying officials; and the funding centre of the Cold War's intelligence-backed groups.
United States.imp: Many rules that touch daily life, from whether a plane is certified safe to what a state law says, are drafted or checked by people outside elected government, and the public usually learns this years later from a court or a Senate report. A foreign spy service sat inside the phone network. Things to watch: who writes the bills in your statehouse, whether foreign-agent cases end in a verdict or a pardon, and whether penalties for banks that carry drug money come back.

Uruguay.d:
Nothing on the map shows an outside force sitting inside Uruguay's government today. What Uruguay's record holds is the long tail of its military dictatorship, and one modern fight with a tobacco company.

The heaviest cases come from Operation Condor, the cross-border pact through which South America's military governments of the 1970s hunted each other's opponents. Gregorio Álvarez, the army commander who became Uruguay's last de facto president, was sentenced in October 2009 to 25 years for 37 homicides, including forced disappearances; several victims had been moved to Argentina in 1978 under the Condor plan, and the Supreme Court upheld the sentence in September 2011. In July 2019 a Rome appeals court gave life sentences to 24 people in its Condor case, among them Juan Carlos Blanco, Uruguay's former foreign minister. Most were sentenced in absentia, and the verdict can still be appealed to Italy's highest court.

Under the same military rule, in 1981, the Unification Church, the movement founded by Sun Myung Moon, bought 49% of Banco de Crédito, one of the country's oldest banks. It also started a daily paper that declared itself 'fully identified' with the military 'process', and bought Montevideo's Hotel Victoria Plaza. The bank closed in 2002, and a parliamentary commission found it had lent about US$100 million of its roughly US$600 million in loans to Moon-linked companies. That same year Uruguayan police seized files at the Montevideo villa of Licio Gelli, head of the Italian lodge P2, who had fled there from an Italian arrest warrant; what became of the files rests on press reports.

The modern case: in 2010 Philip Morris International sued Uruguay over graphic health warnings covering 80% of cigarette packs. In July 2016 the World Bank's investment tribunal ruled for Uruguay and made the company pay its costs.

Uruguay sits in the map's anticommunist-web and industry-and-regulator patterns, mostly as a place where these networks were later exposed and tried.
Uruguay.imp: For people in Uruguay, the record shows courts and parliament doing the exposing: a former de facto president and a foreign minister convicted over disappearances, a parliamentary commission tracing where a failed bank's money went, and a government that defended its health warnings against a tobacco company and won. What to watch now is quieter: companies using investment treaties to challenge new health or environmental rules, and who owns the country's banks and newspapers.

Venezuela.d:
Venezuela's government is in upheaval. On 3 January 2026 US forces seized President Nicolás Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores in Caracas and flew them to New York to face a narco-terrorism indictment. Vice-President Delcy Rodríguez became interim president,; Congress did not authorise the operation. In October 2025 Trump had confirmed that he had authorised the CIA to carry out covert action inside Venezuela, while the US military struck boats it said carried drugs. The UN human-rights chief called for an investigation of the strikes.

The US case is that drug trafficking runs through the Venezuelan state itself. Prosecutors charged Maduro and more than a dozen officials in 2020 as leaders of the 'Cartel de los Soles', a network they say runs through the officer corps. Most of this is accusation: no trial has been held, and analysts dispute that it is an organised cartel at all, while agreeing officials are involved in the trade. Some parts have been tested in court. Two nephews of the first lady were convicted in 2016 of offering 800 kilograms of cocaine, then released in a 2022 prisoner swap. Former military intelligence chief Hugo Carvajal pleaded guilty in 2025, and retired general Cliver Alcalá was sentenced in 2024. Others named, including Diosdado Cabello (interior minister from 2024), former anti-drug chief Néstor Reverol and former vice-president Tareck El Aissami, face US designations or indictments that have never been tried. The US also says the Tren de Aragua gang, born in a Venezuelan prison, acts on the government's orders; its own intelligence council doubted that in April 2025.

A foreign government is documented inside the army. Under 2008 agreements Cuba oversaw the restructuring of Venezuela's military intelligence, which turned to watching Venezuela's own soldiers and grew to at least 1,500 agents. Reuters reported Cuban advisers withdrawing after Maduro's capture.

Money is the third thread. A former head of Odebrecht, the Brazilian construction firm, in Venezuela told prosecutors it gave $35 million to Maduro's 2013 campaign; the government denies it and no Venezuelan court has examined it. Under an energy deal announced after the capture, the US is to sell Venezuelan oil into US-controlled accounts.

The older background includes the 2002 coup: the director of Cedice, a Caracas think tank in the Atlas Network that received US NED money, signed the decree dissolving the National Assembly and Supreme Court.

Venezuela is at the centre of the map's organised-crime-in-the-state pattern.
Venezuela.imp: For Venezuelans, the people accused of running the drug trade have held the posts meant to police it: the anti-drug office, the interior ministry, military intelligence. Few of those accusations have been tested by any court, and the evidence is not public. Now a foreign government has removed the head of state by force and controls how the country's oil is sold. Watch who holds the interior ministry, military intelligence and the oil accounts during the transition, and whether any of the charges reach a trial.

Kosovo.d:
Kosovo's former prime minister and president, Hashim Thaçi, is on trial for war crimes at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, a court set up after an EU task force reported compelling indications of such crimes. The road there began with a Council of Europe report. In December 2010 Swiss senator Dick Marty told the Council's assembly that a 'Drenica Group' of former Kosovo Liberation Army commanders, which he said Thaçi led, controlled criminal trades including heroin, and found 'credible, convergent indications' of organ trafficking after the 1999 war. The assembly endorsed the report in 2011; Thaçi denied it. The organised-crime claims have not been tested in court, so they remain suspected.

The second case shows a foreign government reaching into Kosovo's security services. Turkey calls the movement of preacher Fethullah Gülen a terrorist group. In March 2018 Kosovo police and intelligence seized five teachers and a doctor accused by Ankara of Gülen links and flew them to Turkey. Prime Minister Ramush Haradinaj said he had not been told and sacked the interior minister and the intelligence chief. In 2023 a Pristina court sentenced former intelligence chief Driton Gashi to four years and eight months for abuse of office. Kosovo's conditions scores borrow North Macedonia's figures.
Kosovo.imp: For people in Kosovo, the record shows two risks: wartime commanders carrying networks into government, and a foreign government able to get local officers to hand over residents without the prime minister knowing. The courts have acted on both, with a war-crimes trial and a conviction for abuse of office. Watch the outcome of the Thaçi trial and whether security services stay answerable to elected leaders.
